offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That a Commission of Bankrupt was, on the 6tn Day of February 1790, awarded against Joseph Freeman and Thomas Grace, of Devonshire Square, Bishopgate Street, London, Warehousemen, Dealers, Chapmen, and Co-partners, under which they were found and declared Bankrupts, and the Petitioners were chosen Assignees of their Estate and Effects; and that, at the Time of the issuing of the said Commission of Bankrupt, there was due from Matthias de Gan-dasequi to the said Joseph Freeman, for Principal and Interest, on a Mortgage bearing Date the 15th Day of January 1789, of certain Premisses in or near Saint James's Square, in the County of Middlesex, the Sum of £. 13,700, and upwards; and that such Premisses were subject to a prior Mortgage, bearing Date the 26th Day of October 1785, for securing the Sum of £. 3,500, and Interest, to John Wilmot, Esquire, who, in order to recover the Money due to him upon such ‘prior Mortgage, filed a Bill of Foreclosure against the said Joseph Freeman and Matthias de Gandasequi in the Court of Chancery, to which Suit the Petitioners, as Assignees as aforesaid, were made Parties; and that an Account of the Principal, Interest, and Costs, due to the said John Wilmot, w-as directed to be taken in the said Suit, by one of the Masters of the Court of Chancery, and in pursuance thereof the said Master, on the 7th Day of May 1792, certified that there would be due to the said John Wilmot, for Principal, Interest, and for Costs, on the 2 2d Day of the said Month of May, the Sum of £.4,676. 165. yd.; and that the Petitioners, on the 14th Day of June 1792, with the Money in their Hands, as such Assignees, and other Money advanced by other Persons, Creditors of the said Bankrupts, paid the said Sum of £. 4,676. so due

to the said John Wilmot, and thereupon the said John Wilmot conveyed all his Interest in the said mortgaged Premisses to John Wilkinson, Esquire, a Trustee named by and on the Part of the Petitioners, and the said other Persons who advanced Money for the Purpose of making up the said last mentioned Sum, and the legal Estate of and in the same Premisses now remains vested in the said John Wilkinson as such Trustee: That the Petitioners were induced to pay off the said Sum of £. 4,676. 16 s.yd. so due to the said John Wilmot, from a Belief that they, as Assignees as aforesaid, w'ere Second Mortgagees of the said Mortgaged Premisses, and that the said Mortgaged Premisses might be sold, and that the Surplus which should remain of the Money arising from the Sale thereof, after deducting the said Sum of £.4,676. 16$. yd. would be thereby secured for the Benefit of the Creditors of the said Joseph Freeman and Thomas Grace, and accordingly the Petitioners caused the said Premisses to be put up to Sale, and the Sum of £9,817. 10 s. being bid for the same, and no higher Sum being offered, the Party bidding that Sum was declared the Purchaser; and that the said Matthias de Gandasequi is an Alien born, and as, by the Law of this Realm, an Alien cannot purchase Lands for his own Benefit, but takes them for the Benefit of the Crown, the Purchaser of the said Premisses has refused to complete his Purchase thereof: That there is now due, from the said Matthias de Gandasequi to the Petitioners, as Assignees as aforesaid, upon the said Mortgage so made to the said Joseph Freeman, the Sum of £. 15,000, and upwards, besiaes 1 the

Petition from the Assignee! of Messrs. Freeman and Grace.

Burford in- A Petition of John Esquire, Lord of the

Pe* Manors of Burford and Bury Barns, in the County of Oxford, and principal Proprietor of Lands within the same Manors, and within the Hamlets of Signet and Upton, in the said Parish of Burford, the Reverend Robert Clarke Caswall, Clerk, Lessee of the Great Tythes, and Proprietor of Lands, within the same Manors, Parish, and Hamlets, the Honourable and Reverend Francis Knollis, Clerk, Vicar of the said Parish of Burford, and the several other Owners arid Proprietors of Lands or Grounds in the Manors of Burford and Bury Barns aforesaid, and in the Parish of Burford and Hamlets of Signet and Upton aforesaid, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Manors, Parish of Burford, and Hamlet of Signet, several Open Common Fields, Common Pastures, and Commonable Lands, called Signet and Burford Fields, which lie intermixed and dispersed in small Parcels, and, in their present Condition, are incapable of any considerable Improvement, but, if the same were divided and inclosed, it would be of Advantage to all Parties interested therein; and that the Lands within the Hamlet of Upton aforesaid, being now subject to Tythes, it would be also of Advantage to all Parties interested in the said last mentioned Lands, if the same were exonerated from Tythes, and Lands allotted, within the said Fields of Signet and Burford, in Lieu thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Open and Common Fields, Common Pastures, and Commonable Lands, called Signet and Burford Fields, and that specific Parts and Shares thereof may be assigned and allotted unto and amongst the Petitioners and others interested therein, according to their respective Shares and Interest in the same, and also for exonerating the Lands within the Hamlet of Upton aforesaid from tythes, and for allotting Lands within the said Fields of Signet and Burford in Lieu thereof, by such Ways and Means as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Brassey Halhed and Mr. FrancisAnnesley do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had received, from the most Noble Charles Marquis Cornwallis, Knight of the most Noble Order of the Garter, the following Letter, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 19th Day of December, in the last Session of Parliament:

Sir,

I had the Honour to receive your Letter, dated the 9th of January 1793, a few Days before I embarked <for Europe; and I lost no Time in publishing to the whole Army, at the Three Presidencies, the Testimony of High Approbation which the House of Commons have expressed, in the Resolutions that you inclosed to me, of the Conduct and Exertions of the European and Native Officers, Non-commissioned Officers, and Soldiers, who served under my Command in the Field during the late War in India.

Being sensible that the favourable Opinion of the Representatives of the Commons of Great Britain, reflects the most distinguished Honour upon any British Subject, I request that you will assure the House, that the flattering Manner in which they have been pl< jased to declare their Approbation of my own Conduct during that War, has impressed me with tl*.e strongest Sensations of Satisfaction and Gratitude .* and K beg that you will accept of ray best Ackuov /ledgments for the very obliging Personal Expression'^ regarding my-

self, which yon did me the Honour to make use of in communicating these Resolutions.

I have the Honour to be,

With Respect,

Sir, Your most obedient

most humble Servant,

Cornwallis.

London, the 9th February 1794.

Right honourable Henry Addington

within the Parish of Manchester, in the County Pala-tine of Lancaster', and that the said Grammar School is a very ancient Foundation, being founded by Hugh Oldham, then Bishop of Exeter, in the early Part of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, for the Instruction of Youth in Grammar, and' the Advancement of Knowledge and Learning, by further assisting them in their Education at Oxford and Cambridge, and the said School is free for the Whole British Empire; and that the Estate of the said Free School (vested, in the Petitioners) consists, in a great Measure, of Mills situate upon the River Irk, in Manchester aforesaid; and that, in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, an Act of Parliament was passed, by which the Inhabitants of the Town of Manchester were discharged from the Custom of grinding their Corn and Grain, except Malt, at the said Mills, but that the Custom of grinding Malt at the said Mills was established and confirmed by the said Act, and the Petitioners are obliged, by the said Act, to repair and maintain the said Mills, so as to be sufficient to grind for the Inhabitants, and that, without a sufficient Supply of Water, the said Mills will be unable to grind for the Town, and a Failure in this Respect will be productive of irreparable Damage to the Trust Estate vested in the Petitioners; and that the Stream of the said River Irk, on which the said Mills are situate, is already so scantily supplied with Water, that at some Times, and especially in a dry Season, the said Mills are unable to work for several Hours in the Day, through Want of Water; and that the Petitioners are well assured, that the said intended Canal, upon the Line proposed, cannot be effectually supplied with Water, without taking those Resources which feed the Stream of the said River Irk, and that the making such Canal will unavoidably cut off many Springs and Streams, and take away from the Petitioners that from which a great Part of the Income of the said Trust Estate arises: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same Bill may not pass into a. Law, and that the Petitioners may have such further or other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Mills upon the Rivers Roach, Irwell, and Irk, and their Feeders,* was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill mentioned in the last preceding Petition; and Setting forth, That there are upon the said Rivers Roach, Irwell, and Irk, and their Feeders, a considerable Number of Water Mills, many of which are of great Value, and the Petitioners conceive the said Navigation will be the Means of depriving them of the Supply of Water, which, ever since the said Mills have been erected, they have derived from the said Rivers, and their Feeders: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall appear just and proper.

A Petition of the several Owners and Occupiers of Mills, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Also taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are the Owners or Occupiers of several valuable Water Mills, which are so situate, that the Petitioners have great Reason to apprehend that it is not practicable to make and maintain the said intended Canal, according to the Line and Level proposed, without taking or intercepting most of the Sources and Feeders of the Rivers which supply the said Mills with Water, and thereby deprive the said Mills of their necessary and usual Supply, not only to the essential Injury of the Petitioners, but to the great Detriment of the Trade of the Country, and of the Public: And

therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same Bill may not pass into a Law.

Downham, Coveney, Witchford, Witcham, Wingford or Wentworth, Witburton, Haddenham, Mepal, Sutton, March, Doddington with Wimblington, Benwick, Chat-

teris, Whittlesea Saint Mary, Wittlesea Saint Andrew, and Wisbech, within the Isle of Ely, and in certain Extra-parochial Places adjoining, or lying near to, the aforesaid Parishes or Townships, or some or one of them, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the River Ouze^ in the County of Norfolk, is the Great Outfall for the Waters from the Middle and South Levels of the Fens, the Country of Marshland, and divers other Lands which drain to Sea thereby, through the Harbour of King's Lynn, in the said County of Norfolk, and that IJart of the said River Ouze, between Saint German's Bridge and King's Lynn aforesaid, is in a State very insufficient for the Purposes of a complete Drainage and safe Navigation, occasioned principally by the Channel or Bed of the said River being too wide, and bending very considerably between the said Place called Saint German's Bridge and King's Lynn aforesaid, by Reason whereof the Drainage of large Tracts of Land, lying in the said Parishes or Townships, is greatly impeded, and the Trade and Navigation to and from the Port of King's Lynn are materially injured: and that in order effectually to improve and assist the Drainage of the said Lands, and to amend the Navigation to and from the said Port, it is necessary that a Cut, or River, of sufficient Dimensions to afford a free Passage for the Waters draining from the said Lands, and to answer the Purposes of Navigation, should be made to branch out of the said River Ouze, from the Common Salt Marsh, at or near a Place called Eau Brink, in the Parish of Wiggenhall St. Mary, in the said County of Norfolk, and again to join the said River Ouze, at or near the Harbour of King's Lynn aforesaid; and that, by Levels and Surveys, lately taken and made by experienced Engiheers, it appears that a Cut, or River, as above described, may be made, and the Petitioners conceive? the making thereof, with such other Works as may be found requisite to attain the Ends above-mentioned, would be highly beneficial to the Owners and Occupiers of Lands within the Districts above specified, and would tend greatly to promote the Trade and Commerce of the Town and Port of King's Lynn, and of the adjacent Country, and that the Expence of executing such Cut, or River, and other Works, may, with great Ease and Convenience, be provided for by Means of a Tax on the Lands to be benefited by the said Cut and Works, aided by a certain Tonnage Duty on Goods, Wrares, and Merchandize, navigated on the said Cut, or River: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given. to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred-to Sir John Wodehouse, Mr. Jodrell, 8cc.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, Mr. Benjamin Morland being examined, said, That the Footways in the several Streets, Lanes, Passages, and Places, within the said Town are very ill paved, and the said Streets and Places are not sufficiently cleansed and lighted, and are subject to various Encroachments, Obstructions, and Annoyances, and are also in some Parts very incommodious and unsafe for Travellers — That it would tend gready to the Benefit, Convenience, and Safety of the Inhabitants of the said Town, and to all Persons resorting thereto, if the said Footways were properly paved, and the said Streets and Places were well and sufficiendy cleansed, lighted, and tegulated, and all Encroachments, Obstructions, and Annoyances removed and prevented.

In Support of the Allegations of the Second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Morland being further examined, said, That it would tend gready to the Safety and Accommodadon of the Inhabitants, and of all Persons resorting to the said Town, if Powers were given for establishing a Nightly Watch therein.

A Petition of the Woolcombers and others, in the Borough of Wilton: And also,

A Petition of the Woolcombers of the Town and Borough of Ashburton, in the County of Devon: And'

also,

A Petition of the Woolcombers of the Town and Borough of Tavistock;

Were severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That, by the Invention of a Machine for combing of Wool, which diminishes Labour to an alarming Degree, the Petitioners entertain just Fears, that they and their Families will speedily become a heavy Burthen to the State, it appearing to the Petitioners, that One Machine only, with the Assistance of One Person and Four or Five Children, will perform as much Labour as Thirty Men in the customary Manual Manner: And hoping, That the House will apply such Remedy as to them shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or Canal from Leeds Bridge, in the County of York, to the North Lady's Walk, in Liverpool, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and from thence to the River Mersey, was read; whereby the said Company were empowered to borrow the Sum of £. 200,000; but, in case the said Sum should be found insufficient, they were enabled to raise a further Sum, not exceeding £.60,000, to be applied for the Purposes of the Act. — Then,

Mr. John Hardy being examined, said, That in making and completing certain Parts of the said Canal, and in purchasing and improving the Navigation of the River Douglas, alias Aslana, in the said County of Lancaster, which, by virtue of an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of His present Majesty, is now consolidated and incorporated with the said Canal, the said Company have expended a Sum of £. 300,000, and upwards — Then,

An Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, was read, empowering the said Company to make a certain Variation, and in order to complete and finish the said Canal, to borrow, in Manner therein mentioned, the Sum of £. 200,000. — And the Witness further said, That since the passing of the 6 said

Petitions re- A Petition of the Mayor and Aldermen of the Bo-specting the rough of Newark upon Trent, in the County of for Hun'0" tingham, and of the Merchants, Tradesmen, and other

Docks' Bill. Inhabitants of the said Borough: And also,

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and principal Inhabitants of the Town of Wakefield, in the County of York, and of the Vicinity thereof;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by virtue of an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, a Legal Quay has been made at the Port of Kingston upon Hull, with a Dock large enough to receive the Shipping trading to the Port at that Time, but, in Consequence of the great Increase of Trade and Shipping which has since taken Place, the said Dock has become greatly insufficient for the Accommodation thereof, and the Trade of the Country is much injured by the Want of Dock Room at the said Port; and that not only an Extension of the Wet Dock at Hull, but also an Entrance thereinto direct from the River Humber, is absolutely necessary, the present Passage to the Dock and Quay, through the long narrow River or Haven of Hull, being very frequently blocked up by the Ships to and from Foreign Voyages, Coastwise, River Craft, and Rafts of Timber, so that the manufactured Goods, sent down for Exportation by the Petitioners, frequently meet with the most disadvantageous Delay thereby: And that the Petitioners, having been informed that a Bill is intended to be brought into the House for Relief in the Premises, therefore pray the House will take into Consideration the present Restriction, Loss, and Delay, hereby occasioned to the Trade and Manufacture of the Country connected with the Port of Hull, and to grant such Relief as to them shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, George Maxwell, Esquire, being examined, said, That the River Ouze, in the County of Norfolk, is the great Outfall for the Waters from the Middle and South Levels of the Fens, the Country of Marshland, and divers other Lands which drain to Sea thereby through the Harbour of King's Lynn, in the said County of Norfolk: — And being further examined, he said, That Part of the said River Ouze, between Saint German's Bridge and King's Lynn aforesaid, is in a State very insufficient for the Purposes of a complete Drainage and safe Navigation, occasioned principally by the Channel or Bed of the said River being too wide, and bending very considerably between the said Place, called Saint Germans Bridge, and King's Lynn aforesaid, by reason whereof the Drainage of large Tracts of Land lying in the said Parishes or Townships is greatly impeded, and the Trade and Navigation to and from the Port of King's Lynn are materially injured. — And being further examined, he said, That in order effectually to improve and assist the Drainage of the said Lands, and to amend the Navigation to and from the said Port, it is necessary, that a Cut, or River, of sufficient Dimensions to afford a free Passage for the Waters draining from the said Lands, and to answer the Purposes of Navigation, should be made to branch out of the said River Ouze, from the Common Salt Marsh at or near a Place called Eau Brink, in the Parish of Wiggenhall Saint Mary, in the said County of Norfolk, and again to join the said River Ouze at or near the Harbour of King's Lynn aforesaid. Then,

Mr. Robert Milne, an Engineer, being examined, said, That he is clearly of Opinion, from the Levels and Surveys lately taken and made, that a Cut or River, as above described, may be made; and that the making thereof, with such other Works as may be found requisite to attain the Ends above-mentioned, would be highly beneficial to the Owners and Occupiers of Lands within the Districts above specified, and would tend gready to promote the Trade and Commerce of the Town and Port of King's Lynn, and of the adjacent Country. — And being further examined, he said, That the Expence of executing such Cut or River, and other Works, may with great Ease and Convenience be provided for by Means of a Tax on the Lands to be benefited by the same, aided by a certain Tonnage Duty on Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes navigated on the said Cut, or River.

And the House being informed that several other Amendments are necessary to be made to the said Bill;

Resolved, That the said Bill be re-committed. Resolved, That the said Bill be re-committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, immediately, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill, considered. The House accordingly resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

' Mr, Serjeant Watson took tire Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Serjeant Watson reported from the Committee, That they had made several other Amendments to the Bill; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received, reported. Mr. Serjeant Watson accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning, if the said Bill shall be then ingrossed.

Turkey Com- A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer-gany s Peti~ chants of England trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protect His Majesty's Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary, that an Ambassador should be sent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in the other Parts of Turkey, where British Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which together with other Expences incident to carrying on this Trade, have of late Years amounted to about £. 8,000 per Annum; and that the Petitioners acknowledge with Gratitude the several Grants they formerly received from Parliament, and, although they did not apply for farther Assistance so long as they found themselves in a Situation to support their Expences, they are sensible that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter* nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not declare their present Inability to support their necessary and unavoidable Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into consideration, and grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table*

A PETITION of several Inhabitants, Housekeepers of the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, paying Scotland Lot within the said Town and Port, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Electors of Members to represent the said Town and Port' in Parliament, on Behalf of themselves and other Electors for the said Town and Port, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth That, upon the 19th Day of March 1792, the Select Vol. 49.

Committee, who were appointed to try and determine the Merits of a Petition of Sir Godfrey Webster, Baronet, and John Tarleton, Esquire, against the Return of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford, reported to the House, that they had determined, " That the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants, Housekeepers of the said Town and " Port, paying Scotland Lot, and in such Inhabitants " Housekeepers only;" and that certain Persons pretending to be Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port, having, on the 27th Day of January last, presented a Petition to this House, praying that they may be admitted as Parties, according to the Form of the Statute in that Case lately made and provided, to oppose the said Right of Election, in Favour of which the said Select Committee have reported as aforesaid, and the Petitioners, insisting that the said Right of Election, in Favour of which the said Select Committee have determined as aforesaid, is the true Right of Election for the said Town and Port of Seaford, therefore praying the House, That they may be admitted as Parties to defend such Right of Election so reported to the House as aforesaid, and that they may have such further and other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and others, being legal Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, shall be takeri into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary, by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Memorandum:

That Notice of the said Petition, and of the Time appointed for taking the same into Consideration, w as inserted, by the Order of Mr. Speaker, in The London Gazette, and also sent to the Returning Officer of the Town and Port of Seaford, according to the Directions of an Act, passed in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the further Regulation of the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament.

The House w-as moved, That the Order, made upon the 27th Day of January last, for taking into Consideration, upon Monday the 10th Day of March next, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and others, being legal Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, respecting the Right of Election for the said Town and Port, might be read.

A Petition of the Ship Owners and Ship Masters, for Hull °" &c. of Newcastle and Shields, in the County of North- Docks Bill. umber land]

Were severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That, by virtue of an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, a Legal Quay has been made at the Port of Kingston upon Hull, with a Dock large enough to receive the Shipping trading to the Port at that Time, but, in consequence of the great Increase of Trade and Shipping which has since taken Place, the said Dock has become greatly insufficient for the Accommodation thereof, and the Trade of the Country is much injured by the Want of Dock Room at the said Port; and that not only an Extension of the Wet Dock at Hull, but also an Entrance into the same direct from the River Humber, is absolutely necessary, the present Passage to the Dock and Quay, through the long narrow River or Haven of Hull, being very frequently blocked up by the Ships to and from Foreign Voyages, Coastwise, River Craft, and Rafts of Timber, so that the manufactured Goods, sent down for Exportation, frequently meet with the most disadvantageous Delay thereby: And that the Petitioners, having been informed that a Bill is intended to be brought into the House for Relief in the Premises, therefore pray the House will take into Consideration the present Restriction, Loss, and Delay hereby occasioned to the Trade and Manufacture of the Country connected with the Port of Hull, and to grant such Relief as to them shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered' to lie upon the Table.

Sir John Ingilby reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and others, Trustees for putting in Execution Three several Acts of Parliament, one passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for repairing the Roads from the Town of Leeds, through Harwood, to the South West Comer of the Inclosures " of Harrogate, and from thence in Two Branches u (one through Ripley, over Burage Green, and the " other through Knaresborough and Boroughbridge)

" to Ripon, and from thence to the First Rill of " Water, or Watercourse, on Hutton Moor, in the " County of York, and for repairing the Sloughs or " Ruts, on the said Moor," another passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of his said Majesty's Reign, to explain- and amend the said first-mentioned Act, and the other, passed in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for enlarging the Term and Powers of the above recited Acts, with respect to those Parts of the said Roads from Harrogate through Ripley and Ripon, to the North East Comer of Hutton Moor, and from the East Ehd of Kirby Hill Moor to the Town of Ripon aforesaid, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. Charles Harrison being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Acts, and have borrowed considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, which, together with the Tolls, have been applied according to the Directions of the said Acts; but the said Roads cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair, nor the Money due be repaid, unless the

Terms of the said Acts are continued, and some of the Powers altered and enlarged.

Mr. Rose presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to His Majesty,

A Copy of the Preliminary Articles for taking into

British Pay a Body of His Majesty's Electoral Troops: And also,

A Paper, intituled, " Return of His Majesty's Hatioverian Forces taken into the Employ of Great,

" from 2 2d February 1793 And also,

A Copy of the Article of Agreement relative to an additional Body of His Majesty's Electoral Troops to be taken forthwith into the Pay of Great Britain.

And the Titles of the said Papers were redd.

The said Papers are as followeth; viz.

PRELIMINARY ARTICLES relative to a Body of His Majesty £ Hanoverian Forces, consisting of Eight Regiments of Cavalry, of Fifteen Battalions of Infantry, and of a Detachment of Artillery (specific States of which are hereunto annexed) which are to be taken into the *Pay of Great Britain, and employed upon the Continent, on such Service as the Exigency of Affairs may require.

1st. These Troops are to Serve and to be employed in Europe only.

lid. The Extent of their Pay, and of all other Allowances, Privileges, and Advantages, being dependent upon the particular Country in which they may be employed, is to be governed by established Precedent, and the fixed Tariff, or Ordonance, declared and confirmed by His Majesty for the Use of His Electoral Troops, on Emergencies similar to die present, and on all Occasions where they are called upon to serve out of their own Country.

IHd. Their said Pay is to commence from the 22d Day of February 1793, being the Day on which the Orders for their March were given; and is to be continued to them for the Space of Three Months after their Return to their own Country.

During the Time they shall be employed on this Service, they are to perform all Duties in common with the other Troops, with which they may occasionally serve, in Proportion to their Numbers; and their Officers are to take Rank on all Duties and Commands According to Seniority of Commission, in Conformity to the general Rules established in all Armies.

IVth. They are to have their own Chaplains, and to be allowed the free Exercise of their Religion, according to the Rites and established Modes of Worship of the German Church.

Vth. In all Cases of Military Delinquency, the Offenders are to be tried, judged, and punished by their own Martial Law and Articles of War: And the Officers commanding the different Regiments, as well as the Commanding Officer of the whole Corps, shall be enjoined to adhere strictly to the said Martial Law and Articles of War; and to take Care that the same be, on all Occasions, duly observed by the Officers and Soldiers under their Command.

Vlth. It being very remote from His Majesty's Intention to suffer His Electoral Military Chest to reap any pecuniary Profit or Advantage from the Circumstance of this Corps of His Hanoverian Troops passing upon the present Emergency into the British Service; it is on the other Hand but reasonable and just, and must accordingly be understood, that Great Britain is to defray all such Expences as may be found necessary for enabling the said Corps to take the Field, as well as for its Maintenance and Support during the Time it remains in the British Service upon an equal Footing with the Troops of any other Nation with which it may be destined to serve; and in particular, that not only a reasonable and fair Allowance shall be made for supplying die Deficiencies whlfch must necessarily be occasioned in His Majesty's Electoral Army by the Employment of this Corps out of His own German Dominions, but that due Provision shall also be made for recruiting and keeping it complete so long as it remains on that Service, and for malring good such Losses as it may sustain in Action, according to the present Practice in other Armies.

Vllth. It is stipulated further, that such Non-commissioned Officers and Private Men as may become disabled by Wounds, or other Casualties happening to them, while actually in the British Sendee, shall be allowed the usual Pensions at the Expence of Great Britain; which said Pensions are moreover to be paid to them in their own Country, upon authentic and satisfactory Certificates of their Existence and Identity being, from Time to Time, produced by His Majesty's Hanoverian Chancery of War.

prosvenor Square, 4th March 1793. Alvensleben.

ARTICLE of AGREEMENT, relative to an additional Body of His Majesty's Electoral Troops, to be taken forthwith into the Pay of Great Britain.

It having been found expedient for the Public Service to augment the Corps of Hanoverian Troops now serving in the Pay of Great Britain in Flanders; and His Majesty having accordingly been pleased to order this Augmentation, a State of which is hereunto annexed, to be completely equipped, and in Readiness to take the Field, at the Opening of the next Campaign; it has in consequence thereof been agreed upon, and is hereby made known and declared,

That this additional Corps of Hanoverian Troops shall be put, in all Respects, upon the same Footing with that which is at present employed in the British Service; and shall enjoy the like Advantages, Privileges, and Emoluments of every Kind, as were granted to the said Corps, and are particularly detailed and specified in the Preliminary Articles relative thereto, agreed upon and signed the 4th Day of March 1793; which Articles are deemed to be hereby confirmed and extended to this additional Corps, in full Force, and to the same Effect, as if herein inserted Word for Word.

And as this additional Corps is engaged to march from Hanover as early as possible in the Month of February next, so as to join the Army in Flanders in the Month of March following, it is therefore agreed, that its Pay is to commence from the Twenty-second Day of January 1794.

Grosvenor Square, the 7th of January 1794.

(Signed) Alvensleben.

Hope that in Time, by propel* Application, the Importation of Foreign Yarn may be much lessened, and the Manilfactuters supplied with Yarn of a superior Quality, and at a lower Rate, the Produce of our own Nation, which at the same Time will find Employ- ment for a great Number of Women and Children, many of whom, for Want of Work, are a Burthen to the Community; but the said and Tho-

mas Port house have been hitherto greatly deprived of the Benefit they expected to have received from the Sale of their said Inventions by the Artifices of Workmen, and certain Persons, who had received Instructions and Models from them, and, after having obtained those Ends, endeavoured to evade the Patents,

by making Alterations in the Arrangements of the Machinery; and that the said Undertaking, on Account of its Originality, hath been attended with very great and unforeseen Expences, as well as many Years Labour and Study, before it arrived at its present State, and as the Time of the Patents is so far expired, and no Advantage hath arisen, nor is likely to arise, unless the Grant be prolonged, and the Property of the said Invention secured to them for an additional Term, they cannot receive an adequate Recompence for their Labour, Expences, and Time: And therefore praying, That leave may be given to bring in a Bill to extend the Term of the said Grant for such a Number of Years as shall appear to the House to be due to the Design of the said Patents, so far as relates to the Spinning of Flax by Mills or Machinery.

A Petition of the Mayor and Corporation, Clergy, Churchwardens, Landholders, and Inhabitants, of Tiverton, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are given to understand, that a Petition is already, or is about to be, presented to the House by a few Persons of Tiverton, and its Neighbourhood, for Leave to bring in a Bill for paving and improving the Town of Tiverton, which Petition is signed by several Persons of no Property in the said Parish; and that, at Two numerous and respectable Meetings of the Landholders and Inhabitants of Tiverton, held, pursuant to Public Notice, in the Months of September; and October last, it was resolved, that an Act of Parliament for improving the Town was wholly unnecessary, and that the Parish would oppose every Scheme to obtain an Act to levy new Burthens, unless they had the reasonable Prospect of receiving adequate Benefits in Return; and that the Petitioners conceive an Act of Parliament for paving and improving the Town of Tiverton is wholly unnecessary, and would be extremely burthensome and oppressive to the Inhabitants of the said Parish, who are already groaning under a Load of Taxes from a sinking Trade and a numerous Poor; and that the Inhabitants have always been, and still are, ready and willing to repair the several Streets of the Town when Occasions require, and the Petitioners conceive that the existing Laws are fully sufficient to enforce such Repairs, when necessary, without the further Aid of Parliament; and that the Town of Tiverton stands out of the grand Travelling Western Road, and would not derive any material Benefit from the proposed Alterations, or pretended Improvements, and the Petitioners therefore hope the House will reject the Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, and prevent the Petitioners and the Public from the Expences and Burthens which are intended, and must necessarily arise from such Act, if obtained.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That an Act was made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of King William the Third, intituled, "An Act for " the Explanation and better Execution of former " Acts made touching Watermen and Wherrymen " rowing on the River Thames, and for the better " ordering and governing the said Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, upon the said River,

" between. Gravesend and Windsor;" and that, in pur-

suance of the said Act, certain Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, have, from Time to Time, been made for the better Rule and Government of the Society or Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, upon the said River, between Gravesend and Windsor, but the same have hitherto proved inadequate and ineffectual, by reason that the Right of suggesting and proposing such Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, is exclusively vested in the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the said Society or Company, and the Cognizance of the several Offences committed against

C o

the said Rules, Orders, and Constitutions is vested in Eleven of their own Members; and that it would tend to the more speedy and effectual Administration of Justice, and be of great Public Utility and Convenience, if the Court of Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London, for the Time being, were authorized and empowered to make, frame, and set down in Writing, reasonable and necessary Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, for governing and regulating the Wherrymen, Watermen, ana Lightermen, upon the River Thames, between the Limits aforesaid, and if the Lord Mayor, Recorder, or any one Alderman of the said City for the Time being, or any Justice of the Peace within the Shires and Places next adjoining to the River Thames, between Gravesend and Windsor, were empowered to carry such Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, into Execution and Effect: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for making the lliver Nine or Nen, running from Northampton to Peterborough, navigable, and also, an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for making more effectual the above-mentioned Act, were read.: And,

John Bramston, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Commissioners appointed to put the said Act in Execution, did, by Indenture bearing Date the loth Day of September 1726 (and which he produced to your Committee) contract with, constitute, authorize", and appoint Robert Wright and Thomas therein

named, to make, and to be Undertakers for making, perfecting, maintaining, and keeping the said Navigation, and for their Charges and Expences therein to have, take, and enjoy, to and for the Use and Behoof of them, their Heirs and Assigns, the Tolls and Rates therein particularly mentioned; and that the said Commissioners did also, by a certain other Indenture bearing Date the 29th Day of April 1736 (and which he also produced to your Committee) contract with, constitute, authorize and appoint the said Thomas Squire to make, and to be Undertaker for making, perfecting, maintaining, and keeping the said Navigation, and for his Charges and Expences therein to have, take, and enjoy, to and for the Use and Behoof of him the said Thoma , his Heirs and Assigns, the Tolls and Rates therein particularly mentioned.

And being further examined, he said, That by virtue of the said Acts, and the said Indentures, the said River Nine or Nen has been made navigable from Peterborough to Thrapston Bridge aforesaid, but that the Powers by the said Acts granted to the said Commissioners, for the good and orderly Usage of the said Navigation, have, in several Instances, been found insufficient for the Purposes thereof; and, for Want of due and proper Exercise of some of the Powers vested in the said Commissioners, at the Time the said Contracts were made and entered into, and the said River made navigable, additional Difficulties have arisen. — And the Witness added, That it is expedient and necessary that some further Powers and Remedies should be given for the better carrying the said Acts into Execution.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to remove 'certain Difficulties in the Execution of the Powers vested in the Commissioners appointed by Two Acts, passed, in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, and in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, for making the River Nine, or Nen, running from Northampton to Peterborough, navigable, so far as the same relate to the Navigation between Peterborough and Thrapston Bridge: And that Mr. Dickins and Sir William do prepare, and

bring in, the same.

A Message from the Lords, by, Mr. Holford and Mr. Spranger:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty certain additional Duties on Foreign Spirits imported into Britain; with-

out any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty certain additional Duties upon Worts, Wash, and other Liquors, brewed or made in England, for extracting Spirits for Home Consumption, and upon Spirits made in Scotland, and imported into England; without any Amendment: And also,

A Petition of Susanna Palmer, Widow, and John Petition Francklin, Esquire, was presented to the House, and against Ea* read; Setting forth," That the Petitioners are joint Proprietors of the Right of Navigation on the River DraLage Bill Ouze, from Saint Ives's Staunch, in the County of Huntingdon, up to Barford Bridge, in the County of Bedford; and that the Petitioner, Susanna Palmer, is the sole Proprietor of the Right of Navigation on the said River, or of the Tolls and Profits thereof, from the said Bridge, up to the Town of Bedford, and is also sole Proprietor of the Tolls and Profits of the Navigation on the River Lark (which is a Branch of the said River Ouze) from the Town of Bury Saint Edmunds, in the County of Suffolk, to Worlingfon, in the same County; and that the Petitioners have been informed, that a Bill is depending before the House, to authorize the altering the Course and Channel of a certain Part of the said River Ouze, by making a new Cut from a Bend in the said River, at, or near, Eau Brink, in the Parish of Wiggenhall Saint Mary's, in the County of Norfolk, into, or near, the Harbour of King's Lynn, and, in order to defray the Expences. of the said Work, it is intended by the said Bill to impose certain Tolls on all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize (except Manure) to be navigated through such new Cut; and that the intended new Cut, if it should answer the Purpose of improving Drainage, will necessarily tend to impede the Navigation, by reducing the Depth of Water in the said Rivers, which, in several Parts thereof, particularly in the Old Ouze, above Denver Sluice, is, at present (owing to that Sluice, and the Neglects of the Corporation of Bedford Level) scarcely sufficient for the Passage of the Vessels employed thereon, but the said Cut will, in the Opinion of able Engineers, be productive of Effects immediately prejudicial, and eventually destructive, of the Harbour of Lynn, as well as the Navigations of the River Ouze, and its several Branches, in which Event the Value of the Properties of the Petitioners in the Navigations above described (acquired by great Labour and Expence, and held under the Sanction of a Royal Grant, and several Acts of Parliament) must be annihilated, to the Ruin of their private Fortunes; and that the Tolls, intended to be imposed by the said Bill on Commodities to be navigated through the said Cut, will (by enhancing the Price of such Commodities to the Consumers beyond those at which they can be supplied from other Quarters) have the Effect of turning Part of the Trade, now carried on by the Navigations belonging to the Petitioners, in other Channels, whereby the Profits of the said Navigations must be

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for improving the Drainage of the Middle and South Levels, Part of the Great Level of the Fens, called Bedford Level, and the Low Lands adjoining, or near to, the said Levels; as also the Lands adjoining, or near to, the River Ouze, in the County of Norfolk, draining through the same to Sea, by the Harbour of King's Lynn, in the said County, and for altering and improving the Navigation of the said River Ouze, from or near a Place called Eau Brink, in the Parish of W Saint Mary's, in the said County, to the said Harbour of King's Lynn, and for improving and preserving the Navigation Of the several Rivers communicating with the said River Ouze, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Sir Wat kin Letces reported from the Committee, to Swansea whom the Petition of the thereunder mentioned Per- Canal Pe-sons, Proprietors of Lands in the Counties of Glamor- titio".re' gan and Brecon, as well as others, most of whom are 1)0 interested in the Trade and Commerce of the Port of Swansea, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that' the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him. to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Rhys Davies being examined, said, That he is resident in the Neighbourhood of the Line of the intended Canal; and that there are great Quantities of Iron Ore, Iron Stone, Coal, and Lime Stone, in the Vale of Tawe, and the adjacent Country, at present unworked, or worked in but small Quantities, from a Want of Water Carriage therefrom to any Port, and that a great Part of the Country adjoining remains in a very uncultivated State, on Account of the Defect of such Mode of conveying such Lime Stone, and other Manure, and some Iron and other Works are now carried on therein, which may be greatly enlarged, and many more may be established, to the great Benefit of that and the adjoining Counties, and the Town of Swansea — He further said. That he is of Opinion, that the making a Navigable Canal or Navigation from a Place called Hoi noyadd, through the several "Parishes mentioned in the Petition, to or near a Place called The Brewery, in the Parish of Mary in Swansea, together with Navigable Cuts, inclined Planes, Railways, Roads, and Conveniencies, to communicate with the Canal, will be an Object of great Public Utility, and will be the Means of enabling such Mines of Iron Ore, Iron Stone, Coal, and Lime Stone, being worked, and of Lime Stone, and other Manure, being conveyed to cultivate the Line of Country at present so indifferently cultivated.

Mr. Thomas Lane being examined, confirmed the above Evidence: And,

Mr. Thomas Sheasby being examined, said, That he has surveyed and levelled the Line of the proposed Canal, and is of Opinion, that it is practicable to make the same as described in the Petition.

A Petition of the Right honourable Henry Earl of Uxbridge, and the humble Petition of the several Gentlemen, Clergy, Land Owners, Merchants, Tradesmen, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appears, by a Survey lately taken, that a Navigable Communication, for the Passage of Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, with heavy Burthens, may be conveniently made from the present Navigation of the River Trent, by and from the Town of Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, along a Part of the said River, and from thence, by a Cut or Canal, to join and communicate with the Coventry Canal upon Fradley Heath, in the said County, where it will unite with the Inland Navigations to the Ports of London, Hull, Bristol, Liverpool, and the intermediate Places, and afford an Opportunity of bringing to Market, upon very advantageous Terms, the Produce of the several Alines of Lime, Limestone, Coals, Ironstone, Grindingstone, Buildingstone, and other Minerals, on the South Side of the River Trent, and considerably reduce the Price of the Carriage of those several Articles, and of all Mercantile Goods, and will also greatly facilitate the Trade of the River Trent from the Ports of HulL Gainsborough, See. and be of great Utility to the Public in general: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining the said Navigable Communication, by such Ways and Means, and with such Powers, and finder such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Villiers, the Lord Paget, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of John Kenrick, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Kelshall, in the Parish of Kelshall, in the bounty of Hertford, and Owner of the greater Part of the Lands within the said Manor and Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Manor and Parish, certain Commons and Waste Grounds, and certain Old Inclosures and Open Field Lands, which, in their present Situation, are incapable of Improvement, but, if divided and inclosed, the same might be put in a State of Cultivation, and considerably improved: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Old Inclosures and Commons and Waste Grounds, and Open Field Lands, in such Manner, and subject to such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Elijah Impey, Mr. Plumer, and Mr. Baker do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, Bill to extend by an Act, passed in the Thirty-second Year of the the Lancaster Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act Canal Navi- " for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or gation. Canal from Kirkby Kendal, in the County of Westmorland, to West Houghton, in the County Palatine " of Lancaster, and also, a Navigable Branch from " the said intended Canal at, or near, to, or

" near, War Ion Cragg, and also, another Navigable " Branch, from, at, or near, Gale Moss, by Chorley, to " or near Duxbury, in the said County Palatine of " Lancaster," certain Persons were united into a Company, and authorized to make and complete a Canal, to be called The Lancaster Cana/, navigable and passable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, from, at, or near KirkbyKendal aforesaid, through the several Parishes and Townships in the said Act mentioned, into the Township of West Houghton, in the County Palatine of Lancaster; and that the said intended Canal was proposed to be carried very near the Mansion House of Ashton Holland Park?, belonging to the Petitioner, to the great Inconvenience and Dislike of the Petitioner, but the Petitioner was persuaded to consent to the making of the said Canal upon having the Line of the Canal carried through his Estate, in the Manner described in the Map or Plan, and Book of Reference, mentioned in the said Act, and upon repeated Assurances that the said Canal would be of great Advantage to the Petitioner and his Tenants, by passing Seven Miles through the Estates of the Petitioner, and that the said intended Canal should not deviate from the Course or Direction delineated in the said Map or Plan, and set forth in the said Book of Reference, in such Part of the Line of the said Canal as should pass through the Petitioner's Estate; and, in Confirmation of the said Assurances, it is by the Said Act particularly enacted, that nothing therein contained should extend, or be construed to extend, to authorize or enable the said Company of Proprietors or their Successors, or the said Commissioners, in making the said then intended Canal to deviate from the Course or Direction delineated in the said Map or Plan, and set forth in the said Book of Reference, in such Part of the Line of the said Canal as should pass through the Estates, Lands, or Grounds, of, or belonging to, the Petitioner, without the Approbation or Consent, in Writing, of the Petitioner, his Heirs, or Assigns, under his or their Hand and Seal for that Purpose first had and obtained; and that, notwithstanding the before stated Assurance

of the Agents concerned for the said Company, the Petitioner observes, from the Votes of the House, that a'

Bill is depending for enabling the said Company of Proprietors of the Lancaster Canal Navigation (amongst other Things) to vary the Line of the said Lancaster Canal Navigation, and that such intended Variation is proposed to be made by making and completing a Canal navigable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, from, or out of, the said Original Line or Course, at, or near, a Place called Cabus Nook, in the Township of Cabus, in the said County Palatine of Lancaster, through the same Township, and into, or through, the several Parishes of Cookesham and Garstang, Church Town, and in, or through,'the several Townships of Winstanley, Nateby, Garstang, and Bonds,

all in the said County Palatine of Lancaster, and to join and communicate with the said Lancaster Canal at or within the said Tow'nship of Barnacre with Bonds, and that a very considerable Part of the Line of the said Canal, intended to be abandoned by the aforesaid Deviation, runs nearly through the Centre of the Lands and Estate of the Petitioner, and a large Part of the Line proposed to be adopted in Lieu thereof, is also intended to be made through other Part of the Lands of the Petitioner, but at the Extremity of his Estate; and that, if the present Bill should pass into a Law, it will not only defeat the Agreement made with the Petitioner, sanctioned by the said Act of Parliament, but deprive the Petitioner and his Tenants of the principal Benefit to be derived from the said Canal, the Deviation will lengthen the Course of the Canal nearly One Mile, and will be productive of no Public Benefit whatever, the Protection extended to the Petitioner by the said Act will be unjustly violated, and an additional Expence of Tonnage fall upon the Persons who make Use of the said Canal; and that the Petitioner will also be highly injured and aggrieved by other Parts of the said Bill, if the same should pass into a Law: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by his Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill, whereby he feels himself aggrieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Lancaster Canal Navigation to extend such Navigation, by making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the said Lancaster Canal Navigation, at or near a certain Place called How Croft, in the Parish of Wigan, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, to join the Canal of his Grace the Duke of Bridgewater in the Parish of Eccles, in the said County, and also to vary the Line of the said Lancaster Canal Navigation, and for other Purposes, is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is comftiitted.

that Time, but, in consequence of the great Increase of Trade and Shipping which has since taken place, the said Dock has become greatly insufficient for the Accommodation thereof, and the Trade of the Country is much injured by the Want of Dock Room at the said Port; and that not only an Extension of the Wet Dock at Hull, but also an Entrance thereinto direct from the River Humber, is absolutely necessary, the present Passage to the Dock and Quay, through the long narrow River or Haven of Hull, being frequently blocked up by the Ships to and from Foreign Voyages, Coastwise,

Uxbridge A Petition of the Innholders and Publicans of the Innholders Town of Uxbridge, in the County of Middlesex, was **»Petition Presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That cao* e ' the Petitioners are, and have been for several Years past, very heavily oppressed by the great Number of Military, who-have uninterruptedly been quartered upon them, and which they peculiarly feel, owing to the exorbitant Price of Provisions and Fodder of every Denomination; and that Two of the Petitioners, one of whom keeps The Crown, the other The White Horse, in the Town of Uxbridge, have, each of them, fre-Vop. 4Q.

questly had Twenty Horse Soldier's and Horses, Thirty Militia Men, and Six and Eight Officers quartered on them at the same Time, and, upon an accurate Calculation, they have each sustained ah Annual Loss of £. 300, and the Other Petitioners Loss has been proportionably heavy, according to the Size and Accommodations of their respective Houses; and that the very small Allowance, made by Government as a Compensation for quartering the Military, is so perfectly inadequate to the Expence Occasioned thereby, that it renders the Petitioners Situation insupportably hard, and compels them to implore the Attention of the House, and to declare, that, if some Relief is not afforded them, from the heavy Losses they sustain, the Petitioners will be inevitably prevented from supporting themselves and Families: And therefore praying.

That the House will take these Circumstances into Consideration, and relieve them from their oppressed Situation, by ordering Barracks to be erected, or by such other Measures for their Relief, as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Com Dealers thereto subscribed, being Growers of, or Dealers in Petition. Com, or concerned in buying and selling of Com and Grain, in several different Parts of the Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That notwithstanding it seems to have been the Object of the Legislature from the beginning of the Thirteenth Century to the present Time, to establish, throughout the Kingdom, One uniform Measure for Corn, and many Acts of Parliament have been passed, and other Means used, to effect the same, it is notorious that in many or most Parts of the Kingdom, there is an arbitrary Provincial or Customary Bushel, or Measure for Com, used, and almost every Market Town, and every Part of the Country, in some Respect, differs from another in the Shape and Size of the Measure, and in the manner of filling and measuring the same, or in some or one of those Particulars, and the Dimensions and solid Contents of the Brass Bushels, and other Measures, which have been sent to various Parts of the Country, and kept as Standards, and supposed to be according to those in the Exchequer, differ, some in a greater, and others in a lesser Degree: That the several Acts of Parliament, passed ior regulating Measures, enact.

That there shall be but one Measure, and that according

By Acts of Parliament, of 16 Charles I. C. 19. 22 CharlesII. C. 8. and 22 and 23 Charles II. C. 12. in all Cases relating to Buying or Selling of Corn, the Use of a Bushel, agreeable to the Standard marked in His Majesty's Exchequer, commonly called The Winchester Bushel, there said to contain Eight Gallons to the Bushel, and no more or less, is directed under several severe Penalties as there mentioned. — The Act of 13

IV. III. C. 5. which was (amongst other Things) for laying a Duty of Six Pence a Bushel upon all Malt in Hand on the 9th of March 1701, and upon all that should be made from that Time to the 24th of June 1703, enacts, that by the Bushel there mentioned is meant and intended a Bushel according to the Standard remaining in the Custody of the Chamberlain of His Majesty's Exchequer, commonly called and known by the Name of The Winchester Bushel; and in the latter Part of the Act it is stated, " That, to the End " all His Majesty's Subjects may know the Content " of the Winchester Bushel, whereunto this Act refers, and that all Disputes and Differences about " Measure may bet prevented for the future, it is " hereby declared, that every round Bushel, with a " plain and even Bottom, being made Eighteen Inches " and an Half wide throughout, and Eight Inches " deep, shall be esteemed a legal Winchester Bushel, " according to the Standard in His Majesty's Exchequer;" and all,- or most of the Acts, which, since the Expiration of this Act, have passed annually, for laying a Duty upon Malt, direct the Duties to be collected under the like, or nearly the like, Rules and Regulations as are mentioned in this Act: That, in the Year 1758 and 1759, some Reports were made by Committees of the House of Commons appointed to enquire into the Original Standards of Weights and Measures in this Kingdom, and to consider the Laws relating thereto, these Reports were ordered to be printed, bat no further Proceedings were had respecting the same; and by those Reports it appears, that the Bushel used at the Exchequer as a Standard is less than Eight of the Standard Gallons there, a Gallon less than Four of the Standard Quarts, and a Quart more than Two of the Standard Pints; viz.

The Bushel, which is dated 1601 (in the Time of Queen Elizabeth) contains - - 2,124 Cubical Inches.

That it appears also, by those Reports, that all Duties of Customs payable by the Bushel, are collected by the Winchester Bushel, made agreeable to the Act of \$W. III.; that the Bushel is struck, and, to strike it, is used a round circular Strike, which is of the same Diameter from one End to the other, and, by Order of the Commissioners of the Customs, it is to be used in all Ports of the Kingddm; and, by the said Reports, it also appears to be the Opinion of the Committee, that Measures of Capacity should be ascertained by the Number of Cubical Inches therein contained; and that all Goods, measured by any such, should not be heaped, but stricken with a round Strike of the same Diameter from one End to the other; and they further pointed out to the House what they thought were the proper Contents of such Measures: That several late Acts of Parliament have recognized, and, in some Respects tolerated, a Customary or Provincial Measure, and the Use of it, in a great many Places, is general: That several Informations, on the Statutes of Charles II. for selling Grain by a Measure different from the Winchester Measure, have been lately made, Vol. 49.

and several Persons have been convicted in the Penalties there mentioned; and some of those Convictions have been removed into the Court of King's Bench, and there have been argued and affirmed:

Those Convictions have awakened the Attention of many People, and many Sellers and Buyers of Corn have provided themselves with new Bushels, according to the Standard, or what they thought according to . the new Standard; but these, coming from different Makers, in London and elsewhere, are different in Shape, and are found, by a Comparison, not to be of equal Size: That, from w'hat has before been stated, it appears, that a Bushel sized by, or made according to, 13 W.III. From these Contradictions it is probable the Inequality which now exists in Measures might originate; and, as the Laws now stand, it seems equally legal to adopt a, Measure according to 13 W. III. or of any other Form, if equal to the Standard Bushel, or Eight of the Standard Gallons, which will differ from each other about One Part out of Forty, or, perhaps, to adopt a Measure containing 32 of the Exchequer Quarts, or 64 Pints, which will differ from some of the first-mentioned Measures about One Part out of Twenty: That the Shape of the Measure, and the Manner of filling and striking the same, being different (as is the Case in many Parts of the Kingdom now) will occasion a considerable Difference in the real Quantity contained in a Measure of any given Number of solid Inches; and that, owing to these Inaccuracies and Uncertainties, many Inconveniencies and Disputes do, and are likely to arise, to the great Hindrance of Trade, and Grievance of the Petitioners, and others of His Majesty's Subjects: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and that a Bill may be brought in, and passed into a Law, exactly to define the Form, Dimensions, and solid Contents of a Bushel, or some other Measure, for Com, and the Manner it is to be filled and stricken, under such Rules and Regulations as to the House shall seem proper, or to grant to the Petitioners such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
