A Petition of the Planters of the West India Colonies resident in Great Britain, and of the Merchants trading to the said Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for abolishing the Trade carried on for supplying Foreign Territories with Slaves; and Setting forth, That the Supply of Negroes, which the British Sugar Islands have hitherto had, has depended in a great Measure on the Encouragement which the African Merchants have met with in having different Markets to resort to besides those of the British Colonies, and if they are now deprived of the Liberty of supplying Foreign Markets, Foreigners must of Necessity take up the Trade for themselves, and this will of Course raise new Competition on the Coast of Africa, by Means of which the Price of Negroes will be advanced, the Supply of our Islands be rendered precarious, and a valuable Branch of the British Commerce diverted to other Channels, while no one good Purpose, either of

Policy

Petition against the Bill for abolishing the Trade for supplying Foreign Territories with Slaves.

Petition against the hill for abolishing the Trade for supplying Foreign Territories with Slaves.

236 25° Februarii. 1794.

Policy or Humanity, will be answered by the Measure; and that the Ends of Wisdom or Philanthropy not being attainable by the proposed Bill, various Provisions of the same are, and must be, in their Nature most vexatious, and tend to impede Communication, and diminish, and ultimately annihilate, the Trade, between the several British Colonies in British Vessels navigated according to Law, and in those Seas principally by Negro Slaves: That, at this alarming Conjuncture, when such Proceedings have taken place in the National Convention of France, and in some of the French West India Colonies, as must tend to destroy all Subordination, and produce universal Anarchy and Destruction throughout all the French Colonies in the Wiest Indies, the Petitioners are apprehensive that any farther Proceedings on the said Bill may suggest Grounds of Mischief, and have the most alarming Consequences in our o<vn Sugar Islands: And therefore praying. That they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against the Principle and Provisions of the said Bill.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the Town of Liverpool, was also presented to the House, and read; Likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will be attended with the most fatal Effects, not only to the Petitioners in particular, but to the African and West India Trade in general, and to the Manufactures, Commerce, and Navigation, of this Country; that the Supply of Negro Labourers to the Foreign Colonies in the West Indies and America has always been considered as one of the Branches of the African Trade the moot beneficial to this Country, the Merchandize employed in the said Trade being chiefly British Manufacture, the Navigation British, and the Returns generally in hard Specie; that the British Islands in the West Indies derive many great and important Advantages from the said Trade, among which the Petitioners beg Leave to state the following: It encourages the African Merchant to bring into their Ports a much greater Number of Labourers than they themselves have occasion for, from whence they draw a considerable Revenue by the Import Duties thereon; it gives them a more certain and a more abundant Supply for their own Plantations, leaving only the Refuse of the Market for their Neighbours; it leaves to the Profit of the Islands One Tenth Part of the Value of all such surplus Slaves, besides considerable Sums expended in Charges attending the Sale of the same; it brings a Number of Foreign Vessels into their Ports, and thereby opens a Door for Commercial Intercourse of infinite Advantage, as well to the said Islands as to the Mother Country; and, it enables the Slave Factors to grant such great Indulgencies to our own Planters in the Payments for their Slaves as they never could afford if it were not for the Resources which they draw from the said Trade: That this particular Branch of the African Trade has been always justiy held to be of infinite Value to the Commerce of this Country; that Government, sensible of its great Importance, has given every possible Encouragement and Protection to the British Merchant in the Prosecution of it, and has used great Exertions to extend and to secure it exclusively to this Country, more particularly by the memorable Treaty of Utrecht; and that the Petitioners, under the Sanction of various Acts of Parliament, and under the most watchful Protection of Government, have been encouraged to embark very large Capitals in the Prosecution of the African Trade at large: That before the Depression of Commerce, occasioned by the present War, there were 140 Ships employed in the Trade from the Port of Liverpool alone, which, from their peculiar Form and Construction, are unfit for any other Trade; that the said Ships, with their Outfits and Cargoes, consisting

chiefly of British Manufactures, formed an actual Capital of about £. 1,190,000, and, if to this be added the repeated Investments by the same Ships before the Returns for former Adventures could come in a Course of Payment, the whole Property in Circulation, on Account of the said Trade, would amount to a Sum not less than £. 1,920,000 besides the great Sums employed therein from other Ports: That of this immense Capital, at least Two Thirds has been employed in that particular Branch of the Trade, the Abolition of which is intended by the present Bill; and, if its Operation were even to stop there, its Effect would he of the most fatal Consequence to the Petitioners and others concerned in it; but it is with the most serious Alarm they beg Leave to represent, that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it will go to an Abolition of almost the Whole of the British Trade for Slaves, because no Merchant of any Prudence will risk his Property for the Supply of a Market where it must be altogether at the Mercy of the Purchaser; besides, the Competition upon the Windward and Gold Coast of Africa with other Europeans has been of late Years so great, that it would be altogether impossible to supply our Islands from thence, and the Trade to all the other Parts of Africa must be totally abandoned, the Slaves from thence being of little Estimation in our Islands, and the Adventures, necessarily large, hearing no Proportion to the Littleness of the Demand for them; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that, while the present Bill would deprive this Nation of a most important Branch of its Commerce, and ruin our West India Islands, it would not, at the same Time, have any Effect in the Attainment of that particular Object for which it is intended, it being utterly impossible, by any Law of this Country* to hinder Foreigners from obtaining Negro Slaves the certain Consequence then would be the Transfer of this Trade, with all its attendant Benefits, to other Nations, who would rejoice at this Prohibition, as they would be thereby enabled to avail themselves of the British Intelligence and Industry, which they are now actually courting, to carry it on from their own Ports; and that the Petitioners finally beg Leave to observe, that, if ever there was a Time when the Distresses of Individuals might claim a more than ordinary Attention and Indulgence from Parliament, it is the present, when the Commerce and Industry of the Country labour under the heaviest Depression and Discouragement; they therefore humbly presume to hope, from the Justice and Humanity of the House, that they will not suffer them to be disturbed in the Pursuit of what remains to them of a fair and honest Trade, which they have enjoyed for a long Course of Years under the Security and Encouragement of Parliament, to the infinite Advantage of this Country and its Colonies: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, that they will not suffer the said Bill to pass into a Law, and that they will grant such further Protection and Relief as to the House may. seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

and that the Town Of Borrowstoun-ness has a considerable Foreign and Coasting Trade, and large Quantities of Coal and Salt, from the Works belonging to the Petitioner, Douglas Duke of Hamilton, in the Neighbourhood, are shipped off from that Harbour, and much Benefit has arisen to the Trade from the Repairs and Improvements made upon the Piers, supported by the Impost above-mentioned, for, since the Commencement thereof, not only have the Two main Piers been much extended, but a Bason Wall with Sluices so constructed as has effectually cleaned the Harbour, and continues to preserve a Depth of Water enjoyed by few Harbours in the Forth, and from that Wall a middle Pier has been run out, and all the Works kept in constant good Repair; and that a further Extension of the East Pier for more Accommodation to the Shipping, and for defending them from the North Easterly Storms, has been founded; which important Improvement, with the continual Annual Repairs, will more than exhaust the Funds, and, unless a renewal of the said Duty on Ale and Beer shall be granted, the Petitioners must look forward to a great Reverse in the State of the Harbour,-which would soon become ruinous, and of Course the Trade of the Port dwindle away; and that the Repairs and Improvements on the Harbour have always been considered of the first Consequence, and the Funds have never yet been adequate for enabling the Trustees to attempt a very desirable Object, the bringing in good Water, the Want of which has long been severely felt by the Town of Borrozcstou: It is intended also to have the middle Pier extended, and a dry Dock constructed, a Work highly necessary for the Safety of Shipping under Repair, and Part of the Funds will also be necessary for keeping the Streets in Order; and* that the said Duty on Ale and Beer has greatly declined in the Annual Amount during the last Twenty-five Years, so as now not much to exceed Half of the Amount Twenty Years ago, and the Trustees will thereby be prevented from carrying forward those Works, so necessary to the Prosperity of the Trade of the Town, and the Convenience and Health of the Inhabitants, unless Parliament shall think fit to increase the Fund by a Mode which appears very natural, an Anchorage on the Shipping, of One Penny Half-penny Sterling per Ton, which it is thought may prove sufficient, with the former Impost, for all the Purposes mentioned, and so moderate an Anchorage will be cheerfully paid by the Ship Owners, in view to the increased Improvement of the Harbour, and the additional Security thereby offered the Shipping resorting the reto: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the aforesaid Purposes, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Stoke upon thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and ^D^ure* others, Inhabitants within the Parishes of Stoke upon Trent, Bur stem, and Woolstanton, in the County of Staff Small Debu ford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting Petition, forth, That the said Parishes are very populous, ana much Trade is carried on, and a great Number of Persons employed in the several Works and Manufactories established therein; and that the Tradesmen and Inhabitants residing in the said Parishes are necessarily obliged to give Credit, particularly as to the Common Necessaries of Life, for very small Sums of Money, to many Persons who, although of sufficient Ability to pay the same, very frequently refuse so to do, presuming upon the Discouragements, and taking Advantage of the Difficulties their Creditors lie under, from the great Expence they must unavoidably incur, and the Delays they meet with, in suing for such Debts in the County Court, and which is more than ordinarily oppressive upon the Suitors residing within the said Parishes, on Account of the great Distance of the said Parishes from the Town of Stafford, where such County Court is held, to the great Injury of the fair Trader, and the Prevention of useful Credit; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the establishing of a Jurisdiction within the said Parishes, under proper Powers and Regulations, for the Recovery of Small Debts, in a Way less expensive, and more expeditious, than the present Method, would not only tend to promote honest Industry, support useful Credit, and be of great Advantage to the Tradesmen and Inhabitants in general of the said Parishes, but would likewise relieve the Persons contracting such Debts from the notorious Oppressions Daily exercised over them by Bailiffs, and other illiterate Persons, practising in the said County Court:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts within the said Parishes, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to the Earl Gower, Sir Edward Littleton, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

the said Roads, at all Seasons of the Year, which greatly damage the said Roads, raise a sufficient Fund for effectually maintaining and repairing the said Roads, and keeping down and paying the Interest of the Money already borrowed, unless some additional Tolls be granted and made payable on the said Roads, and the Terms and Powers of the said Acts be further continued and enlarged.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Merchants, Traders, Freeholders, and others, residing in the Cities of Bath and Bristol, and in the Counties of Somerset, Wills, and Berks, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by Levels and Surveys lately made, it appears practicable to make and maintain a Navigable Canal and Communication for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, from the River Kennelt, at, or near, the Town of Neiobury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at, or near, the City of Bath, and a Navigable Branch or Cut out of the said Canal, in the Parish of Rowd, near Devizes, In the County of Wilts, to, or near, the Town of Caine, in the said County, and also a Navigable Branch or Cut, out of the said last mentioned Branch or Cut, to, or near, the Town of Chippenham, in the said County of Wilts; and that the making and maintaining of such Canal and Communication and Branches will greatly facilitate and render less expensive, than at present, the Conveyance of Com, Coals, Stone, Iron, Timber, Lime, Chalk, Manure, and all Kinds of Merchandize, and heavy Commodities, not only to and from the said City of Bath, and the several Towns of Bradford,

Devizes, Caine, Chippenham, Great -

ford, Newbury, Reading, Windsor, and other adjacent Towns and Places, but also to and from the Ports of London and Bristol\and such Navigable Canal and Communication and Branches will be of great Public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effectuating the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall judge proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

' Resolved, That this House doth agree with the

Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That, towards defraying the Expence of conveying Letters between this Kingdom and the Islands of Guernsey and Jersey, there be granted to His Majesty, upon the Portage and Conveyance of Letters and Packets between the Port of Weymouth, or from or to any other convenient Port in Great Britain, to or from any of the Ports of Jersey and Guernsey, or either of them, and to or from the Ports of Jersey, from or to the Ports of Guernsey, for every single Letter Two Pence, for every double Letter Four Pence, for every treble Letter Six Pence, and for every Ounce Eight Pence; and so in Proportion for every Packet of Deeds, Writs, or other Things.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, several Amendments were proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Words " for the Inland Port or Conveyance of all " Letters and Packets sent or conveyed by the Post within the said," and inserting the Words " towards

defraying the Expence of conveying Letters within " the," instead thereof.

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the Said Resolution, so amended, That, towards defraying the Expence of conveying Letters within the Islands of Jersey and Guernsey, or either of them, there be charged the like Rates of Postage, in Proportion to the Number of Miles or Stages such Letters and Packets are carried or conveyed by the Post, as are paid for the Inland Port or Conveyance of Letters and Packets within that Part of Great Britain called England.

A Petition of Henry Duke of Buccleuch, and James Earl of Cardigan, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Petition has been presented to the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for amending and repairing the Road leading from Saint Martins Stamford Baron, in the County of Northampton, to Weldon, in the same County, and also the Road from Oundle to Middleton Lane, in the same County; and Representing to the House, that the Road leading from Weldon aforesaid to Kettering, in the said County, is in a ruinous Condition, and, in many Places, narrow, incommodious, and dangerous, and cannot be effectually widened, amended, improved, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course of Law: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said intended Bill for amending and repairing the said Road from Weldon to Kettering aforesaid, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners of Estates in the County of Northampton, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of Owners and Occupiers of, Messuages, Lands, and Hereditaments, upon and near to the Line of the Lancaster Canal Navigation, commencing at Kirkby Kendal, in the County of Westmorland, and ending at West Houghton, in the County of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by several Acts, passed in the Thirty-second and Thirty-third Years of the Reign of His Vol. 49.

present Majesty, Power is given to make a certain Canal, with divers Branches, commencing at Kirkby Kendal, in the County of Westmorland, and ending at West Houghton, in the County of Lancaster, in the effecting of which Navigation a considerable Progress is already made; and that such Canal and Works will be of the highest Benefit and Utility to the Estates and Situations of the Petitioners, and to the Inhabitants of the Country at large, provided the same be not deteriorated by the Consequences of an Application made to the House, on the Part of the Company of Proprietors of the Canal Navigation from Leeds to Liverpool, to deviate and vary the Line of their said Canal, for which Purpose a Bill is depending in Parliament; and that, amongst the Benefits reasonably to be expected from the said Lancaster Canal, one of the most material, in the Apprehension of the Petitioners, is the Opportunity afforded of procuring Coal and Cannel from the Southern to the Northern Parts of the Line; and that the Application, so made to Parliament by the said Leeds and Liverpool Proprietors, tends to interfere with, and intercept, the Coals, Water, and Carrying Trade upon the Lancaster Canal, and will (as the Petitioners are informed) run for several Miles very near to, and parallel with, the said Lancaster Canal, and must, in other respects, injure that Navigation, without offering or affording to the Public any such material Advantage as can compensate for such apprehended Mischief and Inconvenience: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel and Agents, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Petition from thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Proprietors of Owners of Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in the County of Lancaster, was also presented to the House, and read; against d« Setting forth, That there is a Bill depending in the Bill.

House, to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Canal Navigation from Leeds to Liverpool to vary the Line of the said Canal Navigation, and to raise a further Sum of Money for the Purpose of completing the said Canal Navigation, and for other Purposes, which the Petitioners apprehend will be very injurious to their Estates and Interests, if the same passes into a Law: And therefore praying, That they may be at Liberty, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, to be heard against the said Bill, that the same may not pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Canal Naviga.-tion from Leeds to Liverpool to vary the Line of the said Canal Navigation; to raise a further Sum of Money for completing the same; and to amend an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of King George the First, for making the River Douglas, alias Asland, navigable from the River Ribble to Wigan, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and another Act, passed in the Tenth Year of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining the said Canal Navigation, be read a Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the said BUI, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Whitmore being examined, said, That there was formerly an ancient River or Watercourse leading from the Town of Wisbech to the River Nene, in 7 the

34 Geo. III. 27° Feh'u 251

the Parish of Outwell, in the said Isle of Ely, upon which small Vessels used to navigate, but the same is in many Places so filled up, that a Passage for the Waters cannot be obtained, and that Part that runs at the Back of the Town of Wisbech, has of late Years been filling up, and several Buildings have been erected thereon, and by the Sides thereof, without any Right whatever.

Mr. James Golborne and Mr. John Watth being examined, said, That it appears, by Levels and Surveys, that a Navigable Cut or Canal may be made from the River of Wisbech, at or near a Place called The Old Sluice, through the Parishes of Wisbech, Saint Peter, Elm, Emneth, and Outwell, to join and communicate with Well Creek, and the River Nene, in the said Parish of Outwell. — That for making the said Canal, it will be necessary to throw out, cleanse, and widen the said River or Watercourse, from the said Old Sluice to a Place called Elm Corner, and to remove the several Buildings erected on and by the Sides of the said River.

Then an Act, made in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for improving and preserving the River Nene, and Well Creek, was read: And,

hit. Golborne and Mr. being again examined,

said, That Part of the said River, between Outwell Church and Salter's Load Sluice, in the County of Norfolk, has been of late Years filling up, and is at present in a very imperfect State; and that if the before-mentioned Communication from Wisbech to Outwell is made, it would be necessary that a good Navigation should, at all Times, be maintained from Outwell Church to Salter's Load Sluice, that proper Provisions should be made for that Purpose, and the said Act, 30 far as respects the Navigation between Salters Load Sluice and Standground Sluice, in the said Isle of Ely, should be amended and made more effectual. — And both the Witnesses added, That the carrying the before-mentioned Purposes into Execution, will be the Means of opening a short Communication between Wisbech River and the River Nene, and Well Creek aforesaid, and of making a safe and easy Communication between the Port of Wisbech and the Counties of Cambridge, Huntingdon, Bedford, Norfolk, and Suffolk, and other Parts, which will be of great Public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from Wisbech River, at or near a Place called The Old Sluice, in the Town of Wisbech, in the Isle of Ely, and County of Cambridge, to join the River Nene, in the Parish of Outwell, in the said Isle of Ely, and in the County of Norfolk, and for improving and maintaining the Navigation of the said River from Outwell Church to Salter's Load Sluice: And that Mr. Charles Yorke and General Adeane do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The Order of the Day being read;

The House resumed the adjourned Debate on the Motion, made upon Monday last, for bringing up a Petition of the Reverend Thomas Fyshe Palmer, Clerk, a Prisoner in His Majesty's Ship or Vessel Stanislaus, at Woolwich.

The House was moved, That the Entry in the Votes of the House, of the 22d Day of January last, of the Order, " That the Grand Committee for Courts of " Justice do sit every Saturday in the Afternoon in the " House," might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

Ordered, That the said Petition be brought up.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, at a Circuit Court of Justiciary, holden at the Town or Burgh of Perth, on the 12th and 13th of September last, the Petitioner was tried and convicted upon a certain Indictment exhibited against him at the Instance of Robert Dundas, Esquire, His Majesty's Advocate, for composing, printing, and circulating, or causing to be composed, printed, or circulated, a certain Address resolved at the Berran Meeting House, which, in the said Indictment of His Majesty's Advocate, was and is particularly set forth and charged to be a felonious, seditious, and inflammatory Writing, and the Petitioner was thereupon sentenced by the said Court of Justiciary to be transported beyond Seas, during the Space of Seven Years, to such Place as His Majesty, with the Advice of His Privy Council, should declare and appoint: That the Petitioner is advised, and humbly apprehends, that the Proceedings against him, and the Sentence pronounced upon him, were and are illegal, unjust, oppressive, and unconstitutional, inasmuch as they are not founded on, or supported by, any Statute or other Authority constituting Law in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and particularly because the said Sentence is directly contrary to certain Statutes in force there; and he further humbly submits to the House, that the said Proceedings and Sentence were and are oppressive and unconstitutional, inasmuch as the same were and are unprecedented and excessive, and consequently not warranted by the Free Spirit and the Mild Practice of the British Constitution: And the Petitioner therefore, asserting the Right of a Briton, solemnly appeals to the House, the Constitutional Guardians of the Liberties of the Subject, against the said Proceedings and Sentence, and humbly prays for such Relief in die Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till Saturday Morning next, Ten of the Clock.

A Message by Sir Francis M Gentleman Royal Assent Usher of the Black Rod: to Bills.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses,. do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence,

His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Privy Seal, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for punishing Mutiny and Desertion, and for the better Payment of the Army and their Quarters:

An Act for preventing Money or Effects, in the Hands of His Majesty's Subjects, belonging to or dis-poseable by, Persons resident in France, being applied to the Use of the Persons exercising the Powers of Government in France, and for preserving the Property thereof, for the Benefit of the Individual Owners thereof:

An Act for repealing the Stamp Duties on Gloves and Mittens sold by Retail:

An Act for repealing the Duties on the Registry of Burials, Births, Marriages, and Christenings:

An Act to indemnity such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments, and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications, within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members and Officers in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors; and for indemnifying Deputy Lieutenants, and Officers of the Militia, who have neglected to transmit Descriptions of their Qualifications to the Clerks of the Peace, within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for that Purpose:

An Act for inclosing and otherwise improving certain Lands and Grounds within the Lordship and

Mary, in the County of Norfolk, to, or near, the Town and Harbour of Lynn, and, in order to carry such Work into Execution, and to defray the necessary and other incidental Expences attendant thereupon, it is intended to impose a certain Annual Tax upon a very large and extensive Tract of Commonable and Low Grounds, in which not only all and singular such Lands, as well Commons as Severals, lying within the said several Parishes, as are subject to Land or Sea Floods, but also all and every such Low or Fen Grounds, usually called Adventure Land, and already subject to the Payment of an heavy Annual Acre Tax to the Corporation of Bedford Level, to defray the Expence of such Works as are necessary to preserve the Drainage thereof, and also all and singular such other Lands lying ‘within the Parishes aforesaid as are formed into Districts, the more effectually to secure the Drainage of such Lands, respectively, are included; and that the Petitioners are thoroughly convinced, that whatever Benefit or Advantage the Projectors of the said Scheme, and the Promoters of the said Bill, may derive to themselves from such intended Cut, if carried into Execution, it is totally impossible that the same can be of any Utility, or render the least Service whatever, to the several Lands belonging to the Petitioners, and others, and situate in the several Parishes aforesaid, or in any, or either of them, but, on the contrary, that the Low or Fen Grounds in the said Parishes, and in many others, may thereby became subject to frequent Inundation; and the Petitioners beg Leave further to submit, that by the said Bill it is also intended to impose a certain Tonnage upon all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, which shall be conveyed through the said intended new Cut to, or from, the Port of Lynn, whereby not only the Growers of the Corn, Grain, and other Produce, as well of the Upland as of the Low or Fen Country in the said Counties and Isle aforesaid, and many other Counties, which is now conveyed to Lynn by Means of their respective Navigations, but also the Consumers of Coals, Deals, Wine, and other Articles of Merchandize, with which they are supplied from Lynn, will become subject to an oppressive Tax towards the Expence of a doubtful and hazardous Scheme of Drainage, from which they have no Benefit or Advantage whatever to expect, but much Loss and Inconvenience to apprehend, and the Petitioners are fully persuaded that the said Bill, in its general Tendency, so far from being of any Utility, will be extremely prejudicial and detrimental to the Country at large: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that the Petitioners may be heard against the same, by themselves, or their Counsel.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, Commonalty, and other Inhabitants, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, of the Borough of Thetford, in the County of Norfolk, on Behalf of themselves and others, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed that a Bill is brought into the House, to authorize the altering the Course and Channel of the River Ouze, by making a new Cut from a Place at or near Eau Brink, in the Parish of Wiggenhall Saint Mary's, to or near the Town and Harbour of Lynn, and that, by the Navigation of the Brandon River, which is a Branch of, and unites in, the said River Ouze, the Inhabitants of the said Borough* of Thetford, and its Vicinity, are supplied from or through the Port of Lynn, with Wine, Coals, Deals, Iron, and various Articles of Merchandize, and the Farmers and Occupiers of Land, in and about the Neighbourhood of the said Borough of Thetford, are enabled to export their Com, Grain, and other Produce of their Lands, by Means of such Navigation, which, in its present State, answers the general Purposes of the said Borough of Thetford and its Vicinity, and the Petitioners therefore disapprove of any At-

tempt to alter the same; and that the Petitioners are advised, that the intended new Cut (the real End and Design whereof is to improve the Drainage of certain Fen and Low Lands) is not likely to amend, but will, if carried into Effect, materially injure, and may eventually destroy, the said Navigation; and that, by the Tolls proposed by the said Bill, the Consumers of Goods imported, and the Growers of Articles exported, by the said Brandon River, through the Port of Lynn, will be unjustly taxed towards defraying the Expence of an hazardous Experiment, from which they have no Benefit to expect, but much future Loss and Inconvenience to apprehend: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, but that the Petitioners may be heard against the same, by themselves, or their Counsel.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Petition Worcester and Birmingham Canal Navigation, under against the

C/ vat 1

their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending in the House for making a Canal Navigation from the Warwick and Birmingham Canal, to join and communicate with the Oxford Canal at Braunston, in the County of Northampton; and that an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament for making a Canal Navigation from the Dudley Canal at, or near, Netherton, where there are very large and valuable Coal Mines, to join the Worcester and Birmingham Canal at a Place called Selly Oak, in the Parish of Northfeld, in the County of Worcester, and also, another Act, passed in the last Session, for making another Navigable Canal from the Town of Stratford upon Avon, in the County of Warwick, to join and communicate with the Worcester and Birmingham Canal at King's Norton, near Selly Oak aforesaid; and that, by Means of those Canals, an easy and eligible Line of Communication may be opened with the Braunston Canal, which the Petitioners apprehend would be of meat Importance to the Public, particularly in the Conveyance of Coal and Merchandize, along the aforesaid Canals, between the Cities of Bristol and Worcester, and the Town of Birmingham, Dudley, and other Places, to Braunston aforesaid; and that the Petitioners apprehend the proposed new Canal from Warwick, to join the Oxford Canal-at Braunston aforesaid, is not calculated to serve the Public, as the Lockage from the Town of Birmingham to the Birmingham and Warwick Canal is exceedingly great, and will be attended with much Inconvenience, and that the intended Canal is not founded on any Principles of real Public Utility, and has been hastily adopted, and the Petitioners conceive that a much more eligible Line, to communicate with the above-mentioned Cities and Towns, and the Braunston or Grand Junction Canal, and with the City of London, may be adopted: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

otherwise Goggushland, Cowbitt Common, Langtoft Common, Boston Common, Spalding Common, and Pinchbeck Common, and also of Other Lands called Cowbitt Wash, and Crowland Fodder Lots and Wash, all in the 'Said County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Outfall of the Waters of the River. Welland is very defective, and the Navigation thereby is much impeded, occasioned principally by the Channel or Bed of the River being too wide between a certain Place called Hole, in the said

Parish of Surfleet, and the Junction of the Waters of ,the said River Welland with the Waters of the River Witham, in the said County, and certain Parts of the said Fen Lands, Low Grounds, and Marshes, are subject to be Overflowed by the Downfoll of Rain thereon, and also by Upland Waters, and are: greatly injured by the said Downfoll 'and . Upland Waters not having a proper Passage to the Sea; and that in order effectually to improve and assist the Drainage of the said Lands, and to amend the said Navigation, it is necessary that the present Channel of the River Welland

should be cleansed from a certain Place called The Reservoir to the said Shepherds Hole, and that a Dam should be made across the said Channel, and a new River or Cut of sufficient Dimensions to afford a free Passage for the Waters draining from the said Lands, and to answer the Purposes of Navigation, should be made to commence below the said Shepherds Hole, and to continue from thence down to Wyberton Roads, in the Parish of Wyberton, in the said County, between the Port of Boston and a certain Place called Boston Scalp, and for the Convenience of Passengers, that a Bridge should be built over the said new River or Cut, at, or near, Fosdyke Inn, in the said Parish of Fosdyke; and that, by Levels and Surveys lately taken, it appears that a Cut or River, as above described, may be made, and the Petitioners conceive that the making thereof, with such other Works as may be found requisite to attain the Ends above described, would be highly beneficial to the Owners and Occupiers of Lands in the Places above specified, and would tend greatly to promote the Trade and Commerce of the Town of Spalding, in the said County, and of the adjacent Country, and the Expence of making such Cut or River, and other Works, and also of building the said Bridge, may with great Ease and Convenience be provided for by Means of a Tax upon the Lands to be benefited by the said Cut and Works, aided by a certain Tonnage or Duty on Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, navigated on the said Cut or River, and by a Toll to be taken from Passengers, Cattle, and Carriages, passing over the said Bridge: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

To prove thfe Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Charles Truss being examined, said, That there is a' very considerable Intercourse carried on between the Cities of London and , and the Western

Counties, by Means of the River; that the

Navigation of the said River from Mill,

near Boulter s Lock, in the County of Bucks, to Isle-worth, in the County of Middlesex, is frequently obstructed by the Lowness of the Water in Summer, and the Floods in Winter, whereby the necessary Sup>-plies of Timber, Bark, Malt, Cheese, Flour, and other Articles of Provision for the Metropolis, are rendered uncertain, and frequently damaged, and the Cargoes of Coals and Merchandize for the Supply of the Western Counties are frequently delayed; that by making a Canal from Taplow Mill Head, near Boulter's Lock, to the said River at Isleworth, Eighteen Miles of Navigation will be saved ip; a Distance of Thirty-seven Miles, the Expence of Towing will be considerably reduced, a great Saving made in the Article of Freight, and the Voyage will be performed with Certainty and Expedition, and the same will thereby be of very great Public U tility.

A Petition of the several Owners and Occupiers of Petition Mills situate upon the River Colder, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the an/castlf6 House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for mak- Field Can»l ing and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Bill-Colder Navigation at, or near, Sowerby Bridge Wharf, in the Parish of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, to join the Canal of his Grace the Duke of Bridgewater, in the Parish of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and also certain.

Cuts from the said intended Canal; and Setting forth,

That the Petitioners conceive that the passing such Bill into a Law would not only be very prejudicial to the Mills, Estates, and Interests, of the Petitioners, but also to the Woollen and Stuff Manufactories of that Part of the West Riding of the County of York; and that there are on the said River upwards of Thirty Mills, within the Distance of Twenty Miles, for the milling of Woollen Cloth, scribbling and spinning Wool, scouring of Stuffs, and grinding Com, which produce to the Proprietors thereof a very considerable Annual Rent, and those Mills in Times of Drought experience a very considerable Loss for want of Water, many of them in such Times are not able to work more than Twelve or Fourteen Hours in the Day, and, should a Diminution of Wetter (sufficient to supply a Canal) take Place, the Petitioners apprehend many of those Mills would be thereby rendered nearly useless in the Summer Months and the Manufacturers be obliged, as has been the Case lately, to carry their Cloths and Stuffs to distant Mills on other Rivers to be milled and scoured; and that the River Colder and its Feeders, in its present State, is not equal to the Powers wanted, and, if any Diminution of Water takes Place, those Mills will be very materially injured, as well as the Trade and Manufactories of that Neighbourhood: And therefore praying.

That they may be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against so much of the said Bill as affects the said River Calder, or its Feeders.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.' 1

Earl of New- A Petition of the Right honourable Anthony James burgh and ‘Earl of Newburgh, Viscount Kinnaird, Baron Levingston,

Jou" of Flacraig, in the Kingdom of Scotland, and of Sir John ton'sPetition. Throckmorton, of Buckland, in the County of Berks,

Baronet, as the next Friend and Trustee for, and on Behalf of Thomas Giffard, of Chillington, in the County of Stafford, Esquire, and of his Infant Children, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petitition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Honourable William Radclyffe, late of Ambell, in the County of Northumberland,

Esquire, died on, or about, the 4th Day of November, 1732, seised in Fee Simple of, and in the Manor of, Ambell, and several Lands and Hereditaments situated in Ambell, Hawxley, and Warkworth, in the said County of Northumberland, and the said William Rad-clyffe, by a Will, or Testamentary Instrument in Writing, dated the 24th Day of July 1730, devised, or intended to devise, all his Real Estates to James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh, his little Nephew, and the Father of the Petitioner, the said Anthony James Earl of Newburgh; and that, although the said Will or Testamentary Instrument were executed by the said William Radclyffe, in the Presence of Three credible Witnesses, yet, inasmuch as it was not subscribed by them as Witnesses to his Execution thereof, the said William Radclyffe died intestate as to his Real Estates: That upon Account of the Attainders of the Two Nephews of the said William Radclyffe, viz. James late Earl of Derwentwater, and Charles Radclyffe, for having been concerned in the then late Rebellion of 1715, no Person could become Heir to the said William Radclyffe, deceased: That, upon an Inquisition taken at Morpeth in the said County of Northumberland, on the 4th Day of November 1742, it was found that the -said Manor of Ambell, and all other the Lands and Hereditaments of which the said William Radclyffe died seised or intitled unto, had escheated to the Crown for want of an Heir: That, inasmuch as some Doubts were conceived concerning the Alienage of the said James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh, the little Nephew, and the intended Devisee of the said William Radclyffe, because he was born Abroad, after the Attainder of his Father, the aforesaid Charles Radclyffe, his late Majesty King George the Second was most graciously pleased to mitigate the Rigor of the Laws, by which the said James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh, was disabled to take and hold the Estates of his said great Uncle, deceased, and therefore by Letters Patent, bearing Date the 3d Day of November 1744, demised unto the Most noble Charles, late Duke of Richmond and Lenox, and to the Honourable James Brudenell, Esquire, (Nominees and Trustees of and for the said James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh) all the said Manor of Ambell, and the Lands and Hereditaments therein mentioned to be situated in Ambell, Hawxley, and Warkworth, in the said County of Northumberland, to hold the same unto the said Charles Duke of Richmond and and

James Brudenell, their Executors, Administrators, and Assignees, from thenceforth for and during the Term of Thirty-one Years, at and under the ancient Yearly Rent of Sixteen Pounds Nine Shillings, and his said Majesty did thereby moreover assign and make over to them the said Charles Duke of Richmond and Lenox, and James Brudenell, for the Benefit of the said James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh, all the Rents and Arrears of Rent of the said Hereditaments and Premisses that had accrued from the Death of the said William Radclyffe, up to the Day of the Date of the said Letters Patent: That, by other Letters Patent, bearing Date the 25th Day of August 1768, His present Majesty was also most graciously pleased to demise all the said Manor, Hereditaments, and Premisses, to the Right Honourable George Henry, late Earl of Litchfield, and John Lord Bellew (Nominees and Trustees of and for the said James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh) to hold the same unto the said George Henry Earl of Litchfield, and John Lord , their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, for the Term of Twenty-three Years and Six Months, from the 14th Day of November 1775 (which was the Time of the Expiration of the aforesaid Term of Thirty-one Years) at and under the said Yearly Rent of Sixteen Pounds Nine Shillings: That the aforesaid James Bartholomew, late Earl of Newburgh, is dead, and the Petitioner, the said Anthony James Earl of Newburgh,

Mr. Kemeys' A Petition of John Kemeys Gardner Kemeys, on Be-

Petition. half of himself, his Mother, and his Two Sisters, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Year 1756, pursuant to an Order of the Court of Chancery, the Estates of the Petitioner's Father and Mother, consisting of a Moiety of a Plantation, w'ith the Negroes and Appurtenances, in Jamaica, then producing, communibus Annis, £ 1,200 Sterling, and of several Freehold Manors and Farms in Monmouthshire, in England, then of the Yearly Value of £.352, were yoi. 49.

(subject to prior Portions and Incumbrances, amounting to £ 3,300) settled upon the late John Gardner, the Petitioner's Father, for Life, without Impeachment of Waste, Remainder for securing a Jointure to the Petitioner's Mother of £ 500 per Annum, and £ 4,000 Portions for the Petitioner's Sisters, Remainder to the Petitioner in Tail in strict Settlement'; and that the said John Gardner took the Name of Kemeys, in pursuance of the Will of Reginald Kemeys, his Wife's Father: That it is with the deepest Concern, though under the Impulse of absolute Necessity, the Petitioner is obliged to state, that his Father, having contracted very considerable Debts, conceived a Plan for extricating himself out of his Difficulties, by laying such a Case before the Legislature as should induce them to pass an Act (though to the Disinherison of the Petitioner when an Infant of about Fourteen Years of Age) for making the above settled Property a Fund to discharge his Debts, and accordingly, in the Year 1772, he applied for and obtained (and induced his Wife, the Petitioner's Mother, to consent to) an Act of Parliament in Great Britain, wherein, by way of Inducement to the Fraud then practising on the Legislature, it was, according to the false Evidence produced to the Committees of both Houses of Parliament, stated, that the Petitioner's Father was seised in Fee of an Estate in Monmouthshire, adjoining to and intermixed with the settled Estate, then of the Yearly Value of £ 566, in which had been discovered some Ore that was likely to prove very beneficial; and further, that the Petitioner's Father, since the execution of the said Settlement, was become seised of a convenient Tract of Land contiguous to the said Plantation, and that he had expended considerable Sums in lasting Improvements for the Use of the Plantation, and in extending the Plantation, by cultivating a large Tract of Waste Lands, which before was of little or no Value, and in purchasing an additional Number of Negroes proper for the Improvement thereof, by Means whereof the Annual Income of the Plantation had been increased, from £. 1,200 a Year, to the Annual Sum of £. 2,500, and the Annual Income was likely, in the Course of a few Years, to be much further increased; and further, that the Petitioner's Father had also expended very considerable Sums upon the Monmouth settled Estate, in repairing and enlarging the Mansion House, in rebuilding and repairing Farm Houses, and by inclosing and cultivating great Part of the barren and unprofitable Lands, by planting a very considerable Quantity of Oak and other Trees, which were in a very thriving Condition, and in other lasting and permanent Improvements, by Means whereof the Annual Income of that Estate was increased in Value to £981 per Annum and upwards, and, by the Annual Growth and Increase of the Trees so planted, the Inheritance of the said Premises would, in a few Years, be considerably improved; and further, that there was then growing upon the settled Monmouth Estate a considerable Quantity of Timber and other Trees in a very thriving Condition, which, upon a fair Value, were worth then to be sold £. 6,000 and upwards; and it was also further stated, that, to enable the Petitioner's Father to make the several Purchases and Improvements aforesaid, and thereby to increase as well the Yearly Income as the Value of the Inheritance of the settled Estates, for the Benefit of the Issue Male claiming under the Settlement to the Amount before-mentioned, and without which no such Advantage could accrue to them, the Petitioner's Father had been necessarily obliged, not only to contract Debts to the Amount of £31,976 or upwards, but to grant several Annuities out of the settled Estates, during his Life, to the Yearly Amount of £. 1,300, which were redeemable, and which (with the Incumbrances on the settled Estates prior to the Settlement) made together £44,026 or thereabouts; and it was further stated, that the Pe-

and the Petitioner, instead of coming into Possession, ps he had a Right to expect, of the above settled Property, viz. an English Estate of £352 per Annum, and a Jamaica Estate of about £. 1,200 per Annum, clear of Incumbrances, except his Mother's Jointure of £. 500, and except £. 7,300, being the Incumbrances charged thereon previous to and by the Settlement, he now finds himself intirely stripped of all Provision intended for him by the Settlement, and indeed of all Means of Subsistence, as he has no other Fortune; for there is every Reason to apprehend, that the Mortgaged Estates, if now sold, would fall short of raising sufficient to pay the Principal and Interest due to Mr. Rigby's Executors; and, besides this, the Petitioner's Mother and his Sisters are also, by the Consequences of the Act, totally deprived of the Jointure and Portions intended for them by the Settlement: That the Petitioner now finds, and is able to prove, that the grossest Imposition was practised on Parliament in obtaining the Act; for, instead of the unsettled Monmouth Estate being, as stated in the Act, of £. 566 Yearly Value, and the settled Part being then of £. 981 Yearly Value, making together a Rental of £. 1,547 i and> instead of Ore being found in the unsettled Estate likely to prove beneficial, and the Timber on the settled Estate being at the Time of die Act, as therein stated, worth to be sold £. 6,000 and upwards, the Fact really is, that the whole settled and unsettled Estate in Monmouthshire has never been let at a gross Rent of more than £. 700 or £. 800 per Annum, and that no Ore whatever has been, or is likely to be, discovered therein; and the Petitioner's Father, but a few Years before the Act passed, purchased the unsettled Monmouthshire Estate for a Sum of £. 3,443 only, although the Rental thereof was stated in the Act at £. 566 per Annum; and the Value of the Timber, as stated in the Act, was equally fallacious, for the Timber, on both the settled and unsettled Estates, is now valued at £. 3,000 or thereabouts, and none has been felled since the Act, except for the necessary Repairs; and further, the Jamaica Estate, instead of producing an Income, as stated in the Act, of £. 2,500 per Annum, has not, for the last Seven Years, yielded more than £. 1,000 a Year, nor the English Estate more than £. 500 a Year nett upon an Average, making in all £. 1,500 per Annum, a Sum greatly insufficient to pay the Interest of the Mortgage, by which it is increased from £. 41,386. 13 v. 6 d. to £. 53,000 or thereabouts: That Mr. Rig/y, the Mortgagee of the aforesaid Estates, died indebted to Government in a

Mr. Atkin- A Petition of Christopher , of Park Stt'eet,

son's Petition. Westminster, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in July 1783, the Petitioner had the Misfortune to be convicted upon an Indictment in His Majesty's Court of King's Bench for Perjury, alledged to have been committed by him in an Affidavit denying a Charge contained in a libellous Publication against the Petitioner, imputing to him Fraud in his Transactions with the Victualling Board, and afterwards suffered the direful Consequences annexed by Law to the Crime of Perjury': That, at the Trial, Mr. Lee, the then Solicitor General, who conducted the Prosecution on Behalf of the Vol. 49*

Crown in opening the Case, declared in Substance, that, if no Fraud were found in the Petitioner's Transactions, no Perjury could be imputed to him; to which Lord Mansfield, the then Chief Justice of the Court, and who tried the Indictment against the Petitioner, expressed his Assent: That the Verdict was given by the Jury under an Impression of Fraud, for want of a sufficient Conception of the Nature of the Petitioner's Accounts, and the Mode of keeping them, which Accounts, most unfortunately for the Petitioner, were of too great a Magnitude and Extent to be fully investigated and understood in the short Space allotted for the Trial of an Indictment at a Nisi Prius Sittings:

That the Petitioner, at the Time of his said Conviction, was a Member of this Honourable House, but' in consequence thereof expelled from, it by a Resolution which now appears upon the Journals: That His Majesty's then Attorney General, in Michaelmas Term 1782, filed his Information, in the Court of Exchequer, for a Restitution of the Overcharges alledged against the Petitioner, and which Information particularly involved the Transactions which had been ‘ the Subject of the Trial for Perjury, and proceeded entirely upon the Idea of the supposed Fraud which had led to the Petitioner's Conviction, so that the Question in Effect was, whether the Petitioner had been guilty of that Fraud, the Belief of which was the Ground of his Conviction for Perjury? That, in November 1790, Eight Years from the filing the Information, the Court,. after Twelve Days hearing Counsel, and a solemn and thorough Investigation of the Petitioner's Accounts and Transactions, and reading the Evidence of respectable Commercial Men that had been taken on the Occasion, so far from discovering any Fraud in the Petitioner's Transactions with the Victualling Board, wras pleased to intimate that the Petitioner had Merit with the Public upon the whole of his extensive Transactions with that Board:

That, on the 26th of May 1791, His Majesty's Attorney General, the present Lord Chief Baron, having taken Time to consider whether he ought, on Behalf of the Public, to pray any Account against the Petitioner, was pleased to signify to the Court, that he declined to pray any Account, which the Court not only approved, but observed it was a prudent and honourable Decision, and such Decision, the Petitioner humbly submits, manifests that the Conviction was founded in Misconception: That the Petitioner, on the 14th of June 1791, presented a Petition to His Majesty, stating, in Substance, the above Facts, and praying that His Majesty w ould, in respect thereof, be graciously pleased to pardon the said Conviction, and restore him to his Franchises, w'hich Petition was by His Majesty referred to the said Attorney General, who had conducted the Suit in the Exchequer on the Part of the Crown against the Petitioner, as before-mentioned, and, on a Report from the said Attorney General, His Majesty was pleased to pardon the said Conviction, and to restore the Petitioner to all his former Franchises: And therefore praying, That the House will take these Circumstances into Consideration, and that the Resolution for his Expulsion may be expunged from the Journals, as the Grounds on which he was supposed unworthy to sit in Parliament, now clearly turn out to have been erroneous.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Charles Pierrepont, Esquire, Samuel Crawley, Esquire, and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Roads leading from the Turnpike Road heretofore made between Markham Moor and Dunham Ferry, at or near the MillhiUClump in Ragnall Field, through the Parishes of Ragnall, Fledbrough, Marnham, Normanton, Grass-thorpe, and Sutton upon Trent, to join the Great North ' Road at Sutton aforesaid, in the County of Nottingham, are in a ruinous Condition, and, in the Winter Season, not passable without imminent Danger, and in several Parts very narrow and incommodious; and that, if the said Roads were amended and improved, to become passable at all Times of the Year, so as an uninterrupted Access to Markets and Fairs, and a safe and easy Passage for Cattle and Carriages, might be obtained, it would be a considerable Advantage to the Petitioners and others: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and widening the said Roads, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

and, to the End that the Petitioners might be enabled to carry on so useful an Undertaking, they were thereby empowered to raise among themselves a competent Sum of Money, not exceeding £. 200,000 in the Whole, unless the said Sum should be found insufficient for the Purposes aforesaid, in which Case the Petitioners were enabled to raise among themselves any further Sum, not exceeding £. 60,000; and that the Petitioners, in making and completing certain Parts of the said Canal, and in purchasing and improving the Navigation of the River Douglas, alias Asland, in the said County of Lancaster, which, by virtue of an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of His present Majesty, is now consolidated and incorporated with the said Canal, the said Company of Proprietors have expended the Sum of £. 300,000 and upwards; and that tho Petitioners, by an Act passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, were empowered to vary a certain Part of the said Canal, and, in order to finish and complete such Canal, to borrow, in Manner therein mentioned, the Sum of £ 200,000; and that, since the passing of the said last mentioned Act, other Parts of the said Canal are completed, or are now in Execution; and that the Petitioners, after a careful Examination of that Part of the Line which remains yet unfinished, are well satisfied that making a Deviation therein, and carrying the same from Wanless Banks, in the Township of Barrowford, otherwise rowford Booth, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, to communicate with the Douglas Navigation, at Wigan, in the same County, will be of much greater Advantage to the Public and the Petitioners than the present Parliamentary Line of the said Canal, and such Deviation is practicable; and that, for the aforesaid Purpose, a Bill is now depending in the House, which may happen not to pass into a Law, and, in Case such Bill should not pass into a Law, the Petitioners are desirous of deviating the said Canal, and of making and extending the same to or near a Place called Grimshaw Park, in Blackburn, in the said County of Lancaster, only, as such Deviation and Extension to Blackburn will be more advantageous to the Public and the Petitioners than the extending the said Canal from Wanless Banks aforesaid, along and by the Parliamentary Line, which Extension to Blackburn is practicable; and that the Act for making the said River Douglas, alias Asland, navigable, and the said Act of the Tenth Year of His present Majesty, have been found defective: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to empower the said Company to make a Deviation in the Line of the 1 said

Knaresbo- A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are rough Forest thereunto subscribed, being Owners of Lands, or en-Petitionf* titled to certain Rights and Privileges within the District, called The Forest of Knaresborough, in the County of York, on Behalf of themselves and other Owners of Lands, Rights, and Privileges, in the said District, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by virtue of Two Acts, of the Tenth and Fourteenth Years of His Majesty's Reign, upwards of 20,000 Acres of Waste Land have been, by certain Commissioners thereby appointed, allotted to the Petitioners, and divers other Persons entitled thereto, within the aforesaid District, and great Parts thereof have been inclosed and improved at a great Expence, and, by the Provisions contained in the said Acts, or One of them, the Owners and Proprietors of Messuages, Lands, and Tenements, in the said District, were empowered, at any Time before the Execution of the General Award of the said Commissioners, to exchange, in the Manner therein mentioned, all or any of their Allotments of the said Wastes, Messuages, Lands, or Tenements, so that the same were made with the Consent of the said Commissioners, and declared by their said Award; and that the said Commissioners, having made and executed their said General Award before it could be known what Exchanges the said Owners and Proprietors might be desirous of making, divers of the Petitioners and other Owners of Allotments, who were, and still are, desirous of making such Exchanges, have lost the Opportunity of so doing, and are unable to effect the same, unless the Power of making such Exchanges be renewed and enlarged; and that, by an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Time limited for making Exchanges under the said Acts was renewed and extended, but, from various Causes, the Time so renewed and extended has elapsed, without several of the Owners of Lands, Rights, and Privileges, in the said District, having been able to effect the same: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Commissioners named in, or appointed by, the said Acts, for a limited Time, to confirm and establish such Exchanges as have been agreed upon, or shall be made, by and between any of the Owners or Proprietors of Lands and Tenements in the said District, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem expedient.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Wilberforce and Mr. Duncombe do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Narrow Woollen Clothiers, in the Clothiers West Riding of the County of York: And also, Petitions.

A Petition of the White Broad Woollen Clothiers, in the West Riding of the County of York: And also,

A Petition of the Mixed Broad Clothiers, in the West Riding of the County of York;

Were severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That a very great and extensive Manufactory of Woollen Cloths, of fine as well as inferior Quality, has for many Years been carried on in the West Riding of the County of York, whereby Thousands of Men, Women, and Children, have been kept in Employment, and maintained with Decency and Comfort; and that, compared with the Woollen Manufactories in other Parts of England, this in the said West Riding will be found to have had a decided Advantage as to Constancy of Success, and the consequent Certainty of Employment afforded to the numerous Hands employed in it, which superior Advantages arise principally, if not wholly, from the Difference of the System of carrying on the Manufactory in Yorkshire, and the Mode in which it has hitherto been conducted in other Places: That this System, which so fortunately for the Trade in general, the Individuals concerned in it, and the Public at large, has so happily long prevailed in Yorkshire, is now in Danger of being broken in upon, and destroyed, by the Introduction of the Modes which have prevailed in other Parts of the Kingdom, where the Inconveniences and Mischiefs resulting from it have been frequently and most severely felt, which Modes are founded on a Monopoly erected and supported by great Capitals, and set on Foot by that Description of Persons concerned in the Woollen Trade in Yorkshire, called Cloth Merchants, becoming Cloth Makers; and, of late, several such Merchants in and near the Towns of Leeds and Halifax, in the said Riding, have commenced Clothiers, or Cloth Makers, and others' have manifested , a Disposition to follow their Ex-, ample by establishing large Factories for making Woollen Cloth; and that the Consequence of this Procedure must, as the Petitioners believe, be highly prejudicial to them, who, writh a very trifling Capital, aided by the unremitting Labour of themselves, their Wives, and Children, united under one Roof, decently and independently have maintained themselves

and

276

4° Martii.

A. 1794.

and Families, and kept the Home Trade and Foreign Markets constantly and equally supplied, without an Idea, or perhaps a Possibility, of Monopoly, or any Advantage to themselves, inconsistent with good Faith and fair Dealing, or beyond a necessary and equitable Profit on their Labour, and that, from this comfortable and independent Situation, should such Innovation prevail, the Petitioners must separate from their Families, and be reduced to a State of Servitude, to gain Bread for themselves and dearest Relatives: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for preventing such Monopolies and Factories, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as the Nature of their Case may be found to merit and require.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Robert Forbes, of Gosport, in the Gosport County of Southampton, Merchant, was presented to Bridge Peti-the House, and read; Setting forth, That great In- t,on' convenience having been experienced by the Public in general, and more particularly by the Officers and others belonging to His Majesty's Hospital at Haslar, in the Parish of Alverstoke, in the County of Southampton, for want of a Bridge over a certain Salt Water Lake, or Creek, branching from the Harbour of Portsmouth, to the Village of Alverstoke, called Stoke or Haslar Lake, situate between the Town of Gosport, in the said County, and His Majesty's said Hospital, and the Petitioner having stated this Matter to the Commissioners for Sick and Hurt Seamen, to whom, in order to remedy the Inconvenience, the Petitioner made a Proposal to build a Bridge over the said Lake, and to permit the Officers, Servants, and others, belonging to the said Hospital, to pass over the same, on being paid the like Salary that was allowed to the Ferryman employed for that Purpose, to which the said Commissioners afterwards readily assented, and, in consequence whereof the Petitioner began to erect, and hath now completed, a good substantial Brick Bridge, sufficient for the Passage of Carriages as well as Foot Passengers over the said Lake; and that the said Bridge is, and will be, of great Public Benefit and Convenience, particularly to those belonging to the said Hospital, as heretofore the only Mode of Conveyance for Foot Passengers over the said Lake, to and from Haslar Hospital and the Parts adjacent, has been in Boats, which are frequently prevented passing the said Lake, sometimes from the Lowness of the Water, and at other Times from bad Weather, and Carriages being at all Times, previous to making the said Bridge, under a Necessity to go round from Gosport through the Village of Alverstoke, in order to get to the Hospital, which is a Distance of near Three Miles; and that the building and finishing of the said Bridge hath been attended with a very considerable Expence: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for maintaining the Bridge by him erected across the said Lake, called Stoke or Haslar Lake, from Gosport to the opposite Shore towards Haslar Hospital, in the said Parish of Alverstoke, in the County of Southampton, and for enabling the Petitioner to take certain Tolls for passing over the said Bridge, and other Purposes in such Bill to be mentioned.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House: *

A Petition of Abraham Bosquet, Esquire, late One of His Majesty's Commissaries of Musters, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner having, by much Assiduity and Observation, and a Series of Experiments, discovered certain infallible Means of saving Vessels at Sea in Danger of foundering, preserving their Cargoes, and alleviating the Labours of the Pump by Means the most simple and obvious, always practicable, and in the Power of every Ship's Company to effect, and unattended with Expence to the Nation or the Individual, in the Month of May, presented a Memorial to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, inclosing the necessary Measures, Regulations, and Plan, at the same Time proposing to their Lordships to prove, by actual Experiment, their Practicability and Extent; and that the Petitioner, on the 26th of May, received a Letter from Mr. Stephens, lay Command of their Lordships, acquainting the Petitioner that they had sent his Memorial to the Navy Board for their Consideration and Report thereon, and desiring the Petitioner to attend that Board on the* Subject, but that the Lords Commissioners had npt a Power of granting a Vessel whereon to make the Experiments without the Consent or Concurrence of Parliament thereto; and that, on the 3d of June, the Petitioner received a Letter from the Navy Board, signifying their Desire to see him at the Board on the following Tuesday, and the Petitioner attended, accordingly, and had the Happiness to hod, after a full Investigation of the Principles, that his Measures appeared to meet the entire Approbation of that Board, and SO satisfied did they seem to ho of 2

the Obviousness and Practicability of the Object, that actual Experiment, to evince the Effect, appeared to them on no other Account necessary than to satisfy the less experienced and scientific Pant of Seafaring Men, who might not otherwise credit or adopt Measures so novel, and, at first View so extraordinary; and that, on the 16th of June, the Petitioner received a Letter from Mr. Stephens, by Command of the Lords Commissioners, inclosing a Copy of the Report, which states, " That the Honourable the Navy Board liad " considered the Petitioner's Plan for relieving Ships " at Sea in Danger of foundering, preserving their " Cargoes, and alleviating the Labours of the Pump, " and conversed with him on the Subject, and that " there appeared to them to be good and satisfactory " Reasoning in his Proposals, &c. nor is there a single Point, which the Petitioner adduced, controverted or opposed, all being founded on the most unerring Principles, which the Petitioner will explain and substantiate to the Satisfaction of a Committee of this House, if required so to do: And therefore praying the House to take his Plan into Consideration, and, if he may so merit, grant him a Liberty or Licence to use or employ a Vessel in Tfade, of 200 or 300 Tons Burthen, Duty-free, for Fourteen Years, which Vessel shall have a perpetual Breach or Leak in her Bottom, which no Pump can relieve, and, though even destitute of Pump, yet the Cargo shall not be injured, and the Petitioner will consider such Grant a sufficient Compensation, and would thereby be enabled to evince to the Maritime World, at his own Risque, the Practicability and Importance of this extensive Object, without any Expence to, or further Claim on the House for such Discovery, justly considered to be of greater Magnitude and Import to Mercantile and Maritime Men than any Thing that has appeared at one View in the present, or perhaps any former, Century, or that the House will make him such other Retribution or Recompence as an Object so extensive and salutary may appear to merit.

Ordered, That the said Petitition do lie upon the Table.

John Palmer, Comedian, at an Expence of upwards of £. 18,oooo, and His Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the said Liberty have, from Year to Year, granted their Licence to the said Theatre for Public Music, " Dancing, and other Public Entertainments of the " like Kind," pursuant to Act of Parliament; and that the Petitioner is the Proprietor of the said Theatre, having purchased the same in the Year 1789, and, since the said Theatre has been his Property, opened it for Public Entertainment, with such Amusements as are authorized by the said Licence, but, finding that he thereby incurred very considerable Losses, he caused the same to be closed; and Representing to the House, that, when he adds together the various Sums which have been expended by him in this Undertaking, he cannot state the Total of his Loss at less than 10,000, to reimburse which he finds himself possessed of a yet expensive Property, the most unsaleable in its Species, an unsuccessful and unemployed Theatre; That, towards its original Establishment, Mr. John Palmer raised about £. 7,000 by the Sale of Renters Shares, each Holder of which is entitled to a free Admission to all Performances at the said Theatre, and also to a certain Annuity therefrom for Twenty-one Years from the Year 1787; and the Petitioner believes that, if the Performance of the Drama were permitted at the said Theatre during the Summer Season, the Produce of such Entertainment would enable him to continue the said Theatre open regularly every Year, and while thereby the Interests of the said Renters would be substantiated, and the Losses of the Petitioner in a great Degree repaired, he likewise apprehends that an extensive Public Benefit would be the certain Result of establishing a Place for rational Entertainment in the Eastern Extremity of the Metropolis: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable His Majesty to license as a Play House, during the Summer Season, the Theatre commonly known by the Name of The Royally Theatre, in Well Street, in the Liberty of the Tower of London.

Ordered, That the said Petition be. referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:
