A Petition of the Woolcombers of the Borough of Warwick Warwick, was presented to the House, and read; Set- Woolcombers. ting forth, That, by the Invention of a Machine for FatItion-combing of Wool, which diminishes Labour in an alarming Degree, the Petitioners entertain just Fears, that they and their Families will speedily become a heavy Burthen to the State, it appearing to the Petitioners, that One Machine only, with the Assistance of One Person and Four or Five Children, will perform as much Labour as Thirty Men in the customary Manual Manner: And hoping, That the House wifi apply such Remedy as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the several Petitions, presented to this House in this Session of -Parliament, from the Woolcombers, complaining of certain Machines constructed for the combing of Wool, are referred.

Mr. Robert Anstruther reported from the Com- Queeiwferiy mittee, to whom the Petition of the Persons thereunto ^oads Peti‘ subscribing. Trustees for making and repairing the Uoa report Turnpike Road from North Queensferry, in the County of Fife, to the Town of Perth, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed

rected him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as. followeth;

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the Road from the North through the

Towns of Inverkeithing and Kinross, to the Town of Perth, and also the Road from the said Queensferry, to the Town of Dunfermline, Torryhum, and Culross, and also the Road from the said Queensferry, through Inverkeithing to Bruntisland and Kirkcaldy', and also, an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to continue and render more effectual the said former Act,- were read: And,

Mr. John Sewell being examined, said, That by virtue of the said Acts, the said Road has been made, and a considerable Sum of Money borrowed upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted; that the said Road cannot be effectually repaired, nor the Money so owing be repaid, unless the Term and Powers of the said Acts are continued and enlarged. — And being further examined, he said. That it will be of great Public Benefit to make several Improvements of the said Road, and the Communication thereby.

A Member present confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term and enlarging the Powers of Two Acts, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, and the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty, so far as respects the Road from North Queens-feny, in the County of Fife, to the Town of Perth, and for more effectually making, repairing, and keeping in Repair, the said Road, and to pass by, or near by, the Towns of Inverkeithing and Kinross: And that Mr. Robert Anstruther, Mr. Graham, and Mr. Hobart do prepare, and brings in, the same.

Bath Canal the Petition of several Gentlemen, Merchants, Tra-

Doned°n fe" ders, Freeholders, and others, residing in the Cities of Bath and Bristol, and in the Counties of Somerset, Wilts, and Berks, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with (except, that in the Notices published in The Bath Herald, of the 14th of September, and The Salisbury and Winchester Journal, and Reading Mercury, of the 16th of September, one of the Parishes through which the Line of the Canal goes, viz. the Parish of Pattern, was, by Mistake, omitted to be inserted, and in the same Papers, published on the 21st and 23d of September, the Parish of Saint John, Devizes, was, by the same Mistake, omitted, and in the Two First Notices given in T London Gazette, previous to the 28th of September, the said Parish of Saint John, Devizes, was, by the same Mistake, omitted, but that Notices, containing the Whole -of the Parishes through which the Line of the Canal is proposed to go, were given in The London Gazette of the 28th of September,

and of the 1st and 5th of October, in The Bath Herald of the 28th of September, and the 5th and 12th of October, and in The Salisbury and Reading Papers of the 30th of September, and the 7th and 14th of October; and that complete Notices were also affixed on the Church Doors of Saint John, Devizes, and Pottem, on the Three Sundays immediately following the 29th of September, and also upon the Door of the Town Hall at Devizes on the 6th, 13th, and 20th of October); and that the Committee had examined, the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; arid he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Rennie being examined, said, That by Levels and Surveys lately made, it appears practicable to make a Canal for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, from the River Kennet, at or near Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at or near the City of Bath, and a Navigable Branch or Cut from or out of the said Canal, in the Parish of Rowd, near Devizes, to or near the Town of Caine, and also a Navigable Cut out of the said last mentioned Cut to, or near, the Town of Chippenham, in the County of Wilts.

That the making and maintaining such Canal and Cuts will greatly facilitate the Conveyance of Com, Coals,

Stone, Iron, Timber, Lime, Chalk, Manure, and all Kinds of Merchandize and heavy Commodities, not only to and from the said City of Bath, and the Towns of Bradford, Trowbridge, Devizes, Caine, Chippenham, Hungerford, and other adjacent Towns and Places, but also to and from the Ports of London and Bristol, and such Canal and Cuts will therefore be of great Public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Canal from the River Kennet, at or near the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at or near, the City of Jand also certain Navigable Cuts therein described: And that Mr. Goddard, the Lord Sheffield, the Marquis of Worcester, and the Earl of Wycombe do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Bewley, Co- A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, non, Shin, and for themselves and on Behalf of the other Land Owners Helmsdale and Inhabitants of the Counties of Inverness, Ross, Cro~ attorn*Pe" marty, Sutherland, Caithness, Orkney, and Shetland, and the Towns and Boroughs therein, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the large and rapid Rivers, called Bewley, Conon, Shin, and Helmsdale, run across the Country immediately to the Northward of Inverness, from the Mountains to the East Sea, and it is the singular Condition of those Rivers to be absolutely with* Vol. 49.

out a Bridge from their Sources down to their respective Friths, from which uncommon Circumstance, the large and populous District above-mentioned is sometimes utterly inaccessible, and always reached through dangerous Fords and Ferries with great inconveniency, and not unfrequently with the Loss of Lives; and that the Funds and Abilities of the said District have been totally exhausted by making long Tracts of necessary Roads, and constructing numerous Bridges, some on large, and others on smaller Streams, without the Assistance hitherto of- any Public Aid to effect those laborious and expensive Undertakings in the Counties to the Northward of the said Rivers; and that Two of the said Rivers, viz. Bewley and Conon, run partly through, and partly contiguous to, Two of the most considerably of the late forfeited Estates, now restored to the Heirs of the former Proprietors; and that, during the Time the said Estates were in the Hands of the Public, the Commissioners, appointed for their Management, entered at different Times upon various Proceedings for building Bridges on the said Rivers of Bewley and Conon, and paying the Expences out of the Rents of the said Estates, but those Rents having been, from Time to Time, otherwise applied, neither were the said Bridges, nor any other Public Work, carried on upon the said Northern Estates, nor in that Quarter of the Highlands where they lie, although their Rents were regularly levied for the Public, and were intended by Parliament for general Improvements in those Parts, as well as in other Quarters of Scotland; and that the Estate of Seaforth, in the County of Ross, was forfeited in the Year 1715, and re-purchased from the Public at a large Price by the Heir of that Noble Family, and the Public have of course benefited by that Transaction in the same Manner as if they had retained the Estate in their Possession; and while the Family, owing to that Purchase, could not receive the same Advantage as those who have had their Estates restored, this forms a strong additional Reason for that Benefit being extended to that Part of the Country; and that the Grants of the forfeited Estates are charged, with Payment into the Exchequer in Scotland of certain

Mr. Benjamin Baugh being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Acts, and have borrowed the Sum of £. 1,500, the Whole of which now remains due; that the said Money cannot be repaid, nor the said Roads be kept in good Repair, unless the Term of the said Acts be further continued, and the Powers thereof altered and enlarged. — And the Witness added, That it will be necessary to have an Increase of Toll.

Mr. James Farrer Steadman being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

Mr. James Bourne being examined, said, That a considerable Sum of has been . borrowed, and

is now dpe, upon the Credit of the Tolls collected within the said District; which Money cannot be paid off, and the Road kept in good Repair, unless the Term of the said Acts, so far as relates to the said District, be further continued, the Tolls increased, and some Amendments and Alterations made in the said Acts.

And the Witness further said, That there is a very steep and dangerous Hill, near to the Town of Dudley, and if a direct Road was made from or near the Bush Inn, in Dudley, to communicate with the present Road, at or near the Cinder Banks, in the Parish of Dudley, being only the Distance of about Three Quarters of a Mile, it would not only lessen the Distance between Dudley and Bromsgrove, but also avoid the said Hill, which would be of great Convenience to Persons using the said Road.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging die Term and Powers of certain Acts of Parliament, for repairing several Roads in the Counties of Worcester and Warwick, so far as relates to the Road leading from the Town of Bromsgrove to the Town of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, and for making a more commodious Road near the Town of Dudley: And that Mr. Lygon and Mr. Edward Foley do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Timothy Tyrrell, Esquire, being examined, said, That in pursuance of the said Act, certain Rules and Orders have Hfeeh made for the Rule and Government of the Watermen's Company, but the same have proved inadequate and ineffectual, by reason, that the Right of suggesting and proposing such Rules and Orders, is exclusively vested in the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants of the said Company, and the Cognizance of the several Offences committed against the said Rules and Orders, is vested in Eleven of their own Members: He lurther said, That it would tend to the more speedy and effectual Administration of Justice, and be of great Public Utility and Convenience, if the said Court of Mayor and Aldermen, for the Time being, were empowered to make and frame necessary Rules and Orders for governing the said Company of Watermen, and if the Lord Mayor, Recorder, or any One Alderman of the said City of London, or any Justice of Peace, within the Shires and Places next adjoining to the said River of Thames, were empowered to carry such Rules and Orders into Execution and Effect.

Motion for A Motion was made, and the Question being put, Address re- That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty,

tain Treaties to rePresent 10 His Majesty, that His faithful Corn-laid before the mons, having taken into their serious Consideration the House. various Treaties which have, by His Majesty's Com-Neg. mand, been laid before this House, cannot forbear to express their deep Concern, that His Majesty should have been advised to enter into Engagements, the Terms of which appear to this House, to be wholly incompatible with the Declarations repeatedly made to this House from the Throne, relative to the professed Objects of the present unfortunate War:

To represent to His Majesty the Affliction and Vol. 49.

Alarm of His faithful Commons, that His Majesty should have been advised to make a " Common Cause" with Powers whose Objects are unavowed- and undefined, but from whose Conduct His faithful Commons have too much Ground to dread, that they carry on War for the Purpose of dictating in the internal Affairs of other Countries: Views which have been repeatedly and solemnly disavowed by His Majesty, and His Ministers; and which are utterly abhorrent from those Principles upon which alone a free People can, with Honour, engage in War:

To represent to His Majesty, if the present War had been what His Majesty's Message in the last Session of Parliament stated it to be, a War of Aggression on the Part of France, and of Defence on the Part of Great Britain, that, by a Treaty previously in Existence, between His Majesty and the King of Prussia, the Co-operation and Assistance of that Power were ensured to this Country:

That it does not appear to this House, that the Succours, stipulated by the Defensive Treaty of 1788, have been required by His Majesty, but that a new Convention has been entered into, the Stipulations of which have no other Tendency than the involving us in Schemes, as foreign to the true Interest, as they are repugnant to the natural Feelings of Englishmen, and of imposing Restraints upon His Majesty's known Disposition to avail Himself of any.Circumstances which might otherwise enable Him, consistently with the Honour of His Crown, and the Welfare and Security of the Country, to relieve His People from the present burthensome and calamitous War:

To represent to His Majesty, that the Irruption of the French into Savoy, and their Possession of that Part of the Dominions of the King of Sardinia, did not appear to His Majesty so far to endanger the Balance of Power in Europe, as to induce His Majesty, on that Account, to commence Hostilities against France: That His faithful Commons do therefore express their Disapprobation of that Part of the Treaty recently concluded between His Majesty and the King of Sardinia, by which His Majesty is bound not to lay down his Arms until the Restitution of Savoy shall have been accomplished; a Species of Engagement which it can at no Time (excepting in Cases of the greatest Emergency) be either prudent or proper to make; and much less for an Object which was not deemed, in His Majesty's Wisdom, to be so connected with the Interests of this Country as to occasion a Declaration of War:

To represent to His Majesty, that it appears to His faithful Commons to be the general Tendency of these Engagements to involve us in Connexions of undefined Extent, for Objects which we disapprove, and have disavowed; and this with Powers on whose Principles of Equity and Moderation we are instructed, by Experience, to have no Reliance, and whose complete Success may, in our Opinion, prove fetal to the Liberties of Europe:

To represent to His Majesty, that, having thus expressed our Sentiments respecting the Engagements which His Majesty has been advised to contract, we feel it our bounden Duty most humbly and earnestly to implore His Majesty to consider of such Measures as to His Royal Wisdom shall seem adapted (consistently with that National Faith which, in common with His Majesty, we desire to preserve religiously inviolate) to extricate Himself from Engagements which oppose such Difficulties to His Majesty's concluding a separate Peace, whenever the Interests of His People may render such a Measure adviseable, and which certainly countenance the Opinion that His Majesty is acting in concert with other Powers for the unjustifiable Purpose of compelling the People of France to submit to a Form of Government not approved by that Nation;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for making " and establishing Public Quays and Wharfs at ston upon Hull, for the better securing His Majesty's

" Revenues of Customs, and for the Benefit of Commerce in the Port of Kingston upon , for making " a Bason or Dock, with Reservoirs, Sluices, Roads, " and other Works for the Accommodation of Vessels " nsing the said Port,. and for appropriating certain " Lands belonging to His Majesty, and for applying " certain Sums of Money out of His Majesty's Customs " at the said Porty for those Purposes, and for establishing other neoe6sary Regulations within the . " Town and Port of Kingston upon Hull," was read:

And,

Hugh Ker, Esquire, being examined, said, That a Public Quay has been established at the said Port, together with a Dock sufficient for accommodating the Trade and Shipping of the said Port at that Time, but the great Increase of Trade and Shipping which has since taken Place there, has occasioned the said Dock to be greatly insufficient for the present Trade of the Port, and the want of Room now restrains the Public Revenue, and the Trade and Commerce of the said Port, which are in a State of progressive Improvement; and further Accommodation for the Shipping is absolutely necessary.

That the Revenue arising from the Dock and Quay Duties, being abundantly ample to provide at all Times, and cany into Effect, the Increase of Room necessary for the Improvement of the Public Revenue, and the Benefit of Commerce, if the Dock Company were authorized to receive out of the said Revenue such limited Interest or Dividend upon the Whole of their Money expended as Parliament may think right and proper, during the Time and until the necessary Increase of Room be provided for the increased Trade and Shipping of the said Port, and if the Surplus of the said Dock and Quay Revenue granted for this Use, together with the Land given by His Majesty for that Purpose only, were applied to make Room by extending the said Dock, together with "Conveniencies necessary for Shipping and Trade, the Witness conceives the Intention of the said Act would be carried into Effect, and would be of the utmost Advantage to the Public Revenue, and to the Commerce, Navigation, and Manufactures at the said Port, and in me Northern Part of the Kingdom.

Thomas Robinson, Esquire, a Merchant, and George Bramvell, Esquire, Deputy Town Clerk of Hull, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for extending the Dock and Quay at the Town and Port of Kingston upon Hull: And that Mr. Samuel Thornton ana Mr. John Smyth do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Woolcombers of the North Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in various Parts of this Kingdom, Machines for the Purpose of combing Wool have been, and are, erecting, to the great Detriment, Prejudice, and threatened Ruin, of the Manual Woolcombers; and the Petitioners, aware of the Consequences of so pernicious and destructive a Measure, have ventured, in Conjunction with their Brethren of other Districts, to represent this Grievance to the House: And imploring the Interposition of the House, that so large and useful a Body of People may not be deprived of their Bread, and their Families reduced to a State of Indigence and Beggary.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Society or Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, upon the River Thames, between Gravesend and Windsor, and of the several Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, arid read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of King the

Third, intituled, "An Act for the Explanation and " better Execution of former Acts made, touching " Watermen and Wherrymen rowing on the River " Thames, and for the better ordering and governing " the said Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, " upon the said River, between Gravesend and Windsor;' and that, in pursuance of the said Act, certain salutary Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, have, from Time to Time, been made for the better Rule and Government of the Society or Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, upon the said River, between Gravesend and Windsor, and have been by the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the said Company, proposed to the Court of Lord Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London, to be by them examined, altered, and approved, pursuant to the Directions of the several Acts of Parliament in that Case made and provided, and particularly, that certain Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, which the Petitioners can produce and shew to the House, and which they trust will appear to tend to the speedy and effectual Administration of Justice, and to Public Utility and Convenience, were proposed to the Lord Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London, on the 20th Day of May 1788, to be by them examined, altered, and approved, but the said Lord Mayor and Aldermen have not hitherto approved, or, as the Petitioners believe, in any way examined or taken Notice of the same; and that the Petitioners submit to the House, that the Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, already made, and those which have been so proposed, would have proved adequate and effectual, and such as were reasonable and necessary for governing and regulating Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, and have tended to the speedy and effectual Administration of Justice, and been of Public Utility and Convenience, and that such Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, may at all Times be carried into Execution and Effect in a -speedy and effectual Manner; and that the Petitioners hove been informed, that a Bill is depending in the rHoose to repeal so much of the said before-mentioned Act, of die Eleventh and Twelfth of King William the Third, and also so much of any other Law or Statute, as empowers the Overseers and Rulers of the said Company to make and execute Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, for the Ride and Government of the said

3

Whetryreep^ Waterman, and Lightermen, and to annex Pains and Penalties to the Breach of! such Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, and to impower tbp Lord Mayoj? and Aldermen of the City, of London. to n^He Such Laws, Statutes, Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, for the better Government and Regulation of Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen^ rowing or using any Boat, Barge, Lighter, or other Ves.sel, upon the said River Thames, betweeen Gravesend apd Windsor, as they shall think fit and necessary;

and the Petitioners submit to the House, that noj Charge of Misconduct or Neglect of Duty, or of wanf of due Attention to the speedy and effectual, Administration. of Justice, or to Public Utility and, Convenience, in the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, or any other Officers or Person^ in whom the Right of suggesting, proposing, of making such Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, and carrying the same into Effect] hath hitherto been vested, hath or can be proved, and the Petitioners further submit to the House, that great Mischief and Inconvenience may, and probably will, ensue to the Petitioners, and the Public, if the Power of making such Rules, Orders, and Constitutions, is vested in Persons not conversant in the Art and Mystery of Watermen and Lightermen; and the Petitioners are further ready to shew to the House, that the Company of Watermen and Lighterrnen consists of Ten thousand Persons, and upwards, a°d that they have, in the Course of this War, furnished near Three thousand Men, and who are now serving the Public, either as impressed Men, or Volunteers, in His Majesty's Navy, and that it appears, by the Rooks of the said Company, that Two hundred and Fifty Apprentices are, on an Average, bound every Year, and that since the Report of the said BUI being depending in the House, divers Persons, who had before entered their Names in the Books of the said Company for binding Apprentices, have taken out their Names, and assigned, as a Reason for doing sq, the Apprehensions which they were under of the said Bill passing into a Law, and the Petitioners are w ell assured, that if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Numbers of the said Company would be much reduced, to the great Detriment of His Majesty's Navy, and of the Public, in the Loss of such a Nursery for Seamen; and that the Petitioners have been informed, that, by the present Bill, the Fines levied for Offences are proposed to be at the Disposal of the said Lord Mayor and Aldermen, and submit to the House, that great Hardship would arise to the popr, aged, and infirm Watermen and Watermen's Widows, and other Objects jof the Charity of the said Company, who are now greatly supported and relieved by such Fines, in as much as such Fines are always appropriated by the Rulers of the said Company to the Relief of the poor, aged, and infirm Watermen and Watermen's Widows, if such Fines were otherwise appropriated and disposed of: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the ' same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie nppn the Table, until the Bill for better regulating and governing the Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, upon the River of Thames, between Gravesend and Windsor, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, their Agents, or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if thpy think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bjll, against the said Petition.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly to express to His Majesty the peculiar Satisfaction with which His Majesty's faithful Commons have always contemplated that Security which His Majesty's Subjects possess of applying, in the last Resort, to His Majesty's Justice and Mercy:

His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave to represent to His Majesty, that His Royal Clemency is called forth and exercised, with peculiar Propriety, in Cases where there may be just Reason to doubt either the strict Legality or the sound Discretion which should always dictate the Sentence of a Court of Justice:

That if, within the Limits of British Jurisdiction, such a Case shall have arisen, His Majesty's faithful Commons think it their bounden Duty humbly to call His Majesty's Royal Attention and Consideration to it, that His Majesty may, with that Benignity which distinguishes His Character, extend His Mercy and Justice to those who suffer under it:

His Majesty's faithful Commons, deeply impressed with these Considerations, beg Leave humbly to represent to His Majesty, that, on the 30th and 31st of August 1793, Thomas Muir, Esquire, by the De-Vo l. 4g.

signation of Thomas Muir, Esquire, Younger, of Huntershill, was tried, before the High Court of Justiciary at Edinburgh, for certain Crimes and Offences, corresponding to those Crimes and Offences which, by the Law of England, are denominated Misdemeanors: That the said Thomas Muir, being found guilty by the Verdict of a Jury, was sentenced and adjudged, by the Court, to be transported beyond Seas for the Term of Fourteen Years, and to suffer Death, as in Cases of Felony, without Benefit of Clergy, if he should be found at large in Great Britain within the said Term:

His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave further to represent to His Majesty, that the Prosecution against the said Thomas Muir did originate in the said High Court of Justiciary, which is the highest Court of Criminal Judicature in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland-, and they beg Leave further humbly to represent, that it has been determined by the House of Lords, in its Judicial Capacity, that there can be no Review, by any superior Tribunal, of the Judgments or Sentences of the said Court:

That His Majesty's faithful, Commons, having taken the Circumstances here set forth, and the Case of the said Thomas Muir, into their most serious Consideration, beg Leave humbly, but earnestly, to represent to His Majesty, that great and serious Doubts have been excited, by the Proceedings and Sentence in the said Cause, touching the Legality of the same, and that such Doubts have extended themselves, and do still exist, in the Minds of His Majesty's faithful Commons. That the Crime for which the said Thomas Muir was indicted, and of which he is found Guilty, is a Crime known in the Law of Scotland under the Appellation of Leasing-making, which Crime of Leasing-making is defined and understood, in the Law of that Country, to be, uttering Words, or publishing Matter, tending to breed Discord between the Ring and His People. That, by a Statute passed in the Parliament of Scotland in the Fourth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act " anent (concerning) Leasing-making and Slanders," it is enacted, " That whereas the Crimes thereinmentioned" [meaning the Crimes mentioned in certain recited Acts of Parliament against ]

" are made Capital, and punishable by Death and " Confiscation, and that the said Laws have been " liable to Stretches, and that, in respect of the " Generality, and the various Constructions which " the same may admit, they may be, as to the " aforesaid Capital Punishment, of dangerous Consequence; doth therefore, with Advice and Consent of the Estates of Parliament, abrogate and " annul, in all Time coming, the foresaid Sanction " and Pain of Death and Confiscation contained in the said Act: And statutes and ordains, that the " Punishment of the Crimes therein-mentioned shall, " for hereafter, only be arbitrary, according to the " Demerit of the Transgressor, that is, by Fining " Imprisonment, or Banishment; if the Party Offender " be poor, and not able to pay a Fine, then to be " punished in his Body, Life and Limb always preserved

Yet the said Court, in respect of the Verdict against the said Thomas Muir, ordered and adjudged, " The " said Thomas Muir to be transported beyond Seas,

" to such Place as His Majesty, with the Advice of " His Privy Council shall declare and appoint, and " that for the Space of Fourteen Years from that Date; " with Certification to him, if, after being transported, " he shall return to, and be found at large within, any " Part of Great Britain, during the said Fourteen Years,

" without some lawful Cause, and be thereof lawfully convicted, he shall suffer Death, as in Cases " of Felony, without Benefit of Clergy, by the Law of " England:"

" whereas the Crimes therein mentioned" [meaning the Crimes mentioned in certain recited Acts of Parliament against Leasing-making] " are made Capital, and

" punishable by Death and Confiscation, and that " the said Laws have been liable to Stretches, and " that, in respect of the Generality, and the various " Constructions which the same may admit, they may " be, as to the aforesaid Capital Punishment, of dangerous Consequence; doth therefore, with Advice and Consent of the Estates of Parliament, abrogate and annul, in all Time coming, the aforesaid Sanction and Pain of Death and Confiscation contained " in the said Act: And statutes, and ordains, that " the Punishment of the Crimes therein mentioned " shall, for hereafter, only be arbitrary, according to " the Demerit of the Transgressor, that is, by Fining,

" Imprisonment, or Banishment; if the Party Offender be poor, and not able'to pay a Fine, then " to be punished in his Body, Life and Limb always " preserved:"

Yet the said Court, in respect of the Verdict against the said Thomas Fyshe Palmer, ordered and adjudged,

" The said Thomas Fyshe Palmer be transported beyond Seas, to such Place as His Majesty, with the " Advice of His Privy Council, shall declare and appoint, and that for the Space of Seven Years from " that Date; with Certification to him, if, after being " transported, he shall return to, and be found at large " withiD, any Part of Great Britain during the said " Fourteen Years, without some lawful Cause, and be " thereof lawfully convicted, he shall suffer Death, as in " Cases of Felony, without Benefit of Clergy, by the " Law of England:"

His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave humbly Vol. 49,

to represent, That the Punishment, inflicted by the said Sentence on the said Thomas Fyshe Palmer, seems to them greatly to exceed, in Severity, that which is appropriated to his Offence by the above-mentioned Statute of Queen Anne, in as much as the Sentence inflicts the Punishment of Transportation, and that for a Period of Seven years, with Certification of Death if he returns; while the Statute annuls the Pain of Death, and substitutes that of Fining, Imprisonment, and Banishment, under which Term of Banishment a Sentence of Transportation cannot he lawfully included:

His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave farther humbly to represent, that great Public Mischief and Private Oppression being the necessary Result of all such Stretches of Penal Law, it hecame the Duty of His Majesty's faithful Commons humbly to represent the same to His Majesty, that His Majesty may, in His Wisdom and Justice, avert the Evils likely to arise therefrom:

And His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave further humbly to represent to His Majesty, that, independent of the preceding Consideration, there are strong Reasons to induce His Majesty to extend His Royal Clemency to the said Thomas Fyshe Palmer; because, even if the Law of Scotland vested the Judges with the Discretion of passing the Judgment which they have pronounced, that Judgment seems to His Majesty's faithful Commons, upon a due Consideration and Comparison of similar Coses, to exceed the Bounds of that sound. Discretion which all Courts of Justice ought to exercise in Discharge of that most important Part of their Duty, the Infliction of arbitrary Punishment; in as much as the Punishment of Transportation for Seven Years, with Certification of Death if the Party should return, appears to he greatly dis-proportioned to the Offence, which amounts only to a Misdemeanor, and is greatly aggravated by the humiliating Circumstances attending the Transportation to the Place to which the said Thomas Fyshe Palmer is to be sent, and the Misery with which his Residence there must be attended:

His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave humbly to represent to His Majesty, that the Law of England admits of no such Punishment as Transportation for such an Offence, the ordinary Punishment of which is Fine or Imprisonment; and that it maybe attended with very pernicious Consequences, to have one Measure of Punishment for Crimes against the State or Government in one Part ,of the Island, and another in the other, whilst the same Executive and Legislative Government extends equally to both: And His Majesty's faithful Commons beg Leave humbly to represent, that, in the Consideration of the Punishment of such Crimes, the Measure of Punishment in England might have formed a sound and unerring Guide for the Decision of the Court of Justiciary in the Exercise of their Discretion:

That His Majesty's faithful Commons, under the Circumstances here represented, can only have Recourse to the Royal Lenity and Justice to secure Efficacy to the Law of England, and to mitigate the Severity of that of Scotland:

Under these Impressions, His Majesty's faithful Commons do most /earnestly implore His Majesty tp take into.His Royal Deliberation the various Matters herein humbly get forth; and, in Consideration thereof, -graciously to exercise His Royal Mercy towards the said Thomas Fyshe Palmer, by relieving him from the Severity of the Sentence under which he now labours;

It passed in the Negative.

Sir John Thorold reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Noblemen, and the humble Petition of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, interested in the Navigation of the River Welland, in the County of Lincoln, and also on Behalf of themselves and others, Owners and Occupiers of Land in the several Parishes of Spalding, Pinchbeck,

Gosberton, Sutterton, Fosdyke, and Quadring, and in certain Places called Quadring Hundred, Deeping inclosed Fen, Deeping Common, Crowland Common, otherwise Goggushland, Cowbitt Common, Langtoft Common, Boston Common,- Spalding Common, and Pinchbeck Common, and also of other Lands, called Cowbitt Wash, and Crowland Fodder Lots and Wash, all in the said County of Lincoln, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Navigation and Drainage Bills, and to Bills -for building Bridges, had been complied with; and that the Committee nad examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. George Maxwell being examined, said, That the Outfall of the Waters of the River Welland is very defective, and the Navigation thereby is much impeded, occasioned principally by the Channel or Bed of the River being too wide, between a certain Place called Shepherd's Hole, in the said Parish of Surfleet, and the Junction of the Waters of the said River Welland with the Waters of the River Witham, in the said County; and that certain Parts of the said Fen Lands, Low Grounds, and Marshes, are subject to be Overflowed by the Downfall of Rain thereon, and also by Upland Waters, and are greatly injured by the said Downfall and Upland Waters not having a proper Passage to the Sea: — And being further examined, he said, That in order effectually to improve and assist the Drainage of the said Lands, and to amend the said Navigation, it is necessary that the present Channel of the said River Welland should be cleansed, from a certain Place called The Reservoir, to the said Hole,

and that a Dam should be made across the said Channel, and a new River or Cut, of sufficient Dimensions to afford a free Passage for the Waters draining from the said Lands, and to answer the Purposes of Navigation, should be made to commence below the said Shepherd's Hole, and to continue from thence, down to IVyberton Roads, in the Parish of Wyberton, in the said County, between the Port of Boston, and a certain Place called Boston Scalp; and that for the Convenience of Passengers, it is necessary that a Bridge should be built over tile said New River or Cut, at or near Fosdyke Inn, in the said Parish of Fosdyke.

And the Witness added, That, by Levels and Surveys lately taken and made, it appears, that a Cut or River as above described, may be made, and that the making thereof, with such other Works as may be found requisite to attain the Ends above described, would be highly Vol. 49.

beneficial to the Owners and Occupiers of the Lands in the Places above specified, and would tend greatly to promote the Trade and Commerce of the Town of Spalding, in the said County, and of the adjacent Country; and that the Expence of making such a Cut or River, and other Works, and also of budding the said Bridge, may with great Ease and Convenience be provided for by Means of a Tax upon the Lands to be benefited by the said Cut and Works, aided by a certain Tonnage or Duty on Goods, Wares, ana Merchandizes navigated on the said Cut or River, and by a Toll to be taken for Passengers, Cattle, and Carriages, passing over the said Bridge.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for improving the Outfall of the River Welland, in the County of Lincoln, and for the better Drainage of the Fen Lands, Low Grounds, and Marshes, discharging their Waters through the same into the Sea, and for altering and improving the Navigation of the said River Welland, by Means of a new Cut, to commence below a certain Place, called The Reservoir, and to be carried from thence, through the inclosed Marshes, and Open Salt Marshes, into Wyberton Roads, betweep the Port of Boston and a Place called The Scalp*, and for disposing of the Bare or White Sands adjoining to the said River, and for building a Bridge over the said Cut:

And that Sir John Thorold and Mr. Vyner do prepare, and bring in, the same. ‘

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the River Trent Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by virtue of an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, a Legal Quay has been made at the Port of Kingston upon Hull, with a Dock large enough to receive the Shipping trading to the Port at that Time, but, in Consequence of the great Increase of Trade and Shipping which has since taken place, the said Dock has become greatly insufficient for the Accommodation thereof, and the Trade of the Country is much injured by the want of Dock Room at the said Port; and that not only an Extension of the Wet Dock at Hull, but also an Entrance thereinto direct from the River Humber, is absolutely necessary, the present Passage to the Dock and Quay, through the long narrow River or Haven of Hull, being frequently blocked up by the Ships to and from Foreign Voyages, Coastwise, River Craft, and Rafts of Timber, so that Goods sent down for Exportation, as well as all imported Goods, frequently meet with the most disadvantageous Delay thereby; and that the Petitioners have been informed, that a Bill is intended to be brought into the House for Relief in the Premises: And therefore praying, That the House will take into Consideration the present Restriction, Loss, and Delay, hereby occasioned to the Trade and Manufacture connected with the Port of Hull, and especially to the Trade carried on upon the said River Trent, which communicates with the said Port, and to grant such Relief as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Report Wool- A/TR. Bastard reported from the Committee, to combers Pe- XVA whom foe several Petitions presented to this tit'on. House in this Session of Parliament from the Wool-combers, complaining of certain Machines constructed for the combing of Wool, were refemd; That the Committee had examined the Matter of foe said Petitions, and had directed him to report foe same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report In his Place$ and afterwards delivered k m at

the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followefo; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Daniel Baker being examined, said. He is a Wool-comber, and lives at Exeter, and was brought up to the Trade. — And being asked, Whether it was customary for Persons brought up in that Trade to serve an Apprenticeship? he said, Yes, for Seven Years; and that foe eldest Son of a Woolcorober is entitled to learn the Trade of his Father, without being regularly bound. — And being asked, Whether the Trade required Seven Years Apprenticeship? he said, He conceived it did, to do the Master justice. — And being asked, Whether a Boy who is brought up to the Combing Branch of the W'oollen Manufactory can turn hie Hand to any of the other Branches ? he said, No; he serves an Apprenticeship to that, and to no other Branch, and cannot turn his Hand, or get his Bread, in any other. — And being asked, Whether there was any Regulation among the Woolcombers, with respect to the Number of Apprentices taken? he said, No limited Regulation. — And being asked, What had been the Usage5 he said, Two was the general Rule; the Reason was, to prevent the Trade being overstocked with Hands. — And being asked, Whether he could form any Idea what Number of Hands were employed in the County of he

said, He could not. — -And being asked, Whether he ever saw One of those Machines mentioned in the Petitions? he said, He had, and it was worked by Water. — And being asked, How many Hands were employed in foe Combing of foe Wool? he said, One Man, and Four or Five Children; he saw it at Work, and it appeared to him to be folly employed. — And being asked, Whether he cquld form any Judgment what Quantity of Work might be done by that Machine in any given Time ? he said, As much as Thirty Men could do: The Machine he saw was at Twertom, neat Bath; and that there is great Difficulty in seeing those Machines. — And,

William Eales being examined, said, That he is a WqoleQB&ber, and lives at Plymouth; and was brought up to the Trade by a regular Apprenticeship. — And being asked, Whether there had been any Machines brought into his Neighbourhood? he said, He had seen One at Twer ton, and that he worked at the Combing Trade at Twerton, with the same Master to whom the Machine belonged; it was worked by Water, and that Eleven Children, and One Man as Overseer, were employed at it; the Children were Boys and Girls, some Nine Years of Age, and the oldest about Sixteen; Eleven were employed by Day, and Seven by Night; and that Two Parts of the Machine are necessarily employed double the Space of Time foe Third is, which is foe Reason of their working at Night. — And being asked, Whether any other Men were employed at these Machines ? he said, No, none employed hut as Overseers; he bed Four of his own Children employed at this Manufactory, and that One of them was occasionally employed at foe Machine. — And being asked. What Quantity of Wool the Machine would work within the How? he said, When it went through the last Frame, the finishing' Frames it would clear out Eighteen Pounds an Hour; he had seen a great deal after it came out of foe Frame, and it was worked nearly as well as if it was worked by Hands, in foe old Way. — And being asked. How long a good Workman in the Woolcombing Trade would be* in completely working and finishing off Eighteen Pounds of Wool? he said. Thirty Hours, for One of the best Hands; whe*d there is One can do it in that Time, there are Ten cannot, and that it was very hard Work: And foe Witness said, That a Boy^must have served a great Part of his Time before he is able to be put to the Combs. — And being asked, When he saw the Machine ok Twerton ? he- said,

8 Just

34 Geo. III. 13 M 323

Just before last Whitsuntide. — And being asked, How he

came to go from Plymouth to Tuxrton? ne said, To seek Work; and that he was employed by Mr. Samuel Paul Bamford; and that there was no Machine there when he first went; that Mr. Bamford had a large Trade, and that he, the Witness, thought himself settled there for some Time, and took a House, and sent for his Family from Plymouth. — And being asked, Whether it is usual to go from Place to Place to seek for Employment? he said, It was, and that their Clubs or^ Societies subsist them till they get Work. Mr. Bamford had Twenty Hands when lie first went, and told him he should have Employment for Sixty or Seventy Hands in the Course of a few Months: He, the Witness, went to settle at Twe)'ton last December Twelvemonth. — And being asked, Whether Mr. Bamford did employ that additional Number of Hands that he said he should ? he said, No; Mr. Bamford went into the North, and at his Return, instead of employing an additional Number, as he said he should, he turned all off, except Seven, and that he was One of those Seven; and that Six out of the Seven had Families, which were employed in the Manufactory; and that about Six Weeks after the Dismissal of those Persons the Machine came, and was set to Work about the latter End of February 1793.- — And being asked, What Sort of Wool was worked in that Machine? he said, English Wool; that they work the same Wool by that Machine as they do by Hand, called Combing Wool, and no other; he did not know whether it would work any other Kind of Wool, but at the Time he knew it no other than the Long Combing Wool was worked by it — Aijd being asked, Whether the Societies support the Woolcomtiers when out of Work? he said, Yes; he knew they did in the Counties of Somerset and Devon. — And being asked, Whether there are any Number of Wool-combers who do not belong to the Societies ? he said, There are some, but not One out of One hundred that does not belong to sprue Society. — And being asked, Whether the Children are discharged from the Combing Machine when they arrive at the Age of Seventeen or Eighteen? he said, Yes; they must be, because the Benefit of the Machine depends upon being worked by Children. — -'And being asked, How he was employed during the Time he continued with Mr. Bamford after he brought the Machine ? he said, In combing Wool in the common Way, as likewise the other Six Persons before-mentioned; he was turned away by the Engineer; he knows there are Three of the Six mentioned still employed there in the common Way. — And,

Mr. Joseph Jennings being examined, said, He is a Worsted Manufacturer, and lives in the City of London; he knows the different Sorts of Wool used in this Country, and that there is a Sort of Wool called Long Wool, that is selected from the Short for the sole Purpose of being combed. — And being asked, Whether that Wool is selected from Wool the Growth of this Country? he said, Yes; that there is some Wool imported, but it is not strong enough for combing; besides, it is so dear, it would not answer the Purpose; that there is nothing but English Wool combed, for Foreign Wools would not answer. — And being asked, What has been the Effect of the Machines already erected upon the Woolcombipg Business? he said, He went to a Woolstapler's last January to ask the Price of Wools, and he (the Woolstapler) asked him a Price which he thought too deat'; the Reply was, that be bad unlimited Orders for any Quantity from Davis and Hawxky's for these Machines: He (the Witness) went into, the Warehouse, and was shewn, different Sorts of Wool that was then throwing oven for that Machine, and that all the best and prime was Wool picked from the Fleeces. — And being asked, What Quantity of Noyle would be produced from Vol. 49.

Twelve Pounds of Wool ? he said, He could not answer to a Certainty, but on the Average about Three Quarters of a Pound. — And being asked, Whether any other but English Wool is fit for the Purpose of Combing ? he said, No; he had tried other, but it did not answer; that which he tried, he believed, came from Germany. — And being asked, Whether he ever tried the Foreign Wool mixed with the English Wool? he said, No; but the Price of Foreign Wool is so dear that it would not answer. — And being asked, What Sort of Articles in the Woollen Manufactory must necessarily be made of the Combing Wool ? he said, Sagathies, Duroy plain, Duroy figured, Draughts, Estamanes, Shalloons, Serge plain, Tamies, Poplins, Lastings, Bombazines, Bombazette, Callimanco, Har-ratines, Stuff Damask, Barragon, Camblets, Satti-nette, Crapes, English Shawls, Moncriefs, Russells, Buntings, Grograms, Carpeting, Worsted Plush, Worsted Hose, Worsted Fringe, Lace and Bindings, Worsted Crewels, Drugetts, Rackers, Long Ells, German Serge, Sanfords, Frays, Coarse Eus, and Baize. — And being asked, Whether those Articles were for Home or Foreign Consumption ? he said, Both; the light Goods go to Russia and , and great

Quantities to The East Indies, sent by the Company. — And being asked, Whether any of those Articles are made in Foreign Countries? he said, They imitate them, but the Quality of their Wool being inferior to the English, they cannot make them nearly so good,

no Place in the World can come near to it; and that Goods of these Sorts are preferred to others of the same Kind made in any Country whatever, and that in Times of Peace there is a very great Demand for those Ar-tides for Foreign Markets; and that the Demand, is so great, that the Produce of Wool is not sufficient to supply it. — And being asked, What is the Consequence to the Woolcombers when the English Wool is worked up in each Year? he said, The Combers are out of Employ. — And,

John Osmond being examined, said, He is a Serge Maker, and lives at Tiverton in Devonshire, and served Seven Years Apprenticeship to the Business of a Wool-comber, before he commenced Serge Maker; and that there are Annually, Two or Three Months before Shearing Time, great Numbers of Woolcombers, apply to his House for Employ, by Means of the Scarcity of Wool. — And,

William Eales being again examined, he was asked, Whether whilst he was employed at Mr. s,

he was constantly employed after the Erection of the Machine? he said, No; but constantly before; and that he has frequently been still when the Machine was employed, there not being Wool enough to employ both. — And, .

Jonathan Sowtonbeing examined, said, That he is aWoolcomber, and lives at Exeter. — And being asked, What Assistance a Woolcomber derives from his Family? he said, When a Child is Seven Years old, he is capable of assisting his Father in some Shape to prepare the Wool for nis Father to comb, and may get about Two Pence per Day, and so progressively, till the Age of Fourteen; and then, if strong and healthy, is capable of beginning to work as his Father does. — And,

through, or near, which a Navigable Cut or Canal is intended to be made and maintained from the River Kennet, at or near the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Awn, at or near the City of Bristol, and a Navigable Branch or Cut from, or out of, the said Canal, in the Parish of Rowd, near Devizes, in the County of Wilts, to, or near, the Town of Caine, in the said County, and also a Navigable Branch or Cut from, or out of, the said last mentioned Branch qr Cut, to, or near, the Town of Chippenham, in the said County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners find that the projected Line or Level of the said Canal and Branches is intended to be carried through, or near, several Water Mills, Rivers, Streams, Watercourses, Water Meadows, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in the said Counties of Wilts and Somerset, and the Petitioners, or some of them, are the Owners and Occupiers of the said several Water Mills, Rivers, and Streams, which are very valuable, and are so situate that the Petitioners have great Reason to apprehend that it is not practicable to make and maintain the said intended Canal and Branches, according to the Line and Level proposed without taking and intercepting most of the Sources and Springs of the said Rivers and Streams which supply their Mills with Water, and by that Means deprive them of their usual and necessary Supply; and that the Petitioners, or Borne of them, are likewise the Owners and Occupiers of large Tracts of Meadow Ground usually called Water Meadpws, through, or near, which the Line or Level of the said Canal is intended to pass, which are -almost constantly watered or flooded by the Springs and Streams of Water arising within, or near, the said Meadows, by which Means the said Meadows are made of great Value to the Owners and Occupiers thereof, and of great Public Utility; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive that the intended Line of the said Canal and Branches cannot be made and maintained without taking and diverting all, or many, of the said Springs and Streams of Water from the said Meadows into the said Canal and Branches, by which Means the said Meadows and other Lands and Property of the Petitioners will be very greatly reduced in their Value, and thereby great Prejudice must ensue to the Public, by Reason that, after the said Springs and Streams are diverted by the said Canal from the said Meadows, they will be newly or totally, destroyed as Water Meadows, and the several Arable, Pasture, and Down or Uplands, which lie contiguous to* and are held with, the said Meadows, will be also greatly reduced in Value, as the Produce of the Meadows, chiefly arising, from the watering the same, is now the great, and almost only, Dependance of the Fanner and Occupier for the depasturing of his Sheep and Cattle in the Spring Season, and by the Loss or Decrease of such Produce, the Breed of Sheep, now so considerable in the Farms and Lands in Question, must be lessened in a very great Degree, if nqfc totally destroyed, and, by the same Means, the Farmer and Occupier will he deprived of the present valuable Manure arising from the Flocks, of Sheep, which Manure is one. of the great Sources of the plentiful Crops of Corn, derived from the Arable Lands, now held with, the said Water Meadows; and that the Lands of the Petitioners, through which the said Canal is intended to pass, consist of so deep and tender a Soil that it will be almost impossible with any number of Bridges, especially in Wet Harvests, for the Farmers or Occupiers of such Lands to carry their Corn out of their present Fields, held with, such Meadows, and therefore they will be obliged, with great Loss, and Inconvenience, to Rick their. Com upon the Spot; and that such of; the Petitioners, whose Estates will be affected by

that part of the line of the said Canal proposed to run near Devizes, think they have great Reason to complain of the very short Notice given of a Measure so injurious to them by the Promoters of the Canal in Question, who, for several Years past, fixed on, and gave Notice of, a different Line, and only altered the same, and adopted the last mentioned Cut h few Months ago, by which Means it could not, till very lately, be known by the Petitioners last mentioned, or many of them, how materially they would be injured, and they now apprehend, and are advised by skilful and able Surveyors, that it is impossible for them to ascertain the Extent of their Damages, unless Surveys could be taken at different Seasons of the Year, though they are well assured and convinced, that such Damages must be very great, and many of their Farms in one of the finest Corn Countries, by the making of the said Canal, will be irreparably injured, and the Losses of the Petitioners may fairly be considered not only in a private but in a public Point of View, inasmuch as the Growth of Corn must be much diminished, as well as the Flocks of Sheep and other Cattle decreased, and thereby consequently many poor Labourers be deprived of Employment; and that the Petitioners also conceive, that exclusive of the very serious and important Losses which they will sustain from the Causes aforesaid, their respective Arable, Meadow, and Pasture Lands, through which the said Canal will pass, will greatly suffer, and be much lessened in Value, as well by many of their Lands being intersected and disjointed, as by the Loss of valuable Tracts of Land in a fertile Country, owing to the Cuts proposed to be made for the said Canal, and the numerous new Roads which must be made on such Lands: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem just and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Dock Company at Kingston upon Hull, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act* passed in the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for making and establishing " public Quays or Wharfs at Kingston upon Hull, for " the better securing His. Majesty's Revenues of Customs, and for the Benefit of Commerce in the Port " of Kingston upon Hull, and for making a Bason or " Dock, with Reservoirs, Sluices, Roads, and other " Works, for the Accommodation of Vessels using the " said Port, and for appropriating certain Lands " belonging to His Majesty, and for applying certain " Sums of Money out of His Majesty's Customs at the " said Port for those Purposes, and for establishing " other necessary Regulations within the Town ana " Port of Kingston upon Hull," the Petitioners were incorporated by the Name of " The Dopk, Company " at Kingston upon Hull," and were thereby empowered and required to make a Bason or Dock to extend, from the River Hull, to a certain Place in the Town of Kingston upon Hull, called The Beverley Gales, as described in the said Act, and also a Quay or Wharf of a sufficient and convenient Length, for the Trade and Business of the said Town and Port, and, in Consideration of the great Charges and Expences of making the said Bason, Quay, and other Works, and of maintaining the same in' future, certain, Rates or Duties on Shipping as mentioned in the said Act, were thereby granted to and vested in the Petitioners, the said Dock Company, as their own proper Monies* and to and for their own proper Use and Benefit; for the Purposes aforesaid; and that, although the Time limited by the Act, for the Completion of the Works* was Seven Years from the 31 Bt Day of December 1774; yet, by the great Industry and; Exertions of the Peti*-tioners, the same were completed, as appears by-the Report of‘various Engineers, within Five Years, to the great Accommodation of the Trade of the Port, and the Benefit of His Majesty's Revenue; and that the Petitioners have seen a Bill depending in the House to compel the Dock Company to make, at their sole Expence, other Works than those which the said recited Act required them to execute, which Bill, if passed into a Law, would be subversive of the Rights of the Petitioners, and highly injurious to their Interest, by 'laying on them, the heavy Burthen of making additional Works beyond those which the Petitioners were, by the said Act, bound to perform, and which they have to the utmost Extent executed; and Representing to the House, that, supposing the additional Works, proposed to be executed by the said Bill, are necessary for the Accommodation of the Trade and' Shipping, of the Port of Hull, the Petitioners conceive they are not compellable to execute the same, and that they ap-' prehend the Corporation of, the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull are in the Possession of certain Funds, which are applicable. to the Execution of such additional Works, ,or certain Parts thereof: And therefore praying That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for extending the Dock and Quay at the Town and Port of Kingston upon Hull, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same.Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for the Encouragement of the Exportation of Culm to Lisbon, in the Kingdom of " Portugal,'' which was to continue in Force from and after the 2.5th Day of March 1758 for and during the Term of Fifteen Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, was amended and further continued until the 25th Day of March 1793, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intjtuled, " An Act for making Allowances to the Dealers in " Foreign Wines, for the Stock of certain Foreign " Wines in their Possession, at a certain Time, upon " which the Duties on Importation have been paid,

MR. Poulett reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset, under their Common Seal; and also, the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset, under their Common Seal, 'were severally

referred; That the Committee had examined, ana found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for building Bridges, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. Robert Codrington being examined, said, That the present Bridge over the River Parrett, is very ancient, and the Passage over the same very narrow and incommodious, and many fatal Accidents have been occasioned thereby. — That by reason of the present decayed State of the said Bridge, and the Quays on the said River, it is become necessary that the said Bridge should be re-built, and the Whole rendered more safe and commodious: — And that it is also necessary that proper Regulations should be established, and Powers given for ascertaining and enforcing the Payment of the Quay Dues payable at the Port of the said Borough, and for enabling the Petitioners to claim and receive such additional Duties as, with the present Dues, may be sufficient to defray the Expence of erecting the said new Bridge, and of keeping the same, with the Quays, in Repair.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, the Witness said, That it would be of Advan-r tage to the Trade carried on at the said Port, if Powers were given to regulate the Moorings and Stations of Ships and Vessels, resorting to, and remaining in, the said Port.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a new Bridge over the River Parrett, within the Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset, and for repairing and maintaining the Quays in the Port of Bridgewater aforesaid, and for more effectually collecting and enforcing the Payment of the ancient and accustomed Duties, and for imposing certain new Duties at the said Port, and for regulating the Moorings and Stations of Ships and Vessels Vol. 49.

in the said. Port: And that Mr. Poulett and Mr. Langston do prepare, and bring in, the sante.

A Petition of the Woolcombers of the City of Durham Durham, was presented to the House, and read; Set- Woolcomber* ting forth, That the Petitioners are greatly alarmed Pet, tion-by the Introduction of a newly invented Machine for combing of Wool, and entertain just Fears that themselves and Families will speedily become a heavy Burthen to the State, it appearing to the Petitioners that One Machine only, with the Assistance of One Person and Four or Five Children, will perform as much Labour as Thirty Men in the customary Manual Manner: And therefore praying, That, from the peculiar Hardship of their Situation, and the melancholy Prospect before them, the House will grant them such Relief as the Exigency of their Case may appear to require.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Company of Proprietors of the Canal Navigation from Leeds to Liverpool to vary the Line of the said Canal Navigation, to raise a further Sum of Money for completing the same, and to amend an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of King George the First, for making the River Douglas, alias Asland, navigable from the River Rib-ble to Wigan, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and another Act, passed in the Tenth Year of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining the said Canal Navigation; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the Utility of all Canals, do not oppose the Principle of the said Application, but object to the Execution of so much of the proposed deviating Line as, in the -Map of Reference, lies between certain Places called Heapy Chapel and Hall, in the said County, it appearing to them to be unnecessary that Two separate Canals should be made so near each other in the said Place, when One will fully answer the Purpose of both; and that the Petitioners have been very lately informed, and believe, that die Proprietors of the Lancaster Canal have proposed to allow the Vessels, navigating on the deviated Line, to lock into, and go out of, the Lancaster Canal at the Places aforesaid, with such Provisions as may prevent Loss of Water, or any Cause of Dispute between the Two Companies, and that such Navigation shall be free from all Tonnage, or other Demand, either on Account of making or keeping in Repair so much of the said Line on which they may so navigate, and the Petitioners submit their Opinion that such an Offer is fair and just, and ought to be accepted or enforced: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against the passing of so much of the said Bill as enables the said Company of Proprietors of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal to make the said deviated Line from, or near, Heapy Chapel to Kirklees Hall aforesaid, and that a Junction and Communicable Navigation may take Place between the Two Canals in the Places aforesaid,

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Pepys and Mr. Ord: ,

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enable the Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland further to increase the Capital Stock of the said Company; without any Amendment; And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Christopher Brunswick; without anyAmendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing certain Moors, Commons, and Waste Lands, lying and being within the Parishes of Chappie Allerton, Biddisham, and Wear, in the County of Somerset; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making certain Navigable Cuts from the Towns of Buckingham, Aylesbury, and Wendover, in the County of Buckingham, to communicate with The Grand Junction Navigation, authorized to be made by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, and for amending the said Act; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting the Estate at Little Woodhouse, in the County of York, devised by the Will of Jeremiah Harrison, Gentleman, deceased, in Trustees, to sell the same, and apply the Money to arise by such Sale in the Purchase of other Lands or Hereditaments, to be settled in Lieu thereof; to which the Lords desire the Con* currence of this House.

Mr. Thomas Stanley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Henrietta Maria Atherton, of Atherton Hall, in the Parish of Leigh, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, Spinster, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and, that the House might be the better enabled more fully to understand the Circumstances of the Case, the Committee had directed him to report specially the Minutes of the Evidence taken before them; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: and the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. William Rawstorne, Son of Lawrence storne, Esquire, Guardian to Miss Atherton, cajled in, and examined.

Were you at Atherton when Mr. Mason came there to ask Miss Atherton her Consent to the Lancaster Canal Bill?

I was.

Do you recollect at what Time?

About the 2 2d of January last.

Was you present when any Message was delivered to Miss Atherton, intimating that a Person was waiting to see her?

I was — Miss Atherton's Servant came in, and said that Mr. Mason, the Solicitor to the Lancaster Canal Bill, was come for her Answer, and that he was sent by Mr. Rawstorne; Miss Atherton said, " I do not

" like to go into the Room; but as Mr. Rawstorne has " sent him, I will go;" and desired Mrs. Rawstorne to follow her.

Did Miss Atherton then leave the Room, and did Mrs. Rawstorne and yourself follow her ?

Miss Atherton went into the Drawing Room, and we almost immediately followed her.

Who did you find there ?

Mr. Mason and Miss Atherton.

Relate what passed in your Hearing?

When we came into the Room, Mr. Mason had just shewed the Plan of the Canal to Miss Atherton, and he opened it again, and shewed it to Mrs. Rawstorne — It appeared from the Plan that the Canal w as to pass over the Lawn. — Miss Atherton said, she did not like it should come across her Lawn. — Mr. Mason assured her it would not come within her Gates. — Mrs. Rawstorne then asked Mr. Mason how far it would come over the Lawn. — Mr. Mason said, Not at all — that when it got to the Steward's House, at Platford, it would take the Course of the Brook towards Penning-, ton. — Miss Atherton then said, if it would not come within her Gates that she would not object to it; and on Mr. Masons assuring her that it would not, she said, he had her Consent.

From what you was a Witness to, do you believe Miss Atherton would have given her Consent to the Canal on any other Consideration than that of its not passing through her Lawn ?

I do believe, from what I understood, that Miss Atherton would never have given any Consent, had she not been repeatedly assured by Mr. , that it would not come within her Gates.

Was not Mr. Mason explaining the Plan to Miss Atherton when you came into the Room ?

The Plan was laying on the Table rolled up — A Plan like the One now produced by Mr. Mason to the Committee.

Did you not hear Mr. Mason ask Miss Atherton if the Lands on the other Side of the Division Fence of the Lawn was not her's; and if he did, what Answer did Miss Atherton give him ?

1 did not hear any such thing, that I recollect.

Were you present at the First Interview between Miss Atherton and Mr. Mason, or did you not come in after Mr. Mason had been in the Room some Time ?

I was not present at her First Interview with Mr. Mason, but it could not have been more than Two Minutes after Miss Atherton had entered the Room. — Mr. Mason had been in the Room some Time before Miss Atherton entered it.

And then the Witness was directed to withdraw.

Lawrence Rawstorne, Esquire, called in, and examined.

Have you not been in the Habits of frequently conversing with Miss Atherton on the Subject of the Lancaster Canal ?

1 have had some Conversations upon the Subject with her.

Was she not uniformly persisting in denying her Consent to it's coming through her Lawn and Avenue ?

At all Times when I have heard her mention the Subject.

Did you not go over to Worsley, prior to any Line being surveyed for the intended Canal, and wishing that Mr. Gilbert would assist you in procuring the Canal to come by Leigh, as you apprehended it would be of very great Benefit to Miss Athertons Estate? — I did.

Did not Mr. Gilbert recommend to you to write to some of the Gentlemen who took an active Part in the Lancaster Canal to that effect; and did you not write to Edward Buckley, Esquire, who was the Chairman of the General Meeting of the Proprietors of the Lancaster Canal, to intimate to the Committee how glad you would be if the Cantd did come by Leigh;

and that the Company should have every Assistance which the Family at Atherton could give them ?

I did write to that Purport; but whether I made use of the Name of the Atherton Family, or engaged only for myself at this Distance of Time I can't recollect.

I was acquainted with that Line by Mr. Hodgkinson but I do not recollect, from the Time I wrote to Mr. Buckley until Mr. Mason called at in Novem-

Yes.

Did not Mr. Mason produce to you the Plan of the Lancaster Canal Extension ?

Yes, he did.

Did you not, at that Time, declare to the Gentlemen who attended upon you, that if the Estate of Miss Atherton was your's, you would not hesitate your Assent to that Plan a Moment?

I made a Declaration to that Purport

Did you not say, that you was sorry to inform the Gentlemen that Miss Atherton would not then assent — that you would take the Plan to her, to try to prevail upon her, and that you would return ai^Answer?

I went Twice or Thrice into the Room where Miss Atherton was, with the Plan, and she positively refused her Assent to it.

Did you not desire Mr. Mason not to press Miss Atherton any more at that Time; but that if he would call again at about Christmas, you was in hopes she might be prevailed upon ?

I did.

Had you any other particular Interest in having the Canal to go by Leigh, than that of being Guardian to Miss Atherton?

No Interest whatever, having no Property in that Neighbourhood.

Was it not your Opinion, and is it not now, that the Canal passing by Leigh would be advantageous to the Estate of Miss Atherton?

I have not now the same favourable Opinion of the Canal, with regard to Miss Atherton's Interest, as I had in November last, when I had' the Conversation with Mr. Mason.

What is your Reason for altering your Opinion?

From a Conversation that passed between Mr. John Gilbert, the Duke of Bridgewater's principal Agent, and Mr. Hodgkinson, Miss Atherton's Steward, in regard to the Carriage of Coals upon the Canal; concerning which Mr. Hodgkinson, being present, can inform the Committee.

Are you not Uncle to Miss Atherton ?

Yes; by Marriage.

Whether it was not understood by you, that Miss Atherton's Servant was not authorized by Mr. Mason to say he came from you ?

I was absent from Atherton at that Time — Miss Atherton, I believe, misunderstood the Message brought by the Servant: She thought that Mr. had

come immediately from me; it was a Misapprehension of her's.
