Mr. Richard Hodgkinson, called in, and examined.

Are you in the Service of Miss Atherton — and in what Capacity ?

Yes; Steward to her.

Has not Atherton Hall long been the Place of Residence of her Ancestors, and does she not now reside there herself?

It has been the Place of Residence of her Ancestors for many Generations, and is now her's.

Is it not a Capital Mansion House, and have not large Sums been expended in ornamenting the Place, by extensive Plantations, and other Improvements ?

It is esteemed a large and Capital Mansion House, finely situated, and her Ancestors must have expended immense Sums of Money in the Improvement of the Place.

Does the Line of the intended Canal cross Miss Atherton's Plantations and Avenue, in the Manner laid down in the Plan now produced by you, and for what Distance, in the View of the House ?-

To the best of my Judgment it does for 8oo Yards, and upwards, across the Avenue, within Sight of the House.

Has Miss Atherton any Land lying between the Outside of her Gates and the Town of Leigh, through which she has any Power to direct the Line of the Canal to pass ?

She has not any, without passing through Gardens and Lands held by Life Leases granted by her late Father.

I once passed by them taking Levels over the artificial

I most certainly can perceive that the Line of the Canal does pass between the Gates and Atherton Hall. — In my former Answer to that Question, I perfectly misunderstood the meaning of the Honourable Gentleman who proposed it — The Question, as I then understood it, was, " Could I perceive, by the Plan, Whether " the Canal was passing through any Avenue or Plea- sure Ground," supposing I had been unacquainted with the Place.

Whether or not there is any Avenue of Trees leading from Leigh to Atherton Hall?

There are no regular Rows of Trees upon the Coach Road.

Does the Line of the Canal, as described in the Plan shewn to you, pass over any part of the Lawn, Avenue, or Pleasure Ground belonging to Miss Atherton ?

Most certainly it does.

Mr. Jackson Mason, Agent for the Lancaster Canal Extension Bill, called in and examined.

When was the First Time you saw Miss,

on the Subject of the Lancaster Canal Extension ?

The First and only Time I ever saw Miss Atherton Was, about the 22d of January last, when I was introduced to her — upon Miss Atherton's coming into the Room I accosted her, by saying, that his Grace the Duke of Bridgewater and the Lancaster Canal Committee were exceedingly sorry to understand from me what Mr. Rawstorne had told me in November, that she had an Objection to the Canal going through her Lawn and Avenue — She told me, that was her only Objection — I told her, we were particularly sorry, because, if the Company had known her Objection in Time, it should have been remedied; and that I had the particular Directions of the Committee to do every Thing that could at that Time be done, to make it satisfactory, to oblige her, and that we did not mind a few Hundred Pounds Expence — I likewise told her, that the First Time I understood what her Objections were, was early in November last, and that immediately upon being informed of them, I had desired Mr. John Gilbert, of Worsley, a Gentleman whom I believed, under the Duke of Bridgewater, was One of the first practical Navigators in this Kingdom, to see if the Line could be altered agreeable to her Wishes — that he had accompanied me upon the Line, and we had found that Alterations might have been made, either by taking the Canal up the Brook, by taking along the Division Fence of the Lawn and Avenue, or by taking it on the Outside of that Fence; and that if she pleased I would shew her, upon the Plan itselfi what we could do to oblige her. — I immediately took out the Planr and traced upon it what I have before-mentioned, which was what might be done with her Assent; but as the Township of Pennington was not inserted in our Gazette Notices, we were obliged to deliver the Plan at the Office of the Clerk of the Peace as it was. — I asked her if the Lands in the Township of Pennington, betwixt the Canal and the Town of Leigh, were her Property, and she told me she believed they were. — I then said, You may have the Canal altered in your Grounds, betwixt the Line of the Canal, as laid down in the Plan, and the Town of Leigh, as you please. — She answered me, that she was much obliged to the Duke of Bridgewater, and the Gentlemen of the Lancaster Committee, for their Attention to her, and she certainly would assent. About this Time, I believe .1 let go the Plan, and it being very strong Paper, it rolled itself up again; and I think, to the best of my Recollection, it was at this Moment of Time that Mr. William Rawstorne, came into the Room with a Lady, whom I did not then know, but whom I conceived to be Mrs. Rawstorne, and I think another young Lady, and another young Gentleman, whom I apprehended to be a Mr. Hornby: I recollect entering into some Conversation with the young Gentleman. In the List of Consents is Miss Atherton described assenting absolutely or conditionally ?

She is described assenting absolutely; for I did not know, and I am yet to learn, if there be any other Method of describing her Assent as given to me.

Was there any other Subject upon which Miss is stated to have given her Assent, except to the Canal passing in the Line described in the Plan to which her Consent is annexed ?

Miss Atherton assented, as I apprehend, to the Plan going into the House of Commons as it was, with Liberty for her to alter the Line in any Manner, between the Canal and her other Lands and Grounds nearer Leigh, as she thinks proper; and I did not intend, in framing the Clause before-mentioned, to prescribe to her the exact Place.

Is that Circumstance, which you have stated as Miss Atherton's, only Objection to the Bill, namely the Canal crossing her Lawn and Avenue, removed by the Line described in the Plan, to which her Consent has been given ?

It is not removed by the Plan, because it was out of my Power to alter the Plan lodged at the Office of the Clerk of the Peace; but I trust it is properly removed by the Bill now brought into the House.

Do you now understand, that the Line of the intended Canal cannot pass on the Outside of Miss Athertons Pleasure Ground, without passing partly over Lands not in the Possession of Miss , ana

the Property, of Persons not included' in the Consent List ?

I do not know whose Property the Grounds on the other Side of the Lawn nearer Leigh is, other than by what Miss Atherton herself told me; but if the Property is Miss Atherton's, be it Houses or Lands, the Company

have no Objection to pay the full Price of such Houses and Lands, in order to carry the Canal entirely clear of her Gates as they now stand.

Do you understand, by the Clause in the Bill to which you have referred, that if Miss Atherton should not be able to direct the Line of the Canal nearer to the Town of Leigh, the Undertakers of the Canal Navigation are empowered to carry the Line of the Canal through the Lawn and Pleasnre Ground without her Consent ? ,

Miss Atherton may carry the Canal, without the Assent of any Body, along the Division Fence of that Lawn, which, in my Opinion, would be doing her the least possible injury, and would be making her a complete Boundary Fence between the Town of Leigh and the Lawn; that the Company do not mean to take any more of her Lawn than they can possibly help; but if Miss Atherton should chuse, upon regular

Application by the Company (should the Act be obtained) to refuse to direct in what Manner the Canal should be carried, then I apprehend the Proprietors would be enabled to make the Canal in the Line laid down in the Plan.

Is the Committee, therefore, to understand that under certain Circumstances, the Powers of this Bill are meant to extend to enable the Company to carry the Line of the Canal through any Part of die Lawn or Pleasure Ground of Miss Atherton?

I apprehend that the latter Part of my last Answer has fully answered that Question, that they might.

Do you mean to state that Miss Atherton has given her Consent to a Plan, that, under any possible Circumstances, would authorize the U ndertakers of the Canal to carry it through her Lawn and Avenue ?

I apprehend she has, if she does not chuse to make her Election.

Can she make her Election, if any Part of the Ground

belongs to any other Persons not included in the Lists of Consents ?

She cannot, I apprehend, carry the Canal into any other Person's Grounds; but she may very materially alter the Line of the Canal, as now laid down in the Plan, without any Body's Assent.

Can she do it so as not to go through any Part of her Pleasure Grounds ?

She may do it, as I said before, so as to make it a Boundary to her Pleasure Ground; and I do not know that the Ground on the opposite Side of the Fence is any Body's Property, but her own.

Do you know that it is her own ?

She told me that she believed it was her own.

Can you say, that at the Time you applied to Miss Atherton for her Assent, and held the Conversation about the Variation of the Line, that you did not know the Lands nearer to Leigh were not let upon Leases for Lives ?

I did not know any Thing about Miss Athertons Lands, but what she told me; for, till the Time I went to Leigh in November, I had never been in that Neighbourhood in my Life to my Knowledge; and the Second Time that I was there, was on the 2 2d of January.

Will you say that you did not know, or do not now know, that these Lands were let upon Leases for Lives, when the Bill was presented to Parliament, and which of course must prevent Miss Atherton having the Direction of the altered Line of the Navigation ?

No otherwise than from what I gathered from Mr. Rawstome upon his Examination before this Committee.

You having stated, that on the 2zd of January you had a Conversation with Miss , in which she

gave her verbal Assent to the Canal passing within her Fence, under certain Conditions, which you have stated at large in the former Part of your Evidence; and you having stated, that no Person was present when Mass Atherton gave such verbal Assent — inform the Committee, whether you made any Minute of the Conversation that passed between you and Miss Atherton at that Time ?

I made no Minute of the Conversation that passed betwixt Miss Atherton and me, on the 22d of January.

Did any Conversation pass between you and Miss Atherton in the Presence of any other Person on that Dav?

After Mr. William Rawstome and his Mother came into the Room, the Conversation, very like that which he has stated to the Committee, passed, save that the Words made use of were, to the best of my Recollection, " Lawn and Avenue " — in other Respects he was very accurate as to what passed.

How long did the private Conversation between you and Miss Atherton continue ?

I cannot exactly say as to the Time, further than what I have related did pass prior to any one's coming into the Room, and my shewing her the Plan.

Did you apprize Miss Atherton of your Intention of calling upon her on the 22d of January, for the Purpose of knowing her Answer ?

I did not — but I called prior to my going to London, and in the Manner Mr. Rawstome himself desired me.

Did Mr. Rawstome desire you to call on Miss Atherton, without giving her Notice of your Intention ?

To the best of my Recollection nothing passed between him and me on that Subject, one Way or the other, further than before stated.

Did you propose to Miss Atherton, that you would l put

34 Geo. III. 17° Martii. 343

put upon Paper that conditional Assent which you have ' stated her to have given, and send it to her that she might sign it, if there was no Misconception of her Meaning ?

I don t recollect any Thing of the Sort passing. I have some faint Remembrance, that when I was taking my Leave of her, that she asked me if there was any Thing to sign; and I said, No, we never took Assents in that Manner.

You having stated, that some Conversation passed between you and Mr. John Gorst — inform the Committee whether you first mentioned the Assent of Miss Atherton to Mr. Gorst, or that he first mentioned it to you?

I do pot recollect.

To whom did you first mention the Conversation of the 22d of January, after you first left Leigh ?

It is impossible for me to say to whom I first mentioned it. I mentioned it pretty generally to every Body, and every Body seemed pleased about it.

Can you recollect any particular Person to whom you mentioned it?

I do recollect mentioning it that Evening to the Reverend Mr. Hornby, whom I called upon in my Road to Warrington on some other Business.

Did you relate to Mr. Hornby that Miss Atherton had given her verbal Assent to the Canal in her Conversation with you, under all the same Conditions which you have stated to the Committee?

By no means — the Conversation betwixt Mr. Hornby and me, upon that Subject, was very short indeed; my Business with him being to obtain his Assent to a Deviation in the Lancaster Canal, which I wanted from him, in order to enable the Company to carry the Canal (which by the Parliamentary Line goes to the East Side of Gar stone) to the West of the same Town; and my Time, while with him, was very much taken up in tracing him the Line upon Paper.

You having stated that you gave to Mr. Hornby no full and exact Account of the Conversation that had passed on the 2 2d of January with Miss Atherton — is there any other Person to whom you gave a full and exact Account of that Conversation ?

I will not take upon me to say I did.

Whether you went to Atherton on the 22d of January, knowing that Mr. Rawsto was absent ?

I got to Leigh early in the Morning of the 2 2d of January; and the first Enquiry I made at the Inn was, if they knew whether Mr. Rawstorne was at Home or not; the Landlord did not know, but Somebody in the Bar said they thought that he was gone to Manchester — this was the first Information I had on the Subject. I therefore went up to Athei'ton Hall immediately, as it was necessary for me to see Miss Atherton before I came to London, to know her Assent or Dissent.

And then the Witness was directed to withdraw.

Brooks, and Streams of Water, situate upon the intended Line of Canal, and also, certain Lands, Tenements, and Veins, or Mines of Coal, and Open Col heries, through which the said Canal is intended to pass; and that, in the Year 1754, the Petitioner's late Father, Charles Noel Somerset Duke of Beaufort, granted a Lease of the said Lands and Tenements,

Veins, or Mines of Coal, to the Lessees therein named, for the Term of Ninety-nine Years, with Liberty for them and their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, to work the said Veins or Mines of Coal, and for that Purpose to erect Works, Mills, and other Buildings, and to divert and use the Waters in the said Rivers, Brooks, and Streams, for the more effectually carrying on the same, subject to such Rents for Lana Money and Way Leave for other Persons Coal as therein mentioned; and that the said Lessees have, in consequence thereof, with great Risk to themselves and their Successors, expended very large Sums of Money in sinking Pits and driving Levels, making Rail or Waggon Roads, for the Convenience of working the same, and in erecting Mills and other Buildings, and have established very considerable Works and Manufactories upon the Faith of such Lease, the Enjoyment of which is warranted by the Petitioner's late Father to the said Lessees; and that the Petitioner's Income, arising from his Estates in the said County of Glamorgan, greatly depends upon the Success of the said Works by the Receipt of Land Money and for Way Leave, and other Advantages, and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioner's Property, and also, the Property of his Lessees, will be greatly injured: And therefore praying, That he may be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of Edmund Cartwright, of Doncaster, in Mr. Cart-the County of York, Clerk, was presented to the House, wngbt's Pe-and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner observes, by the Votes, that Petitions have been presented by a large Body of Woolcombers, of the Manufacturing combing Counties of this Kingdom, praying the Protection of Wool, the House against the Effects of certain Machinery for combing Wool; and that the Petitioner is the Inventor of the Machinery alluded to by the said several Petitions, and hath obtained His Majesty's Letters Patent, empowering the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, to exercise and vend his said Invention, for his and their sole and separate Use and Benefit, for a Term of Fourteen Years, a great Part whereof is yet unexpired, and the Petitioner, at the same Time that he submits to the House, that Machines, by which Manufactures are carried on with a Saving of Manual Labour, are beneficial to the Interests of this Kingdom, and therefore proper to be encouraged instead of meeting with Obstructions, yet, nevertheless, is willing to concur in any Plan for limiting him in the Sale of his Machinery to such Number Annually as to the House shall appear expedient, without receiving-any Compensation, byWay of an Equivalent, though he trusts that an Extension of the Term of his Patent will not be considered as unreasonable if the unlimited Use of it is to be restrained:

And therefore praying, That the House wiil take his Case into Consideration, and permit him, if Occasion shall require, to be heard, by himself, his Counsel, or his Agent.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Hobart accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duty of Excise of One Pound One Shilling and Five Pence Half-penny, charged upon-every One hundred We‘ght of all Cast Plate Glass made in Great Britain, and squared into Plates of a Superficies of hot less than One thousand Four hundred and Eighty-five Inches, and of a Thickness according to the Superficies, do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That in Lieu of the said Duty, a Duty of Excise of One Pound One Shilling and Five Pence Half-penny be charged upon every One hundred Weight of Materials, or Metal, or other Preparation, by what Name soever the same are of may be called or known, which shall be made Use of in Great Britain in the making of Cast Plate Glass.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting to His Majesty certain additional Duties on Glass imported into, or. made in, Great Britain, is committed,

That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill pursuant to the said Resolutions.

Mr. Watson's A Petition of George Watson, of OldMalton, in the Petition County of York, Esquire, was presented to the House, against Old and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for dividing, r°ii inclosing, draining, and improving, the Open Fields, Ings, Pastures, Commons, and Waste Grounds, within the Manor and Parish of Old Malton, in the North Riding of the County of York; and Setting forth, That the Petitioner now is the Proprietor and Lessee of divers ancient inclosed Lands and Grounds within the said Parish, under and by virtue of certain renewable Beneficial Leases, for long Terms of Years, held of the Master, Brethren, and Sisters, of worth Hospital, in the said Bill named, of which respective Terms Eighteen Years and upwards are yet to come and unexpired, and divers Clauses have been introduced into the said Bill, without the Knowledge and Consent of the Petitioner, which will, if carried into a Law, materially affect and prejudice his Estate and Interest in the Premises; and that the said ancient inclosed Lands have been long in the Possession of the Petitioner and his Ancestors, and form Part [of the Grounds immediately adjoining to his Mansion House, and have, at various Times, been effectually drained and improved by the Petitioner and his Ancestors at a very considerable Expence, and no Benefit or Advantage whatever, as to such ancient inclosed Grounds, can be derived, from the intended Drainage, to the Petitioner, who will therefore be much prejudiced by any Increase of Rent being directed to be paid to the said Master, Brethren, and Sisters, on Account of such pretended Improvement, during the Continuance of his Leases; and that all, or the greatest Part of, the Timber Trees and other Wood, now standing and growing on the said inclosed Grounds, have been planted by, and at the sole Expence of, the Petitioner and his Ancestors, upon the Faith, and in Consideration of having their Leases, from Time to Time, renewed to them, according to ancient Custom, and the cutting down such Timber and other Trees would greatly injure the Petitioner's Property therein, and deprive him of the Means of having Wood necessary for the future Repairs of his Buildings and Fences on the said Premises; and that the Petitioner is also the Lessee of a Water Com Mill within the said Parish, and has a Mill Dam of Water raised within the said ancient inclosed Lands for the Use of his said Mill, which Mill Dam is not guarded or preserved to the Petitioner by any Clause in the said Bill, and may, by the Diversion of the Watercourses, and making of the Drainage therein proposed, be materially injured, or totally destroyed; and that the Petitioner has many other Objections to the passing of the said Bill, in its Vol. 49.

present Form: And therefore praying, That the House will permit and direct such Clauses to be inserted in the said Inclosure Bill, as shall to them seem most expedient, for the Purpose of protecting and preserving the Petitioner's Right and Interest in the Premises, and that he may be heard, by himself. Agent, or Counsel, against the said Bill's passing into a Law, as it now stands.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by himself, his Agent, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

Mr. Vansittart reported from the Committee, to whom Torquay the Petition of Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, Lord of the Harbour,&c. Manor of Tormoham, in the County of Devon; and also, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names repo are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Inhabitants of the Port of Torquay, in the County of Devon, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, Mr. Robert Abraham, Junior, being examined, said, That the Harbour of Torquay, on the North East Side of Torbay, in the County of Devon and within the Manor of Tormoham, is at present too confined, and very inconvenient for mooring Ships and Vessels; and there are not effectual Powers for enforcing the Payment of the Rates and Tolls due to the Lord of the said Manor.

To prove the Allegations of the Second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Robert Abraham, Junior, being again examined, said, That the Inhabitants of Torquay have lately much increased in Number, and the Trade carried on at the said Port is much increased; that there is not at present any Market at Torquay, and it would be a great Advantage and Accommodation to the Inhabitants thereof, and of the adjacent Country, if a Market was established there, under proper Regulations and Restrictions.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable Sir Robert Palk, Baronet, his Heirs and Assigns, to repair and enlarge, or re-build, the Quay or Pier within the Harbour or Port of Torquay, in the County of Devon, and to improve the said Harbour, and to regulate the Moorings of Ships and Vessels therein, and to establish a Market there: And that Mr. Vansittart and Sir John Call do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Vansklart presehted to the House, according to Order, a Bill for enlarging the Term ana Powers of an Act, of the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty, for repairing the Road between The Bear Inn, in Reading, and Puntfield, in the County of Berks, and several other Roads in the said County: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

A Petition of several Journeymen Bakers, for themselves, and in behalf of other Journeymen in the same Trade, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to explain and amend an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, "An Act for the better Observation of the Lord's Day, commonly called " Sunday;" and setting forth, That the said Bill contains a Clause allowing all Persons, exercising the Trade of Baking, to follow the same, so far as relates to baking of Meat, Puddings, or Pies, on Sundays, until a certain Hour of the Day, under the Regulations in the said Bill mentioned; and, if the said Clause should remain a Part of the said Bill, and the same should pass into a Law, it will be very oppressive to the Petitioners and other Journeymen Bakers, as such an Allowance will lay them under the Necessity either of working till the Hour that may be limited on Sundays, in Addition to the Severity of their Labours during the Week, or of losing their Employment with all such Masters as might choose to avail themselves of such Allowance: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against that Part of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if thqy think lit.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Burdon reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of John Kendrew and Thomas of Darlington, in the County of Durham (to whom the King was graciously pleased to grant His Letters Patent, in the Year 1787, for the Spinning of Flax by Machinery, in England and Scotland, the Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick upon was re-

ferred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it. in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John J'Anson, of Darlington, Linen Manufacturer,

being examined, said, That the Petitioners have brought the Invention of Spinning of Flax, by Mills and Machinery, into such a State of Perfection, as to render the same of great Public Use; which Invention, being t\ie First of the kind ever brought into Practice for the Spinnjpg of Linen Yarn, has been attended with many-Difficulties, great Expence, and Loss of Time, in maturing and bringing forward the same, so as to make it work.with that Ease and Certainty required in Machines intended to work by Water or other Powers; and that the Petitioners, have obtained Letters Patents for England, bearing Date the 19th Day of June 1787, and for Scotland, bearing Date the 10th Day of December in the same Year, whereby the sole and exclusive Right to the said Invention was granted to them, for the Term of Fourteen Years from the Date of the said respective Letters Patents- — and the Petitioners produced to your Committee the said Letters Patents, and the Specifications of the Invention inrolled in the Courts of Chancery of England and Scotland.

And being further examined, he said, That the Linen Manufacturers of Great Britain are now, and for several Years past have been, under the Necessity of using great Quantities of Linen Yam purchased in Germany and other Foreign Countries, which - Importation will be much lessened by Means of the said Invention, and the Manufacturers of this Country supplied with Yarn of a superior Quality, and at a lower Price.

Mf., Frederick.Norman confirmed the above Evi-

dence.

Mr. J1 Anson being further examined, said, That the Petitioners have incurred very great and considerable Expences in the prosecuting the said Invention, and bringing the same to Perfection, previous to their obtaining the said Patents.

Mr. William. Sayer then produced to your Committee, the Accounts of the Receipts and Payments of the Petitioner* siaoe their obtaining the said Letters Patents, whereby it appears they have sustained a Loss of £.4,000 and upwards: — And he further added, That he apprehends the Petitioners will not be able to reimburse themselves the said Monies so lost by them, and receive a proper Recompence for their said Invention, unless the Terms of the said Letters Patents be extended.

Brandling do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of John Brathwaite, of Skelton, in the Parish of Ripon, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there is a Bill depending in the House, for inclosing the Moors, Commons, and Waste Grounds, and also the Common Fields of Skelton aforesaid; and that the Petitioner is legally seised in his own Right of an ancient Messuage, and also of several Scites or Foundations of ancient Messuages and Cottages, within the Town of Skelton aforesaid, and for which he claims a Right of Common for all Commonable Cattle, at all Times of the Year, upon the Moors, Commons, and Waste Grounds, Vol, 49.

and also a Right of Average in the said Common Fields of Skelton so intended. to be inclosed;, and that there is a Clause contained in the said Bill, which requires the Commissioner named therein to set out and allot Two Third Parts of the said Moors, Commons, and Waste Grounds, intended to be divided and inclosed, unto and amongst the several Owners and Proprietors as well of Messuages, Cottages, and Front-steads (such Frontsteads having had a House standing thereon within Forty Years previous to the 1st of January 1794;) and that there have not been any Houses standing upon the Petitioner's said several Scites within Forty Years previous to the said 1st Day of January 1794, and if the said Bill should pass into a Law, in its present State, the Petitioner is advised by his Counsel, that if he makes a Claim, for his said Scites, the Commissioner therein named cannot set out, allot, or award, any Part of the said Moors, Commons, and Waste Grounds, and Common Fields, of Skelton aforesaid, unto the Petitioner, for and in respect thereof, because he has not had any Houses standing thereon within the Forty Years last aforesaid; and the Petitioner, by the said Bill, is prevented from trying his Right, in the usual Way, which will be a real Injury to him: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given him to make such Alterations in the Clauses of the present Bill, and also to insert such other Clause and Clauses, as he shall be advised by Counsel, that will give him an opportunity of putting in his Claim for a Right of Common upon the Grojmds so intended to be inclosed by the said Bill, for and in respect of his said several Scites, and if such Claim be objected to, then a Power to have his Right thereto tried by an Issue at La#, Or to have the same referred to One or more Arbitrator or Arbitrators; and also to have such other Powers and Authorities inserted in the said Bill as is usual and customary in such and the like Cases; and that he may be heard, by his Counsel and Agents, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect him.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Open Common Fields,

Ings, Moors, Commons, and Waste Grounds, within the Township of Skelton, in the Canon, Fee, Manor, and Parish of Ripon, in the West Riding of the County of York, is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, or Agents, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

Mr. Secretary Dundas acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House: and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty thinks it proper to acquaint the House of Commons, That, for the Purpose of more effectually guarding against any Attempt which may be made, on the Part of the Enemy, to execute their professed Design of invading this Kingdom, His Majesty has ordered a further Augmentation of His Land Forces, the Estimate for which He has directed to be laid before the House. It is also His Majesty's Intention to take Measures, in order to be able, in case of Emergency, to assemble speedily a large additional Force in any Part of the Kingdom where it may become necessary; and His Majesty relies, with Confidence, on the cordial and effectual Support of Parliament, and on the zealous and spirited Exertions of His People, in carrying into Execution such Measures as may be requisite for the general Security.

G. R.

Ordered, That His Majesty's said most Gracious Message be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing of a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Perth, in the Room of the Honourable James Murray, deceased.

A PETITION of John En of Foxholes, in the County of Lancaster, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Manchester, Bolton, and Bury Canal, now making at, or nearly at, a Place called Hinde's Mill, in the Parish of Bury, by Rochdale and Littleborough, to a certain Place at, or near to, Sladen, and also, another Navigable Canal from the said Manchester, Bolton, and Bury Canal, at Bolton, to a Place at, or near to, Red Moss, in the Township of Blackrod, all in the County Palatine of Lancaster;and Setting forth, That, by the Will of his Predecessor, the Petitioner, and his Heirs, are obliged to maintain the Dwelling House at Foxholes aforesaid, with the Out-buildings, Gardens, and Pleasure Grounds thereto belonging, and to reside at the said House, as the Family Mansion, and the Petitioner has already expended upwards of £. 5,000 in repairing and improving the same; and that it appears by the said Bill, that it is proposed to carry the Line of the intended Canal within about 127 Yards of his said Mansion House, and within about 55 Yards of his Out-buildings, and within a much less Distance of his Gardens and Pleasure Grounds; and the Petitioner submits, that, if the same should be carried in the Course proposed, it must greatly diminish the comfortable Possession and Enjoyment of his said Mansion House, and, in his Estimation, render the 6ame of but small Value as a Place of Residence: And therefore praying. That he may be heard, by his Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may tend to his Injury or Inconvenience, and may have such Relief as the House shall think reasonable.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses Of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, in Common Hall assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for Thirty Years and upwards last past, been possessed of a Cap-stern, erected and maintained by them at a very considerable Expence, on a certain Wharf, also belonging to them', on the Trent, near Nottingham Trent Bridge, for the Accommodation of the Navigation, of the River, by assisting Vessels passing along the said River Vot. 49.

in their passage through the said Bridge, which is always difficult, and very frequently, from the particular Period of the Season or State of the River, extremely dangerous; and that such Capstem was originally erected' by the Petitioners or their Lessees, and has ever since been maintained by them, in consideration of a small but stipulated Gratuity; agreed to be paid them for the use of such Capstern, by every Vessel passing through such Bridge, whence, from the Number of the Vessels contributing thereto, the Petitioners have long derived a considerable Revenue; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending before the House (the main Object of which, being the further Improvement of the Navigation of the River Trent, has the decided Approbation of the Petitioners) under the Authority of which a Cut or Canal is intended to be made from, the Trent, above the said Bridge, at Beeston Meadow, into the Nottingham Canal, which by diverting the whole Course of the Navigation of the River from its present Course through the Trent Bridge, will deprive the Petitioners of nearly the whole of the Revenue they at present derive from the Money payable for die use of such Capstern; and that, although the Petitioners apprehend that the Bill in question will, if carried into a Law in its present State, have the effect to destroy and render of no Value the whole of the Petitioners Property in such Capstern, by annihilating the Annual Revenue derived therefrom, and also considerably to depreciate the Value of the Petitioners Wharf, which is materially connected therewith, yet, at particular Periods of the Season, the Communication with the Canal being impeded, or totally obstructed, whilst the Navigation of the River will still be practicable, the Safety and Security of all the Vessels navigating the River will, at those Periods, which will Annually occur, be dependent upon their having the Aid of a Capstern (placed in the Situation of that belonging to the Petitioners) in their Passage through the said Bridge:

And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into Law in its present Form, but that the House will afford to the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem' meet, and that in the mean Time, the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to- whom the Bill to alter and amend an Act, of the Twenty-third Year of His present Majesty, for improving the Navigation of the River Trent, and for making and maintaining-a Navigable Canal from the said River, in the Parish of Beeston, to join the Nottingham Canal in the Parish of Lenton, in the County of Nottingham, and also certain Cuts on the side of the said River, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all' have Voices who come to the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed'.

Copy of a CIRCULAR LETTER to the Lords Lieutenants of Counties.

Whitehall, 14th March 1794.

My Lord, or Sir,

Finding, from an Official Inaccuracy, that Copies of the Plans which have been prepared with a View to the augmenting the Internal Force of this Kingdom, have not been communicated to you, I have the Honour of inclosing Copies thereof herewith.

I am, $<?.

Henry Dundas.

GENERAL SUBSCRIPTION.

Whitehall, 14th March 1794.

It is naturally to be supposed, that Gentlemen of Weight or Property in different Parts of the Kingdom, will separately stand forward, in order to carry into Execution the several Parts of the Plan for the Security of the Country: But it seems also desirable a General Subscription should be opened, to be applied, under the Direction of a Committee, for the Purpose of assisting in carrying into Execution all or any of the Measures therein suggested, as Circumstances'.shall appear to require.

PLAN of AUGMENTATION of the FORCES for INTERNAL DEFENCE.

Whitehall, 14th March 1794.

In order to provide more completely for the Security of the Country against any Attempts which may be made on the Part of the Enemy, it may be expedient to adopt some, or all, of the following Measures:

I. To augment the Militia by Volunteer Companies, as was practised in the last War; or by an additional Number of Volunteers, t<f be added as Privates to each Company.

II. To form Volunteer Companies in particular Towns, especially in those situated on or near the

Sea Coast, for the Purpose of the local Defence of the particular Places where they may be raised, according to the accompanying Plan, or such other as may, on Application for that Purpose, be approved of, as best adapted to the Circumstances of any particular Town. .

III. To raise Volunteer Troops of Fencible Cavalry, consisting of not less than Fifty, nor more than Eighty, per Troop; who will be to serve only during the War, and within the Kingdom. The Officers will have temporary Rank only, and will not be entitled to Half Pay. The Arms, Accoutrements, and Cloathing, will be furnished by Government; but the Levy Money for the Men to be furnished by the Persons who undertake to raise such Troops; and the Horses to be found by them, but to be paid for, at a reasonable Price, by Government.

A Person raising Two Troops, to have the temporary Rank of Major; Four Troops, that of Lieutenant . Colonel; and Six Troops, that of Colonel.

IV. To

King's Message for Augmentation of Forces considered; and Address thereupon.

34 Geo. III. 26° Mart*. 379

IV. To form other Bodies of Cavalry within particular Counties or Districts, to consist of the Gentlemen and Yeomanry, or such Persons as they shall bring forward, according to the Plans to be approved of by the King, or by the Lords Lieutenants, under Authority from His Majesty; and the Officers to receive temporary Commissions from His Majesty j and the Muster Rolls also to be approved by His Majesty, or by the Lords Lieutenants, at Periods to be fixed. No Levy Money to be given; and the Horses to be furnished by the Gentry or Yeomanry, who compose the Corps; but the Arms and Accoutrements to be supplied at the Expence of'.the Public. Such Corps to be exercised only at such Times as shall be fixed by Warrant from His Majesty, or by the Approbation of the Lords Lieutenants. To be liable to be embodied or called out of their Counties by special Directions from His Majesty, in case of actual appearance of Invasion; and to be liable to be called upon, by Order from His Majesty, or by the Lord Lieutenant or Sheriff of the County, to act within the County, or in the adjacent Counties, for the Suppression of Riots and Tumults. In either case, while actually in Service, they shall receive Pay as Cavalry; and be liable to the Provisions of the Mutiny Bill.

V. To enroll and appoint Places of Rendezvous for a sufficient Number of Persons in different Parishes mid Districts, particularly in Places near the Sea Cdast, to serve as Pioneers, or to assist the Regular Force in any manner that may be necessary, on the shortest Notice, in Cases of Emergency.

Companies of INFANTRY for Manning BATTERIES on the Coast.

Companies of Infantry for Manning Batteries on the Coast, each to consist of,

1 Captain.

2 Lieutenants. '

3 Serjeants.

3 Corporals.

2 Drummers.

6o Private Men, at least, One Third to be armed with Firelocks, the other to have Pikes, Eight Feet long.

The Officers to be recommended by the Lords Lieutenants of Counties, but to have Commissions from the King.

To assemble Two Days in each Week, to practise. The Officers to be allowed Pay; and the Noncommissioned Officers and Private Men, each One Shilling per Day, for the Days they are at Exercise. To have Cloathing given by Government, that they may be all uniform. Not to be removed more than Five Miles from Home, unless ordered by His Majesty on the Appearance of an Invasion, when they are to be called out, and paid Kke other Militia; but not to be removed out of their County. Officers on Half Pay will be accepted, if recommended.

To be under Military Law when embodied, and under the Command of a General Officer.

professed Design of invading this Kingdom: That with this View I we shall be ready to make Provision for the further Augmentation of His Majesty's Land Forces, and for enabling His Majesty, in Case of Emergency, to assemble an additional Force in any Part of the Kingdom where Circumstances may require it: That, in the Prosecution of the just and necessary War in which His Majesty is engaged, which involves in it the Safety and Happiness of His Subjects, His Majesty may rely on the continuance of our firm and decided Support, which cannot fail to be seconded by the zealous and spirited Exertions of a brave and loyal People; .

A Petition of the thereunto Subscribers, Burgesses, Another Citizens, and Inhabitants of Aberdeen, was presented to Petition from the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for the better paving, lighting, cleansing, and otherwise deeiTVaving] improving, the Streets, Lanes, and other Public Pas- &c. Bill sages of the City of Aberdeen, and the Roads and Avenues leading to and from the same, for the better supplying the Inhabitants with Fresh Water, and for removing ana preventing all Obstructions and Annoyances within the said City and Liberties thereof; and Setting forth, That the said Bill, so far as the same has been published to the Petitioners, and by which they would be essentially injured in their Property and Interest, proposes a heavy Assessment on the Rents of Houses,

Shops, and Warehouses, which they occupy, and that for Improvements altogether undenned, agreeable to neither Plan nor Description which they have seen, and left entirely to the arbitrary, alarming, and uncertain, Determination of Commissioners, vested with the most dangerous discretionary Powers; and that, to heighten the Aggravation of the Petitioners Case, the Bill, far from being a Bill of Experiment, as might have been expected, and contrary to all sound Discretion and commendable Example in such Cases, has no fixed Period of Duration, but is proposed to be perpetual: That the discretionary Power of the Commissioners is, by the said Bill, extended in a most alarming Degree in one Particular, whereby the whole Inhabitants of the said City would be obliged, from the Produce of this heavy Assessment, and on a Principle as unexampled as it is unjust, to furnish a Sum of many Thousand Pounds to provide a few Hundreds of the more wealthy Citizens with Water into their Houses, when the whole Inhabitants of every Description might be amply supplied, agreeable to their most ardent Wishes, by Public Wells, for a Sum not much above as many Hundred Pounds, according to the Plan of an ingenious and disinterested Citizen, whose Propositions for that Purpose have been received by the great Body of the Citizens with Gratitude, and the most Public Testimonies of cordial Approbation; and that, although the Treasury Fund of the said City, destined in its Original Institution for the Public Benefit of the whole Community in Matters of Police, and to which every Burgess largely contributes, has been for many Years in a State of progressive Improvement,

384 27° Mar Hi. A. 1794.

tnent, especially by an Act of the Town Council, whereby the Admission Dues of Burgesses have been doubled, and the Inhabitants have largely contributed in Aid to the said Treasury Fund, for Water, Pavement, and Lamps, for the greater Part of this Century, as well as that Foot Pavements in many of the principal Streets have been made, at the private Expence of Proprietors of Houses, in their Line of Direction, yet an Attempt is now made, by the proposed Bill, to draw from the Fund, to be established by it, a large Sum of several Thousand Pounds, said to be due for Water, but which has been chiefly laid Out, without any previous Authority from the Citizens, or their Opinions taken on the Subject, in opening and paving new Streets, the principal of which leads directly to Grounds the Property of the Public Treasury, and since let on Building Leases, or Feus, to an Advantage of many Hundreds per Cent, and by means of which the Revenue of that Fund has been greatly increased: That this Claim is not only ill founded, and cannot in Justice be demanded from the Citizens, but, if granted, would greatly retard, and tend to effectually check the Improvements proposed by the Bill; and that the Petitioners conceive themselves liable to be affected by no Assessments for Public Improvements except within the Royalty, and present Circuit of the Borough, and then only when it becomes evident, that the Treasury Funds are incapable of furnishing the Aid necessary for such Improvements, and not until those Improvements are regularly described in their Lines and Boundaries, and ascertained by Plans and Estimates, before they are introduced into any Bill to be passed into a Law: That, in the means of Conviction for Offences against the Regulations in the Bill, by the Testimony of one Witness, as well as in the high Penalties annexed to such Transgressions, there is an evident and unnecessary Deviation from the course of the Common Law; and that the said Bill,

/ being in the Particulars already stated, as well as in its general Principle, and in many of its other Enactments, highly arbitrary, exceptionable, and extremely disagreeable, to the Petitioners, as well as to a great Majority of the Citizens, Burgesses, and Inhabitants of Aberdeen, they implore the Indulgence of the House, if, in thus stating their Objections to a Measure, to them very deeply interesting, they shall have in any Degree departed from ordinary Rules, or have erred in point of Form, and, confiding in the Wisdom and Justice of the House, the universial Guardian of the People's Rights, they humbly intreat that the said Bill may not pass into a Law, but that, if insisted in, they may be heard, in Objection to the same, by Counsel, at the Bar of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

and that the said Canal was begun to be surveyed in the Month of May last, and finished in the Month of August following, and that not only the Steward and Land Surveyor, but also the Guardian of the said Henrietta Maria Atherton, were made acquainted with the Line of the said Canal, and acquiesced therein, until the Month of November last, when it was too late to make any Alteration in the Plan; and that the Assent of the said Miss Atherton was given to the Petitioner without any Misrepresentation on the Part of the Petitioner, or, as the Petitioner verily believes, any Misconception on her Part, and the Petitioner offered Evidence before the Committee to prove what Steps had been taken upon such Assent, as also that various Acts had been done, as well before the said Miss Athertons coming of Age as afterwards, by Persons then and still entrusted with the Management of her Estates, all tending to prove an implied Assent or Acquiescence on their Parts, and to confirm the Evidence given by the Petitioner, and the Petitioner conceives and submits to the House, that the same ought to have been, but was not, received by the said Committee; and that the Petitioner apprehends, that an Assent so obtained ought not to be allowed to be retracted, more especially when the Line of the said Canal could easily have been taken another way, but was.conducted in the present by Means, and at the Instance, of the Agent of the said Miss Atherton, and the Lancaster Company have incurred a heavy Expence thereby: And therefore praying to be heard, on the Part of the said Lancaster Canal Proprietors, by Counsel and Witnesses, at the Bar of the House, or, that the said Petition of the said Henrietta Maria Atherton may be re-committed, for the Purpose of hearing-further Evidence, or that such other Relief may be granted as to the House may seem meet.

Petition from A Petition of the Provost* Magistrates, and Town

Montrose for Council of Montrose, in the County of Forfar, in ta* Urn*Forfar* ^ame the Community of the said Burgh, and of Roads Bill. the Commissioners appointed by an Act of the Thirty-second of His present Majesty, for building a Bridge over the River South Esk, at, or near, the said Town of Montrose, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the great Post Road, from the South to the North of Scotland, is intersected at Montrose by the River South Esk, which is Half a Mile in Breadth, deep, and rapid, and at present Travellers must pass the River in Boats, and the Passage is often attended with Delay, Inconvenience, and Danger: To unite the principal Line of Road through the County at the said Place, by Means of Bridges, and thereby to render the Communication between the different Parts of the Country more expeditious and convenient, has long been the Wish of the Public, and, in many Respects, an Object the most desirable; and that the Inhabitants of the Town and Neighbourhood of Montrose, on the 19th Day of October 1787, opened a voluntary Subscription, when the Sum of 5,000 was immediately subscribed by way of Free Gift, and since that Period the Sum has increased by His Majesty's Bounty, and the further Subscriptions of Individuals, to the Amount of £. 12,000, in Consequence of which, Contracts were entered into in the Year 1792, for uniting the Road aforesaid at Montrose, by Two Bridges, and the 'Expence of accomplishing the said Work is estimated at between £. 16,000 and £. 17,000; and that the Money deficient will be about £. 5,000, but the Commissioners appointed for the erecting of the said Bridges, trusting that they would be enabled to borrow, upon the Security of the Toll or Pontage to be levied on the said Bridges, a Sum sufficient for accomplishing the Work, they caused the same to be commenced in the Month of September 1792, and at this Time very considerable Progress has been made, but the Petitioners are much concerned to represent, that the aforesaid Work of the greatest Public Utility, is likely to be interrupted, if not entirely stopped, by a Bill, proposed to be brought into Parliament in this present Session, for raising the Tolls, and granting new Powers to the Trustees appointed by an Act, of the Twenty-ninth of His present Majesty, intituled. " An Act for repairing the Roads in the County of Forfar, " and for regulating the Statute Labour within the " same," wherein, among other Clauses, there is one to authorize the Trustees for the Turnpike Roads of the County to erect Toll Bars upon any Part of the Turnpike Roads they shall think proper, and there' to levy Tolls and Duties, and it has been signified to the Petitioners to be intended, by some of the Trustees for the said Roads, as soon as the Bridges aforesaid shall be completed, to cause a Gate or Bars to be placed at the South End of one of the Bridges, for the Purpose of levying a Toll for the Road, which Measure, if carried into Execution, would prove most oppressive to the Petitioners, and injurious to the Revenue, expected to have been drawn by way of Pontage from Vol. 49.

the said Bridge, because it would be levying a double Toll, and that at a Rate proposed so very high as chuld not fail, in many Instances, to operate as a Prohibition from passing the Bridge with Articles of small Value, such as Lime; Coals, Manure, See. and consequently lessen the Amount expected to have been collected by the Commissioners; by Way of Pontage, not only for discharging the Interest of the Money to be borrowed, but to form a Fund for Repairs, which will, from Time to Time, be necessary for one of the Bridges, composed chiefly of Timber, and render it impracticable to obtain a Loan of Money for com- ‘ pleting the Work; and that the Money, proposed to be levied by the Road Toll at the Montrose Bridge, is meant to be appropriated to increase the Funds of the Line of Road from Dundee to Montrose, being about Thirty Miles, and there are already upon those Thirty Miles no less than Five Gates for levying Tolls, to enable the Trustees to make and keep up the Road, and the whole Expence of making the same does not amount to the Money required for erecting the Montrose Bridges; and that the said Bridges, when completed, will confessedly form the most important Part of the whole Line of Road, and, considering the Trustees have, as above-mentioned, Five different Tolls collected upon the Thirty Miles of Road for keeping the same up, it would be a most oppressive Measure to insist upon placing a Gate at the Montrose Bridge, and thereby double the Toll to be paid there; and that, though the Bridges will cost a Sum of Money far exceeding the whole Expence of the rest of the Line of Road, and that £. 12,000 thereof has been supplied as a Free Gift, the Petitioners require only the Produce of one Single Toll, in the Way of Pontage, to enable them to borrow the £. 5,000 to complete the Work: And therefore praying, That there may be a Clause inserted in the Bill above mentioned, restraining the Trustees therein named from erecting, or causing to be erected, any Gate or Bars for the Purpose of levying a Road Toll at the End of the said Bridge, or within Three Miles thereof, or such Distance, by way of Exemption as the House shall think fit.

Another Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Petition from Town Council of Montrose, in the County of Forfar, Montrose, in Name of the Community of the said Burgh, ,^i1^tT^"lrfaf and of the Commissioners appointed by an Act of the Thirty-second of His present Majesty, for building a Bridge over the River South Esk, at, or near, the said,

Town of Montrose, was also presented to the House,

and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is now depending before the House, for enlarging the Powers, given by an Act of the Twenty-ninth of His present Majesty's Reign, to certain Trustees therein named, for repairing the Roads in the County of Forfar, which will considerably affect the Interests of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by Counsel, against the Clauses in the said Bill, by which they are affected.

A Petition of the several Persons thereunto sub- Petition from scribing, Owners of Land in the Counties of Forfar Owners of and Perth, upon or connected with the Turnpike Road in the former County, leading Westward from against D" Dundee towards Perth, was likewise presented to the Bill.

House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Twenty-ninth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, an Act was passed for repairing the Roads in the County of Forfar, and for regulating the Statute Labour within the same, by which the Trustees thereby appointed were authorized to levy Tolls on the several Roads therein described, to borrow Money on the Credit thereof, and to make and repair the said Roads, with all the usual Powers; and that, by the Terms of the said Act, the several Roads were separated and distinguished as unconnected Lines, and particularly the Road from Dundee Westward towards Perth, to the

Borders of the County of ,was described as

one Line, and the Road from Dundee Eastward to Ferryden was described as another and a distinct Line, and, it was expressly declared, that the Produce of the Tolls or Duties arising on each of the said Lines of Road should be applied towards upholding and repairing that Line on winch the Tolls and Duties were respectively collected, so as each particular Line of Road might have its own Produce, and the Trustees were authorized to borrow Money to an Extent not exceeding £. loo a Mile for the Road for which such Money should be borrowed, and on the Credit of the Tolls of that particular Road; and that, in pursuance of the said Act, the Road from Dundee Westward towards Perth has been completely made, and in a great Measure from the Exertion of the Trustees of the Turnpike Roads in the adjacent County of Perth, who were induced to interfere because the said Road was a Continuation of the Great Post Road from , terminating (so far as they had any Concern) at the Town of Dundee, which is the great Market for the neighbouring Country, and the Perthshire Trustees have engaged to keep a considerable Part of the said Road, though locally situated in the County of Forfar, in Repair, and they have lent Money on the Credit of the Tolls on the said Line of Road, and have besides, by altering the Course, and accommodating the Forfarshire Trustees, shortened it from Four Miles and a Half to Three Miles, which is now all the Extent of Road which the Trustees of Forfarshire, and the Tolls on that Line, under the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of His Majesty, have to maintain, and the Tolls thereby authorized to be levied on it are, from the Average of past Years, and the reasonable Prospect of Increase, fully sufficient to pay the Interest of the Money borrowed, to maintain the Road, and leave a considerable Surplus, gradually to diminish and sink the Principal Debt owing; and that the other Line of Road before-mentioned, from Dundee Eastward to Ferryden, is of Twenty-seven Miles in Extent, or thereby, and is by no Means sufficiently made, or in proper Repair, and is loaded with Debt, contracted on the Credit of the Tolls, which are not sufficient to pay the Interest, and make or support the Road as it ought to be: In these Circumstances, a Bill has been brought into the House, and is depending, for continuing the Term and enlarging the Powers of the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of His Majesty, and for repairing several other Roads in the County of Forfar, which does not state or alledge, that to make or uphold the Line of Road from Dundee Westward towards Perth, needs any further Interposition of the Legislature, but stating, that the Tolls upon the Road from Dundee Eastward to Ferryden (amongst others) are not sufficient for keeping it in Repair, and paying the Interest of the Sums owing or borrowed on the Credit thereof; and alledging, that it would be both just and expedient, that the Road from Dundee towards Perth should be united in the same Trust, and added to the Line of Road leading from Dundee to Ferryden, and prays that the Trustees may be authorized to levy Tolls on all the Roads, according to certain Rates, avowedly much higher than those permitted to be taken by the said Act of the Twenty-ninth of His Majesty, and that the Roads to the Westward and to the Eastward of Dundee may, in future, be considered as one and the same Line of Road, that the same Tolls may be levied on both, and that the Money collected on the said Roads, so united, may form an Aggregate Fund to pay the Interest of the Money borrowed and owing for both Roads, and to repair and maintain both; and that the Petitioners apprehend that this is an Attempt both novel and unjust; it is in Effect to repeal a subsisting Law, on the Faith of which many Transactions have taken {dace, and to Jay a Tax upon one Set of People and one District

of a Country, for the Benefit of a different Set and a different District, with which (to the present Purpose) the Legislature had declared they should not be connected for a Term of Years, of which many are yet to run; and it is not only to continue but to enlarge Tolls and Duties on one Road, though not alledged to be necessary for it, in order to create a Fund for another separate and distinct Road, because the Persons particularly concerned in the last have erred in their Calculations, and are unwilling to supply the Deficiency out of their own Pockets; and, finally, it is to take away and injure the Security of the Persons who have lent their Money on the Faith of the former Act of Parliament, to throw the Load of a Debt, contracted singly on the Credit of the Tolls on the Eastern Road, on the Tolls of the Western, to leave the Persons particularly connected with the last without the Prospect of ever being relieved of their present Burthen, and at the same time increasing it; and that the Interest and Properties of the Petitioners, as well as of all Persons living near to, and connected with, the Road so leading Westward from Dundee, will be materially affected if the said Bill, as now brought in, shall pass into a Law: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against those Parts of the said Bill which respect the Road Westward from Dundee, and the Road Eastward from thence to Ferryden, and the Junction or Communication of the Funds of these separate Roads, and the Tolls proposed to be levied on the former, and that the said Bill may not in so far pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to continue the Term, and enlarge the Powers, of an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for repairing the Roads in the County of " Forfar, and for regulating the Statute Labour within the same," and for repairing several other Roads in the said County, and for building a Bridge over the River South Esk, near Finhaven, is committed; and the Two last mentioned Petitioners are to be heard by themselves, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petitions, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petitions.

A Petition of William Topli the Younger, of Cuck-ney, in the County of Nottingham, Worsted Manufacturer, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner having observed by. the Votes that several Petitions of Woolcombers have lately been presented, praying the Interference of the House to restrain the Use of Machines for combing Wool, entreats the Attention of the House to a Statement of his Interests as an Inventor of a Machine for combing Wool, and as a very great Consumer of combed Wool: That, for several Years last past, the Petitioner has employed from too to 150 Wool-combers in combing Wool, which he has spun into Worsted Yarn by Machinery, and that, experiencing great Inconveniencies from the inadequate Number of Woolcombers for the Purposes of Trade, when the same is extensive and flourishing, and from their irregular and improper Conduct in forming themselves into Societies and Combinations, the Petitioner, after great Labour and Study, invented a Machine for combing Wool, to be worked by Water, and for the exclusive Use and Exercise of which the Petitioner on the 8th day of June 1793, obtained His Majesty's Letters Patent for a Term of Fourteen Years, and by the Machines invented by the Petitioner Wool can be combed as well as by Hand, and with a great Saving of Manual Labour and Expence, whereby the Worsted Yam, and the Goods manufactured from it are produced both better in Quality and cheaper: That in the Year 1792, when the Worsted Manufactory was carried on to a greater Extent than at present, the Woolcombers in some Parts of the Kingdom were found insufficient to comb the Wool wanted, and they are formed into Clubs or Societies in different Parts, and governed by Laws or Rules of their own, by which they are restrained from taking Apprentices (except their Eldest Sons) or extending their Number by instructing the Apprentices or Servants of their Employers; that many of them are single Men, and lead Itinerant Lives, travelling from One Part of the Kingdom to another, and seldom work half their Time; that the Woolcombers employed by the Petitioner can, upon an Average, earn from Twenty-five to Twenty-eight Shillings per Week, when they chuse to work every Day, whereas the Average Wages paid to them seldom exceed Ten Shillings per Week, and this Difference arises solely from their refusing to do more Work, and not from its being withheld from them: That by Means of the Societies or Clubs formed by the Woolcombers in all the Manufacturing Parts of the Country, the Manufacturers are entirely at the Mercy of their Combers, and must pay them whatever Wages they demand, particularly when Trade is in a flourishing 'State, inso much that if a Manufacturer displeases one, Woolcomber all the others Vo l. 49.

either quit his Service entirely, or until he appeases the offended Member, and no other Woolcomber will work for him so long as he continues under the Displeasure of any of the Members of their Society: That there are various Societies independent of, and who refuse to mix or work with each other, so that a Yorkshire or Lancashire Woolcomber could not obtain Employment amongst the Midland Woolcombers, whose Chief Society or Club is held in Leicestershire; and that the Use of Machines for combing Wool will reduce the Quantity of Manual Labour consumed in the Fabrication of Worsted Goods, and consequently enable the Manufacturer to bring them to Market at a lower Price, and to undersell the Manufacturers of other Countries, and the Petitioner submits to the House, that the Principle upon which the Woolcombers oppose the Use of Machines in combing Wool would equally apply to restrain or prohibit every other.

Species of Manufacturing Machinery, as the Object of all such Machinery is the reduction of Manual Labour, and without it die Manufacturers of Great tain could not support a successful Competition with those of other Countries, and the Objection made by the Woolcombers to the Use of combing Machines would equally apply to all the Machinery used in the preparing and spinning of Cotton, Worsted, and Woollen Yarn, and Silk, and in weaving, printing, and dressing, many of the most valuable Manufactures in this Country; and that, in Addition to these Considerations, the House will recollect that all the Inventions and Improvements in the Manufactures of Great Britain are adopted and imitated in other Countries, and, if the House should in any Degree restrain the Use of manufacturing Machinery, it would enable Foreigners by the Use of them to undersell the British Manufacturers: And therefore praying, That in Case the House shall proceed to take the Petitions of the Woolcombers into Consideration, it will, at the same Time, also take the Petitioner's Case into Consideration, and that (if Occasion should require) the Petitioner may be heard, by himself, or by his Counsel, at the Bar of the House, and may be permitted to adduce Evidence'in support of the Allegations contained in this Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Woolcombers of the County and Leicester Borough of Leicester, was presented to the House, and Woolcombers read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are justly Petition, alarmed at the calamitous Consequences likely to arise from the Construction of certain Machines, which, by reducing the Quantity of Manual Labour, threaten to involve the Petitioners in every Distress necessarily consequent on the total Suspension of the regular Business on which they depend for Subsistence, and to which they have been brought up from their Infancy, and the Prospect before them is peculiarly distressing because, in the Business of Woolcombing, it is not possible to increase the Raw Material beyond the present Quantity, and the Number of Woolcombers at this Time in Great Britain is more than sufficient for the Wants of the Manufactory: That, in other Departments of Trade, wherein Machines have conduced to the Extension of the Wealth and Commerce of the Nation, the Raw Material has been capable of indefinite Increase, whereas the Growth of Wool is definite, and never equals the Ability of the Woolcombers to manufacture, and therefore any sudden and unexpected Diminution of the Quantity of Manual Labour will reduce the Petitioners to a State of the most wretched Poverty, and be attended with the most calamitous Consequences to their Wives, Children, and numerous Apprentices: And hoping, That such Measures for theif Relief and Security from the threatened Danger will be adopted by the House as they may judge expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Lottery. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Seven hundred and Forty thousand Six hundred and Sixty-six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence be raised byWay of Lottery, such Lottery to consist of Forty thousand Tickets, at Eighteen Pounds Ten Shillings and Four Pence each; and that the Contributors towards the same shall, on or before the 5th Day of April 1794, make a Deposit, with the Cashiers of the Bank of England, of One Pound Ten Shillings and Four Pence, in respect of the Monies to be paid for every such Ticket, as a Security for making the future Payments to the said Cashiers, on or before the Times herein after limited; that is to say: Two Pounds on or before the 23d Day of May next; Two Pounds on or before the 28th Day of July next; Two Pounds on or before the 5th Day of September next; Three Pounds on or before the 24th Day of October next; Four Pounds on or before the 21st Day of November next; Four Pounds on or before the 13th Day of January 1795; and that Tickets, as soon as the same can be prepared, shall be delivered to the Contributors, so com-. pleting their Payments: That the Sum of Five hundred thousand Pounds shall be distributed into Prizes, for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery; which Prizes shall be charged upon the Aids and Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament, for the Service of the Year 1794, and be paid at the Bank of England, in Money, to such Proprietors upon Demand, on, or at any Time after, the ist Day of July 1795, as soon as Certificates can be made out, without any Deduction whatsoever; and that all the Monies to be received by the said Cashiers shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer, to be applied, from Time

Vol. 49.

to Time, to such Services as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament:'

That every Contributor, who shall pay in the Whole of his or her Contribution Money towards the said Sum of Seven hundred and Forty thousand Six hundred and Sixty-six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, at any Time on or before the 21st Day of November 1794, shall be allowed an Interest, by Way of Discount, after the Rate of £. 3 per Centum per Annum, on the Sum so completing his or her Contribution respectively, to be computed from the Day of completing the same, to the 13th Day of January 1795 -

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Diserth, and Meliden, in the Counties of Denbigh and Flint, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Drainage Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. —

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Matthews being examined, said, That there are within the Parishes of Abergele, Saint Asaph, Rhydlan, Diserth, and Meliden, in the Counties of Denbigh and Flint, several inclosed Lands and Common Marshes, which are yearly worn, inundated, and greatly damaged by the Sea, and by Land Waters. — And that the making of Sea Banks, Fences, Aqueducts, and other Works necessary for securing the Coasts from the Encroachments of the Sea, and for draining the Land Waters, will tend greatly to improve the Port and Harbour of Voryd and Rhydlan, and be of Public Vo l.49-

Utility. — That the Proprietors of Lands, Messuages, and Hereditaments within the said Parishes, have Right of Common on the said Marshes and Waste Low Lands* and are affected in different Degrees by the Encroachments and Inundations of the Sea,

And being further examined, he said, That in order to complete and preserve the Works necessary for fencing and guarding the said Lands, Marshes, and Waste Low Lands from the Sea, and draining the same, it will be expedient that some Parts of the said Common Marshes and Waste Low Lands, in every Parish respectively, should be inclosed, and sold, to defray the Expence of erecting, completing, and preserving such Works.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for embanking hfld otherwise fencing from the Sea the Lands on the Sea Coasts of the Parish of Abergele, in the County of Denbigh, and Rhydlan Marsh, in the several Parishes of Abergele aforesaid, and of Saint Asaph and Rhydlan, and the Franchise of Rhydlan, in the County of Flint, and sundry other Marshes, Commons, and Waste Lands, in the said Parish of Rhydlan, and in the several Parishes of Diserth and Meliden, in the said County of Flint; and to cut and make in or through the same, or some Part thereof, one or more Aqueducts, or other Watercourses and Drains, and to inclose, divide, and sell competent Parts of the said several Marshes, Commons, and Waste Lands, to defray the Expences of the said Works, dnd to raise a Fund for the future Repair and Preservation thereof: And that Sir Roger Mostyn and Mr. Owen do prepare, and bring in, the same.

and that, if the Duties now payable by Law to the Corporation of Bridgewater should be increased, and any such doubtful Duties confirmed and established upon Boats, and other Vessels, or any Goods, Merchandize, or other Things, coming into and sent from the Port of Bridgewater, or passing under the said Bridge, |he same would, by lessening the Quantity of Goods, and other Things, that would otherwise pass upon the said River Tone, between the Towns of Bridgewater and Taunton as aforesaid, be very injurious to the Petitioners, by diminishing the Dudes payable to them by virtue of the said Acts: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as shall affect them, and may have such Relief as the House shall think just and reasonable.
