" Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom of Great Britain, and for the more effectually supporting and " conducting the same, upon an improved Plan, in a " peculiar Manner calculated for the casting of large " Plate Glass," which Act was to have Continuance for the Term of Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and that, besides the Capital Stock raised in Conformity to the said Act, the Petitioners have contracted Debts to the Amount of about £.66,000, and the Company have had in view, for some Time, an Application to Parliament to grant them Relief in the present embarrassed Situation of their Circumstances; but, ffom unavoidable Accidents, the Time for presenting Private Petitions elapsed before the Company could, with Propriety, make Application to the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for dissolving the present, and for creating a new Company for the Term of Twenty-one Years, and for vesting in such new Company the whole of the Corporation Property, subject to the Payment of the Debts affecting the same, and for such other Purposes as shall appear to be necessarily connected with the Subject, and such Petition has been accordingly prepared, and is now ready to be presented to the House; and that the Creditors of the Company have become very importunate for Payment of their Demands, and have even threatened coercive Measures, which, if carried into Effect, would be highly injurious to the Interests of the Petitioners, who have embarked considerable Sums in the Establishment of a Manufactory, which they conceive to be an Object of National Importance, and might totally ruin the same before the next Session of Parliament: And therefore praying, that the House will give Leave to the Petitioners to present their aforesaid Petitioi} for dissolving the present, and for creating a new Company of Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers, notwithstanding the Time' limited for presenting similar Petitions during the present Session, is elapsed.

And the House being informed, by a Member in his Place, that the said Company would have made an earlier Application to the House, but were restrained by the Consideration of the Effects which the Bill for granting to His Majesty certain additional Duties on Glass imported into, or made in, Great Britain, now depending in this House, might have on the State of the Affairs of the said Company;

Petition from Then a Petition of the Governor and Company of the Company the British Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers, was pre-Glass Man*- sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That facturere. by the said Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, the Petitioners were empowered to raise a Capital joint Stock, to be applied for carrying on the said Manufacture, not exceeding £. 40,000; and, in case the same should be found insufficient, an additional Sum of 20,000, in the Manner therein mentioned, and, the said Act contains various Clauses prescribing the Mode in which the said Manufactory was to be carried on, and directing that the said Act should take Place, and have Continuance, from the passing thereof, for the Term of Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and that the said Manufactory was established in the Year 1773, and has ever since been conducted by the Petitioners in Conformity to the Terms of the said Act, first with a Capital Stock of £. 40,000, afterwards with the extended Capital of £. 60,000, and since with that Capital, aided by Loans negotiated by the Company with different Individuals, to the Amount of £. 60,000 or thereabouts; and that, according to an Estimate lately made of the Company's Property, the same is worth upwards of £. 150,000, to be disposed of in the regular Course of Trade, but would not produce Half, perhaps not One-third of that Sum by a forced Sale, under Executions at the Suit of the Petitioners Creditors, nevertheless they have insisted upon immediate Payment of their Demands, and have threatened to use coercive Measures, the Petitioners have therefore had Recourse to different Expedients for relieving themselves from their Difficulties, but the said Act having limited the Capital of the Company to £. 60,000, and the Duration of the Act itself to the next Session of Parliament, the Petitioners find it utterly impracticable to raise Money sufficient to satisfy the Debts owing by them, without an Enlargement of the Term, and an Extension of their Capital, and the said Act having been found, by Experience, to be defective in its Provisions for the Management of such a Concern, and many of the original Proprietors, or those deriving Titles under such Proprietors, having from Death, Insolvency, Infancy, or other Causes, become inefficient Members of the said Company (Circumstances which have a Tendency to impede its Operations) the Petitioners are desirous that the present Company should be dissolved, and a new one created upon such a Scale as will embrace the Objects before pointed out: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dissolving the present, and for creating, a new Company for the Term of Twenty-one Years, and for vesting in such new Company the Whole of the Corporation Property, subject to the Payment of the Debts affecting the same, and for such other Purposes as shall appear to be necessarily connected with this Subject.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Thomas Dundas, Mr. Dun-combe, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the Persons thereto subscribing, Heritors, Land Owners, and Commissioners of Supply, for the County of Kinross, and-principal Inhabitants of the Towns of Kinross and Miln-a-Thort, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for continuing the Term and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, and the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty, so far as respects the Road from North Queensferry, in the County of Fife, to the Town of Perth, and for more effectually making, repairing, and keeping in Repair, the said Road, to pass by, or near by, the Towns of Inverkeithing and Kinross; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive they will be greatly aggrieved if the said Bill should pass into a Law, in as much as it lavs a heavy and severe Toll upon the Heritors, Landholders, and Inhabitants of the said County, without any reasonable Cause, or just Ground for the same: That Kinross is a very small County in point of Extent, whereas the Counties of Perth ana Fife are very large, rich, and populous, each having the Benefit of Water Carriage, whereas the County of Kinross is Ten Miles from any Sea Port; and that great Part of the high Toll, proposed to be raised in the County of Kinross by the said Bill, is with a View of making Roads, Bridges, and Piers, or Improvements on the Ferries, with which the greatest Number of the laborious and industrious Poor in the County of Kinross have no Connection, and it is proposed to lay a heavy Toll on Coal, which to an Inland and Manufacturing County is oppressive and unjust, as well as oppressive, when it is considered that the Money, to be raised by such Toll, will be laid out at the Will and Pleasure of the Two other Counties, who constitute a great Majority of the Commissioners, and who can always overpower the County of Kinross, where there are but few landed Gentlemen to fill the Situation of Commissioners; and that, although the County of Kinross is in itself but vety small, yet the Line of Road to which the proposed Bill relates is as extensive in the County of Kinross as that which goes through the Counties of Fife and Perth, and the Heritors and Land Owners in the County of Kinross are willing to keep that whole Line of Road, being Ten Miles in the County of Kinross, in complete 3

Repair, and they trust free of Drift, with the Tolls as they now stand, and, if they do so, they submit that they do their Duty by the Public; and that they can with Certainty accomplish this desirable End, the Petitioners can prove to the Satisfaction of the House, by shewing the Receipts upon the said Ten Miles of Road to be greatly within the Expenditure, and they can further prove, that the Road through that County has always been in more perfect Repair than any other Part of the Trust: And that, being a distinct ana separate County, with distinct and separate Jurisdiction, and being universally dissentient from the said Junction, because they foresee no Benefit to the Public, and much Detriment to their own Interests, from continuing to be joined in the same Trust with the Counties of Perth and Fife, upon the Footing now proposed, they pmy, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and permit the Petitioners to be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the Second Reading of the said Bill, and in the other Stages of die Proceedings thereon, to the End that the County of Kinross may be struck out from the said Bill, and, should the same pass into a Law for the Counties of Perth and Fife, the Petitioners further pray, that the Trustees shall not be empowered to levy any Tolb on Coals at or near the Bridge of Kelly, or on any Part of the Road leading from thence to the nearest Coal Pits, on the Petitioners undertaking to keep the said Coal Roads in Repair, mid freeing ana relieving the Counties of Perth and Fife from the Expence of supporting the same, and the Petitioners have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr, Vansittart reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Anne Shaw, Widow, and George Edward Allen, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined and found that the proposed Variations of the Kennet and Avon Canal do not exceed One hundred and Twenty Chains in Length, and do not go through any other Parishes than were mentioned in the Notices given for the Bill, and that all the Owners and Occupiers of the Lands through which the Variations go, are consenting thereto; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as lolloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Randolph, and Charles Henry Dundas, Esquire, being examined, said, That since depositing the Plan and Book of Reference with the Clerks of the Peace for the Counties of Berks and Somerset, for making the Canal from the River Kennet, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at or near the City of it hath been found, that, by varying certain Parts of the Line of the said Canal, in the Parishes of Kintbury, Bath Hampton, and Bath Easton, it will not only be an Accommodation to the Petitioners, but would be equally beneficial to the Public as if made in the Line Laid down and described in the said. Plan and Book of Reference.

And the Witnesses added, That the Extent of One of the Variations is only about Twenty-five Chains, and the other about Ninety Chains; and that neither of the said Variations go into any other Parish than was described in the original Notices, given in pursuance of the Standing Orders of this House relating to Navigations, nor through any Land, except the Lands of the Petitioners, and of Four other Persons, who, and also tlje Occupiers of those Lands, are consenting thereto; and that the Subscribers to the Undertaking are willing to make such Variations.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for making a Navigable Canal from the River Kennet, at or near the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at or near the City of Bath, and also certain Navigable Cuts therein described, is committed, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, for varying the Line of the said Canal, in the Parish of Kintbury, in the County of in certain Lands belonging to Anne Shaw, Widow, and the Reverend John Craven, Clerk, and in the Parishes of Bath Hampton and Bath Easton, in the County of Somerset, in cer- -tain Lands belonging to George Edward Allen, Esquire, and the Reverend ..... Sir Thomas Dundas reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Governor and Company of the British Cast Plate Glass Manufacturers, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act to incorporate " certain Persons therein named, and their Successors,

" with proper Powers for the Purpose of establishing " One or more Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom of Great Britain, and for the more effectually " supporting and conducting the same, upon an improved Plan, in a peculiar Manner calculated for the " casting of large Plate Glass," was read; by which Act it appeared, that the Petitioners were empowered to raise a Capital Joint Stock, to be applied for carrying on the said Manufacture, not exceeding £. 40,000, ana in case the same should be found insufficient, an addi- ' tional Sum of £. 20,000 in the Manner, and under the Rules and Regulations therein mentioned; which Act was to have Continuance for the Term of Twenty-one Years: Then,

Mr. Alexander Black (Secretary to the said Company) being examined, said, That the said Manufactory was established in the Year 1773, arKl has ever since been conducted in Conformity to the Terms of the said Act, first with a Capital of £. 40,000, afterwards with the extended Capital of £. 60,000, and since, with that Capital, aided by Loans negotiated by the Company with different Individuals, to the Amount of £. 66,000. — That, according to an Estimate lately made of the Company's Property, the same is worth £. 150,000 and upwards, if disposed of in the regular Course of Trade, but would not produce Half, perhaps not One Third of that Sum, by a forced Sale, under Executions at the Suit of the Company's Creditors, who have insisted upon immediate Payment of their Demands, and have threatened coercive Measures; whereby the Company have had Recourse to different Expedients to relieve themselves from their Difficulties — That the said Act having limited their Capital to £. 60,000, and the Duration of the Act itself to the next Session of Parliament, the Company find it utterly impracticable to raise Money sufficient to satisfy the Debts owing by them, without.an Enlargement of the Term, and an Extension of their Capital. — And he added, That the said Act hath been found to be defective in many Particulars, and it is expedient that the present Company should be dissolved, and a new one created under proper Regulations suitable to the Subject.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to dissolve the Corporation established by an Act; passed in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act to incorporate certain Persons therein named, and their Successors, " with proper Powers for the Purpose of establishing One or more Glass Manufactories within the Kingdom of Great Britain, and for the more effectually supporting and conducting the same, upon an improved Plan, in a peculiar Manner calculated fot " the casting of large Plate Glass," and to provide for the Payment of the Debts of the said Corporation, and also to incorporate certain Persons therein named, and their Successors, with proper Powers for the Purpose of carrying on the Manufactory established under the said Act; and for other Purposes therein mentioned: And that Sir Thomas Dundas and Mr. Hobart do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Chard, and Wellington, and the respective Neighbourhoods, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for building a new Bridge over the River Par ret t, within the Borough of Bridgewater, in the County of Somerset, and for repairing and maintaining the Quays in the Port of Bridgewater aforesaid, and for more effectually collecting and enforcing the Payment of the ancient and accustomed Duties, and for imposing certain new Duties at the said Port, and for regulating the Moorings and Stations of Ships and Vessels in the said Port; and Setting forth, That it appears, by the said Bill, that, in order to defray the Expence of re-building the said Bridge, and repairing and improving the Quays and Wharfs of the said Town of Bridgewater, it is proposed to lay additional

Duties upon Boats and other Vessels, and the Lading thereof, coming into the Port of Bridgewater, or passing under the said Bridge, and also to confirm and establish other Duties, which are at present very doubtful; and, that if the said Bill should pass into a Law, as it now stands, great Quantities of Coals, and a Variety of other Articles used in the Manufactures carried on by the Petitioners, and divers other Persons, in the Several Towns and Places aforesaid, will be charged with much higher Duties than they are now charged with, which will be very injurious to thp Petitioners and the Inhabitants of the several Towns &nd the Neighbourhood thereof, by subjecting them to the Payment of the said increased and doubtful Duties, and for most of which Duties the Petitioners will receive no Benefit or Advantage whatsoever; and Representing to the House, that the Mayor and Corporation of Bridgewater have, for many Years last past, received divers large Sums of Money, which, if duly accounted for, would, as the Petitioners nave goad Reason to believe, be more than adequate to rebuild the said Bridge arid repair the Quays, and that Such Bridge and Quays may be very easily repaired, and the said Bridge widened and rendered safe and commodious, at a moderate Expence: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by th'eir Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as shall appear to affect the Petitioners, and that they may have such Relief as to tjpe House shall appear ream sonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed} and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

The House was moved, That the Petition of the Proprietors, and Conservators, of the River Tone fr, om Bridgewater to Taunton, in the County of Somerset, which was presented to the House upon the 1st Day of this Instant April; and then ordered to lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second Time, might be again read.

Mr. Wilberforce\ reported from the Committee, to Clothiers whom the Petition of the Narrow Woollen Clothiers, ^eti^8 in the West Riding of the County of York', and also, repo the Petition of the White Broad Woollen Clothiers, in the West Riding of the County of York; and also, the Petition of the Mixed Broad Clothiers, in the West Riding of the County of York, were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clefk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed!; viz.

Tq prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr.

Joseph Stancliffe (a White Broad Woollen Clothier of A Airfield, near Wakefield) being examined, said, That there has been for many Years past an extensive Manufactory of Woollen Cloth of different Qualities carried on in the West Riding of Yorkshire, which has employed and maintained, with Decency and Comfort, many Thousands of Men, omen, and Children. —

That, compared with other Manufactories, he thinks this in the said West Riding, has improved much beyqnd the Cloth Trade, in any other Part of the Kingdom; the Success of which he attribute? to the Difference of the System of carrying on this Manufactory, and the Mode in which it has hitherto been conducted in other Places. — Arid being asked, Wherein that System varied ? he said, By Merchants and Manufacturers having, hitherto been, different Persons:

That this System, which, so fortunately for the Trade in general the Individuals concerned in it, and the Public at large, has, so happily long prevailed in Yorkshire, is now in Danger of being broken in upon, by Merchants establishing large Factories themselves, wherein it is intended to employ a great Number of Persons that now work at their own Houses, in the manufacturing of Cloth, which will form a Monopoly, intended to be supported by great Capitals, and set on Foot by that Description of Persons concerned in the Woollen Trade in Yorkshire, called Cloth . Merchants becoming Cloth Makers; and of late, several such Merchants, in and near the Towns of Leeds and Halifax, have commenced Clothiqjrs or Cloth Makers, and others have manifested a Disposition to follow their Example, by establishing large Factories for making Woollen Cloth, which must be highly prejudicial to the Petitioners, who, with a very trifling Capital, aided by the unremitting Labour of themselves and Families, united under one Roof, decently and independently have maintained themselves, and kept the Home Trade and Foreign Markets constantly and equally supplied, without an Idea or possibility of Monopoly, or any Advantage inconsistent with good Faith and fair Dealing, or beyond a necessary and

equitable

432 8° Aprilt. A. 1794.

equitable Profit on their Labour; and that from this comfortable and independent Situation, should such Innovation prevail, the Petitioners must separate from their Families, and be reduced to a State of Servitude to gain their Bread. — Then,

Mr. James Hebden being examined, as to the State of the Improvement of the Woollen Manufactory in the West Riding of Yorkshire; he informed the Committee, That, by an Account which he received from the Treasurer of the said West Riding, it appeared that in the Year 1769 there were made 2,771,667 Yards of Broad Cloth, and of Narrow, 2,144,019 Yards; and in the Year 1792, of the former 6,760,728 Yards, and of the latter 5,531,698 Yards.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Trustees of the Two Cloth Halls in Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, to make Bye Laws and Regulations, under certain Restrictions, the better to prevent Cloth Merchants from becoming Cloth Manufacturers; and for other Purposes: And that Mr. Wilbeiforce, Mr. Duncombe, and Mr. do prepare,

and bring in, the same.

Tibbington Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, to whom Church Peti- the Petition of the Reverend Thomas Shaw Hillier, tion repo Clerk, Curate of the Parish Church of Tipton, otherwise Tibbington, in the County of Stafford, William Underhill, and Isaac Whitehouse, Churchwardens, and the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had* directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Benjamin Horton, Clerk of the said Parish, being examined, said, That the said Parish Church is a very ancient Fabrick, and is become so ruinous that, for the Safety of Persons attending Divine Service, it is necessary that the same should be taken down, and a new Church built; and it is also necessary, either to enlarge the present Church Yard, or to purchase other Land for the Purpose of a Burial Ground for the Use of the said Parish — That it will require a very considerable Sum of Money to defray the Expences of taking down the present Church, and building and fitting up the new Church, and of enlarging the Church Yard, or purchasing Land for a new Burial Ground.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for taking down and re-building the Parish Church of Tipton, otherwise Tibbington, in the County of Stafford, and for enlarging the Cemetery or Burial Ground belonging the reto: And that Mr. Gilbert and the Earl Gower do prepare, and bring in, the same.

And to prove that such Letters Patent were made to the said Duke of Richmond and James Brudenell, in Trust and for the Benefit of the said James Bartholomew late Earl of Newburgh, Mr. Plowden produced a Deed to which the said Duke of Richmond (the said James Brudenell being then dead) was a Party, and in which he is stated to be a Kinsman of the said late Earl of Newburgh, therein called Lord Kinnaird, and by which he covenanted to stand seised of the said Estate of Ambell, during his Estate and Term therein, for the Use and Benefit of the said late Earl of Newburgh's then intended Wife Barbara Kemp, and the Issue.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are common thereunto subscribed, being Common Carriers, in Carriers Pe-that Part of Great Britain called England, using Wag- tition. gons of the several Descriptions hereafter stated, on behalf of themselves, and the several other Common Carriers, using Waggons of the like Descriptions, was presented to the House, and read '; Setting forth, That, by a Clause in an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act " of Parliament, the General Laws now in being for

" regulating

440

8° Aprilis. A. 1794.

' " regulating the Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for other Purposes," the Trustees, appointed by any Act or Acts of Parliament, for the Repair of any Turnpike Road within that Part of Great Britain called , were

authorized to erect Machines, or Engines, proper for the weighing of Carts, Waggons, or Carriages, for conveying of any Goods or Merchandize whatsoever, and they were thereby empowered to receive and take, over and above the Tolls then granted, or thereafter to be granted, the Sum of Twenty Shillings for every Hundred Weight, of One Hundred and Twelve Pounds to the Hundred, which every Waggon or Cart thereafter described, together with the Loading thereof, should weigh, over and above certain Weights thereafter allowed to each of them, respectively, viz. To every Waggon, or Four Wheel Carriage, having the Fellies or Rollers of the Wheels of the Breadth of Sixteen Inches, Eight Tons in Summer, and Seven in Winter: To every Waggon, having the Axle

Trees thereof of such different Lengths, that the Wheels shall roll only one single Surface or Path of Sixteen Inches wide at the least on each Side of the Waggon, and having the Fellies thereof of the Breadth of Nine Inches from Side to Side at the Bottom or Sole thereof, Six Tons Ten hundred in Summer, and Six Tons in Winter: To every Waggon, or Four Wheel Carriage, having the Sole or Bottom of the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Nine Inches, Six Tons in Summer, and Five Tons Ten Hundred in Winter; and, it was declared by such Act, that, for the several Purposes aforesaid, it should be deemed Summer from the 1st Day of May to the 31st of October, and Winter from the 1st of November to the 30th of April, inclusive; and that, by an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for explaining and altering an Act, made " in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, " intituled, "An Act to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the General " Laws now in being for regulating the Turnpike " Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for other Purposes; " so far as the same relates to the Payment of additional Tolls at " Weighing Engines, and the Number of Horses to " be used in Carriages drawn on Turnpike Roads, " and for allowing certain Exemptions with Respect " to Weight and Payment of Toll in particular Cases," the above recited Clause, so far as the same related- to the imposing an additional Toll of Twenty Shillings for every extra Hundred Weight, is repealed, and certain additional Tolls, enumerated in such Act, are directed to be taken in lieu thereof: That every Article, necessary for conducting the Business of a Common Carrier, has so much advanced in Price, since the Year 1773, that the Petitioners, and the other Carriers in this Kingdom, are obliged to expend yearly more than One-third of the Sums with which their Trade was formerly carried on, whereby they are considerably affected, inasmuch as the Rates of the Carriage of Goods are nearly the same now as they "p at the Time of passing the said recited Acts; and

that the Petitioners are unwilling to increase the Rates of the Carriage of Goods if the same can be avoided, as it might tend to injure the Trade of this Country, and be the Means of causing an additional Price to be imposed upon Articles conveyed by them, and the Petitioners apprehend, the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom will be benefited, and the Carriage of the Manufactories thereof to the Metropolis be greatly facilitated, if an Alteration is made in that Part of the Statute, of the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, which fixes lower Weights to be carried in Carriages or Waggons during the Winter Months than the Summer Months, the former of which are therein reckoned from the 1st Day of November to the 30th Day of April, both inclusive, and that, instead thereof, it be deemed Winter from the 1st of November to the last of February, as by that Means the Carriers would be better enabled to comply with the great Demands of the Manufacturers for Carriage of Goods, in order to be exported during the Months of March and April; and the Petitioners hope, that, as Broad Wheels have not been detrimental to the Turnpike Roads in this Kingdom, and as the Petitioners are now subject to such heavy Expences in carrying on the Trade, that the House will grant them Relief, by enabling them to carry in their respective Waggons, an additional Weight of Ten Hundred during the whole Year, and that it may be lawful for them to carry, during the Months of March and April in each Year, such Weights as they are now by Law enabled to carry during that part of the Year which in the said recited Act is deemed Summer: And therefore praying, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as the House shall deem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Bastard, Mr. Rolle, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Petition in A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are HuH Docks t^ereunt0 subjoined, being principal Merchants, Traders, Bui. and Ship Owners, of the Town of Kingston upon Hull,

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen the Petition of certain Persons, denominating themselves the principal Merchants and Traders of the Town of Kingston upon taking Notice of the Bill for extending the Dock at that Port, and stating that tire Old Harbour is the properest Place for making the necessary Accommodation for the Trade and Shipping; and that the Petitioners have no Doubt but it will be proved, to the Satisfaction of the House, that the same Reasons, which the Promoters of the present Dock produced to the Treasury, in order to obtain a Grant of Ground and Money, continue to prevail, as well in Favour of further Dock Room being immediately provided, as against the Old Harbour being used for that Purpose, namely, the Insecurity to the Public Revenue, and the Danger and Inconvenience to the Trade and Shipping, from the confined and shallow State of that Harbour; and that, should the Plan recommended in the said Petition be adopted, not only the present confined and dangerous Entrance into the Port, by which Ships are continually receiving Damage, will be left unimproved, and His Majesty's Revenue again exposed to Risque and Fraud, but the Accumulation of Mud in the said Old Harbour, by which large Ships already frequently experience great Delay and Injury, increased, and thefeby the Passage to the present Sufferance Quays, and Dock, will be much, if not totally obstructed, whereas, should the Dock be extended as proposed by the said Bill, consistent with the Recommendation of the able Engineers employed by Government, and the Concurrence of the Board of Customs, a ready Entrance into the Dock, direct from the River Hum-_ her, with a most essential Advantage of a greater Depth of Water, will be provided, a convenient and safe Mode of discharging and loading Ships afforded, the Revenues of Customs and Excise effectually secured and promoted, and many Inconveniencies, under which the Trade and Public Revenue at present labour, will, be removed; and that the Petitioners have the firmest Reliance, that the Consideration of Objects- of such great Magnitude and Importance to the Nation, as is stated in the Petitions of many of the first Manufacturing and Maritime Places in the North of England, will have a much greater Weight with the House, than the Suggestion of so small a Number as Twenty-one Persons, Nineteen of whom are either possessed themselves of Shares in the Dock required to be extended, or intimately connected with such as are: And therefore praying, That the above-mentioned Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Tabic.

Petition from A Petition of the Persons, whose Names are there-Humlets^ unto annexed> being principal Merchants, Manufac-rrainst the turers, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Di-Application vision of the Tower Hamlets, and the Parts adjoining, to license The was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, Theatre That the Petitioners, having been informed that Two Petitions have been presented to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable His Majesty to license, as a Play House, during the Summer Season, the Theatre commonly known by the Name of The Royalty Theatre, in Well Street, in the Liberty of the Tower of London, beg Leave to represent to the House, that the Building, which it is the Object of those Petitions Vo l. 49.

to convert into a licensed Theatfe, is situated immediately between the great Silk Manufactories of Spital Fields and the numerous and extensive Quays* Wharfs, Warehouses, Docks, Ship Yards, Rope Walks, and other most important Naval Establishments, on the Regularity) good Ordering, and Success* of which, the Prosperity, not of this Metropolis alone* but of the whole Kingdom, does most nearly depend: That Artizans of many Descriptions work there till the Hour of Eight in the Evening, and* on sudden Emergencies, to which, from the Nature of their Business* they are constantly subjected, to a later Hour, and that many of the Petitioners are also busied very late in their Compting Houses, Shops, and Warehouses, when they have Occasion for the Attendance of different Descriptions of-Persons engaged in their Employment^ and it would be a most serious Evil to them if their Journeymen, Servants, Apprentices, Workmen, and Labourers, were exposed to the Temptation (which a Theatre so near at Hand would necessa-; rily offer) of absenting themselves from their several Employments at a Moment when their Services might be most required, and of rendering themselves unfit for the Labour of the following Day, by the Excesses of the Evening: That Multitudes of People are employed below Bridge amongst the Shipping, whose Leisiire depends entirely upon the Tide, and for those Men to be loitering in a Play-house, at the Moment when they are wanted on the River, would be an Evil of the last Consequence, immense Property depending not only upon their Exertions but upon their Punctuality j and that still greater Numbers are employed in the Dock Yards, Rope Walks, and other Places, where Naval Manufactories are carried on, and that Idleness, and Dissipation, and a System of expensive Amusement, introduced amongst them, might prove fatal, in Moments of Public Exertion, to National Equipments, and must be so at all Times to the Interest of Commerce, the most important Venture of the Merchant being often exposed to Failure by a few Hours Delay in the Execution of his Order: And that the Petitioners, being firmly persuaded, as well from the Reason of the Thing, as from their own melancholy Experience, during the short Time the said Building was some Time since opened as a Place of Public Amusement, that these and other Evils would be the inevitable Consequence of its being now converted into a Theatre, and impressed with the most serious Concern and Alarm for the Mischiefs that they conceive must necessarily arise to the Public and themselves, therefore pray, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and that the said intended Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Bastard reported from the Committee, to whom Common the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Camera Pe-thereunto subscribed, being Common Carriers, in that Part of Great Britain called England, using Waggons of the several Descriptions thereafter stated, on Behalf of themselves, and the several other Common Carriers, using Waggons of the like Descriptions, was referred;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Jobling, of Cripplegate, Carrier, being examined, said, That the Expence of conducting the Business of a Common Carrier has increased within the last Twenty Years upwards of One Third, occasioned by the advanced Price of Horses, Oats, Beans, Hay,

Straw, and all other Matters necessary for the carrying on the Business, and the advance in Servants Wages, Blacksmiths and Wheelwrights Charges, and the additional Number of Turnpikes and Weighing Engines: That the Price of, and Allowance for carrying Goods has continued nearly the same for the last Eighteen or Twenty Years: That during the Months of March and April, there are greater Quantities of Goods required to be brought by Land Carriage from different Parts of the Country to London, for Exportation and other Purposes,' and also greater Quantities of Goods sent by Land Carriage from London, than in any other Two Months in the Year: That in those Months the Farmers Teams cannot be spared from Husbandry, and therefore the Goods cannot be conveyed but by Means of Common Carriers, and great Delay often arises from the great Quantities of Goods required to be carried in those Months: That the Common Carriers would be better enabled to comply with the Demands for carrying Goods, and the Public would be very much accommodated, if they were allowed to carry in their Waggons an additional Weight of Ten hundred during the Whole Year, and to carry during the Months of March and April in each Year, such Weights as they are now authorized to carry during that Part of the Year which is deemed Summer, by the Act of Parliament for regulating the Turnpike Roads in England.

Mr. William Holbrook, of Lawrence Lane, Carrier, confirmed the above Evidence.

Report Ex- Mr. Hobart reported from the Committee, who were piling Laws, appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued; That the Committee had made a further Enquiry, and had come to several other Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act to explain and amend the Law's relating to the Transportation, Imprisonment, and other Punishment of " certain Offenders;" and also, so much of an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, as extends to authorize the Removal of Offenders to temporary Places of Confinement, which by an Act, made in the Twenty-eighth Year of His present Majesty, were continued until the 1st Day of June 1793, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, are near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Twenty-fifth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual Transportation of Felons " and other Offenders in that Part of Great Britain " called Scotland, and to authorize the Removal of " Prisoners in certain Cases," as relates to the Removal of Offenders to temporary Places of Confinement, which was to continue in force until the tst Day of June 1787, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is expired, and fit to be revived and continued.

Mr. Darnel Williams being examined, said. That Mr. Steel opened the said Theatre for Public Entertainment, with such Amusements as were authorized by the said Licences, on the 5th of April 1790, but finding that he thereby incurred very considerable Losses, he caused the same to be closed on the 15th of May following. — That he was appointed to receive Subscriptions, which he did, to the Amount of £. 7,200; and Shares of £. 50 each were shotted to the Subscribers, who are thereby entitled to free Admission, and a certain Annuity for Twenty-one Years. That if the said Theatre was opened mr Four Months in the Summer Season, for the Performance of Theatrical Amusements, the Interests of the Renters would be substantiated, and the Lqsses of the Petitioner in a great Degree repaired; and the Witness apprehended it would be for the Public Benefit if a Place of rational Entertainment was established in the Eastern Extremity of the Metropolis.

A Petition of John Johnson, William Hodges, and Petition from Robert Graham, being Persons duly licensed for the pealers in dealing in Tickets and Shares of Tickets, according ^clMits to the several Acts of Parliament made for that Pur- against the pose, for, and on the Behalf of themselves and all other Lottery Bill, licensed Dealers under the said Act, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have regularly taken out Licences under the Sanction of the Legislature for dealing in Tickets and Shares, in foil Confidence that the usual Regulations and Protection afforded to them under the several Lottery Acts would be continued to them, and, m consequence of having taken out such Licence, the Petitioners are obliged to share Fifty Tickets each; and that the Petitioners conceive the Alterations contained in the Lottery Bill now before the House (of which they are but just apprised) to be of such a Nature, that it will not only injure and oppress the Petitioners, but will be such an Extension of Power in the Hands of Justices of the Peace, and their Followers and Dependants, as may deeply affect the Liberty and Property of every British Subject; ansi that the Petitioners more immediately allude to that Clause in the Bill which takes away the Provision of a former Act, namely, that the Persons, authorized by Justices of the Peace to hreak open Houses in search of Offenders against the Act, should be such as are employed by toe Commissioners of the Stamps, and leaves it in the Power of a Justice of the Peace to authorize any Person or Persons to act at his Discretion, and, to the following Part of the said Clause, which has not hitherto constituted a Part of any Act, for granting to His Majesty any Sum or Sums of Money, to be raised by Lottery, " and all Persons, although " not discovered in such House or Place, as aforesaid, who shall employ, or cause to be employed,

" any Person or Persons, iu carrying on any of the " Transactions aforesaid, or in aiding or assisting any " such Person or Persons, shall be deemed Rogues " and Vagabonds, and shall be punishable in like " Manner, as is directed by the said Act of the " Twenty-seventh Year aforesaid and that the Petitioners submit to the House, that the first-mentioped Part of the said Clause subjects the Petitioners, as well as every other Citizen, to have their Dwelling? violated in the Dead of Night, their Desks and Drawers forced, and their Papers examined, upon the Oath of any common Informer, without the Sanction or Intervention of the Commissioners or any other Person, as before provided, and the latter Part of the said Clause, which respects the apprehending and Conviction of all Persons, although not discovered in the House, notwithstanding it is unaccompanied by any Preamble or prefatory Words declaring the Policy of the Enaction, contains, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, Matter so novel, indefinite, and extensive, as to fill the (Minds of the Petitioners with Alarm, and appears to them to be trusting with Justices of the Peace a Power of concluding and punishing from Inference and Implication* which the Petitioners believe has hitherto resided solely, or can, consistent with the Spirit of toe Constitution, reside with a British Jury, aided by the Judges of the Land: And therefore praying the House, in case toe said Bill should be re-committed, to permit the Petitioners to be heard, by Cqpnsel, against the said Clause of the same Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

and that, in Compliance with the Terms of the said Agreement, and in full Confidence that the Period of Continuance thereby provided for must hold good, if the said Company should in any Way, or under any Firm, so long continue their Manufactory at Ravenshead, or elsewhere, the Petitioners did accordingly erect and finish certain extensive Mills, with the necessary Tools and Apparatus which have ever since, been worked, and whereby great Profit and Advantage have accrued to the said Company and the Petitioners, and the said Company are now, by the Means aforesaid, folly and entirely possessed of the said Secret and Discovery heretofore known to the Petitioners only, and which they had the Power of turning to their own exclusive Advantage at the Time they entered into the said Agreement with the said Company; House; and he reac( the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered It in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, when any Application is intended to be made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making any Cut or Canal for the Purposes of Navigation, or any Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, for the Purpose of supplying any City, Town, or Place, with Water, or for varying or altering any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, already made, or for making or improving the Navigation of any River, or for altering any Act of Parliament, passed for any or either of those Purposes (in which Bill for altering any such Act it is intended to give Power for raising any further or additional Rates, Tolls, or Duties, or for varying the Line of such Canal) Notice of such intended Application shall be inserted Three Times in T London Gazette, viz. Once in die Month of July, Once in the Month of August, and Once in the Month of September, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made: And that such Notice shall also be. inserted in some One Newspaper of every County, through which any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, is intended to be carried, or in which such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, already made, is intended to be varied or altered, or in which such River, or such Part thereof as is intended to be made navigable, or the Navigation thereof to be improved, is situated (or, if there is not any Newspaper printed in or for such Counties, respectively, then in the Newspaper of some County near or adjoining the reto) Three Times at the least, Once in the Month of July, Once in the Month of August, and Once in the Month of September, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made: And that such-Notice shall also be given at the General Quarter Session of the Peace which shall be holden for every and each County, Riding, or Division, through which any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, -is intended to be carried, or in which such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, already made, is intended to be varied or altered, or in which such River, or such Part thereof as is intended to be made navigable, or the Navigation thereof to be improved, is situated, at the Michaelmas preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made, by affixing such Notice to the Door of the Session Houses, respectively, where such General Quarter Session shall be holden.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such several Notices shall contain the Names of the Parishes and Townships in, to, or through, which any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, is intended to be carried, varied, or altered, or in which such River, or such Part thereof as is intended to be made navigable, or the Navigation thereof to be improved, is situated.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Map or Plan of such intended Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, and also of any intended Alteration in any Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, already made, shall be deposited, for Public Inspection, at the Office of the Clerk of the Peace of every County, Riding, or Division, through which such Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, is intended to be carried, or such Alteration is intended to be made, on or before the 30th Day of September previous to the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made; which Map or Plan shall describe the Line of such intended Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, or of such intended Alteration, and the Lands through which the same is intended to be carried, together with a Book of Reference, containing a List of the Names of the Owners,

5

or reputed Owners, and Occupiers, of strch Lands respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, before any Application is made to the House for any or either , of the Purposes aforesaid, a previous Application shall be made to the Owners, or reputed Owners and Occupiers, of the Lands through which any such Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, is intended to be' carried, or any such Alteration is intended to be made; and that separate Lists shall be made of the Names of such Owners and Occupiers, distinguishing which of them, upon such Application, have assented to, or dissented from, such intended Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, or such Alteration, or are neuter in respect thereto.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever any Petition is presented to the House for any or either of the Purposes aforesaid, there shall be presented, with such Petition, the Lists mentioned in the last preceding Resolution, and also a Duplicate of the Map or Plan so to be deposited at the Office of the Clerk of the Peace, as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever any Petition is presented to the House for making, varying, or altering, any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, as aforesaid, or making or improving the N avigation of a River, there be annexed to the said Petition an Estimate of the proposed Expence of such Undertaking (in Cases where Provision is intended to be made for raising Money to defray such Expence) such Estimate to be signed by the Person or Persons making the same; send, if such Money is proposed to be raised by Subscription, that there be also annexed to the said Petition, an Account of the Money subscribed for that Purpose, and the Names of the Subscribers, with the Sums by them subscribed respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, whenever any Petition has been presented to the House for the Purposes aforesaid, or any or either of them, the Committee, to whom such Petition shall be referred, do examine, in the first Place, how far the Orders contained in the preceding Resolutions have been complied with, and do report the same, at the Time when they report the Matter of any such Petition, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be Seven Days between the First and Second Reading of such Bills.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons, Owners, or reputed Owners, and Occupiers of the Land through which any such Cut, Canal, Aqueduct, or Navigation, is intended to be carried, or any such Alteration is intended to be made, do Personally attend the Committee, to whom such Bill shall be committed; or if they do not Personally attend, do give their Certificate in Writing, signifying that they have seen a printed Copy of the said Bill, and do give their Consent, or Dissent thereto, or declare themselves neuter in respect thereof; and that the Hand Writing of such Owner or Occupier to such Certificate be proved by One or more Witnesses before the said Committee; and that the said Committee shall report to the House, together with the Report of the said Bill, a List of the Names of such Persons who shall appear to them to have given such Assent or Dissent, or to have been neuter, in respect to the said Bill.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be Seven Days between the Day on which such Bill is reported to the House, and the Day when the said Report shall be taken into Consideration.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, after such Bill is reported to the House, and before the Report is taken into Consideration, the Bill, as amended by the Committee, be printed, at the

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Ord and Mr. Walker:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open Common Fields, Ings, Moors, Commons, and Waste Grounds, within the Township of Skelton, in the Canon, Fee, Manor, and Parish of Ripon, in the West Riding of the County of York; without any Amendment: And also,

TTie Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing the Open Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Commonable Lands, and Waste Grounds, within the Parishes of Long Bennington and Foston, in the County of Lincoln; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Terms and Powers of Two Acts, made in the Twentieth and Thirtieth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing the High Road leading from the North End of the Cow-Cawsey, near the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, to the 'town of Belford, and from thence to Buckton Bum, in the County of Northumberland; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making a Navigable Canal from the River Kermet, at, or near, the Town of Newbury, in the County of Berks, to the River Avon, at, or near, the City of Bath, and also certain Navigable Cuts therein described; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing the Road from Stirling to Dumbarton, and several other Roads in the Counties of Vo h.49.

Dumbarton, and Perth;without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House, That their Lordships will proceed further in the Trial of Warren Hastings, Esquire, on Monday, the 28th Day of this Instant April, at Ten of the Clock, in Westminster Hall.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Portions for tile Daughters of the Marriage, Remainder to the said John Gardner Kemeys in Tail, in strict Settlement.

And the Witness also produced an examined Copy of an Act of Parliament, made and passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for vesting the settled and unsettled Estates of John Gardner Kemeys, Esquire, in u Trustees, in Trust, by Sale or Mortgage to raise tf Money to pay off Portions and Debts, and re-Vo L.49.

" deem Annuities charged upon, and affecting the " same, and for resettling the Remainder thereof, and " Lands to be purchased as in the said Act is directed, " to the Uses to which the said settled Estates do now " Stand settled and limited;" in which it was alledged, that the said John Gardner Kemeys was seised in Fee of an Estate in Monmouthshire, adjoining to, and intermixed with the settled Estate, then of the Yearly Value of £. 566, in which had been discovered some Ore that was likely to prove very beneficial: And further, That the said Gardner Kemeys, since the Execution of the said Settlement, was become seised of a convenient Tract of Land contiguous to the said Plantation, and that he had expended considerable Sums in lasting Improvements for the Use of, and in extending the Plantation, by cultivating a large Tract of Waste Lands, which was before of little or no Value, and in purchasing an additional Number of Negroes proper for the Improvement thereof, by Means whereof the Annual Income of the Plantation had been increased from £. 1,200 a Year, to the Sum of £. 2,500, and the Annual Income was likely, in a few Years, to be much further increased: And being further examined, he said, That the said John Gardner Kemeys had also expended very considerable Sums upon the Monmouth settled Estate, in repairing and enlarging the Mansion, in re-building and repairing Farm Houses, and by inclosing and cultivating great Part of the barren and unprofitable Lands, by planting a very considerable Quantity of Oak and other Trees, which were in a very thriving Condition, and in other lasting and permanent Improvements, by Means whereof the Annual Income of that Estata was increased in Value to £. 981 per Annum and upwards, and by the Annual Growth and Increase of the Trees so planted, the Inheritance of the said Premisses would in a few Years be considerably improved: And further, that there was then growing upon the settled Monmouth Estate, a considerable Quantity of Timber and other Trees in a very thriving Condition, which, upon a fair Valuation, were worth then to be sold £. 6,000 and upwards: And it was also further stated, that to enable the said John Gardner Kemeys to make the several Purchases mid Improvements aforesaid, and thereby to increase as well the Yearly Income, as the Value of the Inheritance of the settled Estates for the Benefit of the Issue Male, claiming under the Settlement to the Amount before-mentioned, and without which no such Advantage could accrue to them, the said John Gardner Kemeys had been necessarily obliged not only to contract Debts to the Amount of £. 31,976 or upwards, but to grant several Annuities out of the settled Estates during his Life, to the Yearly Amount of £. 1,300, which were redeemable, and which (with the Incumbrances on the settled Estates prior to the Settlement) made together £. 44,026, or thereabouts; and that the said John Gardner Kemeys having been threatened with Suits at Law and in Equity by his Creditors, he was advised, and apprehended it would be for the Benefit and Advantage of himself and Family, and all Persons claiming under the Limitations of the Settlement, and be a Means of preserving great Part of the settled and unsettled Estates, if he was enabled by Sale or Mortgage to raise Money sufficient to pay off the Portions, Debts, and Sums of Money so owing by him, and to redeem the Annuities so granted by nim, as he would thereby afterwards have a clear Estate of Inheritance left for the Benefit and Preservation of himself and Family, of the Yearly Value of £. 2,500 and upwards, exclusive of what might thereafter arise from Ore that had been discovered on his unsettled Estate, which he was desirous of preserving, as it might eventually prove very valuable and advantageous to himself and Family; and that in order to make Compensation to the Issue Male inheritable under the Limitations of the

the Settlement, for the Prejudice, if any, that might accrue to him or them by such Sale or Mortgage to be made as aforesaid, the said Gardner Kemeys had proposed and consented that so much of the Plantation and other settled Estates as should not be sold, and the Equity of Redemption of so much as should be mortgaged, should be absolutely discharged from any further Debt he might contract, and that so much of the Plantation Lanas and Negroes as had been purchased by him since the Settlement, together with the Watercourse or Canal, Mills, Erections, Buildings, and Improvements, which, on a fair Calculation, according to the Annual Improvement of the said Estate, might be estimated at £. 18,000 at the least, together with the Estate in Monmouthshi, whereof he was seised in Fee, except the Mines and Minerals within the said Estate, and which was then of the Yearly Value of £.566, and in its then Situation was worth to be sold £. 15,000 at least, should, subject to the raising the £. 44,026 or thereabouts, be vested in Trustees, and settled to the same Uses as the Estates comprized in the Settlement did then stand limited and settled; and as a further Compensation as aforesaid, he was willing and desirous not only to relinquish, for the Benefit of his Issue Male, the Claim he had upon the setded Estates in , in respect of the great Sums expended by him in lasting Improvements, and which might be estimated at £. 8,000 at the least, and also to waive and divest himself of his Power of cutting down Timber and committing Waste on the said setded Estate, which was computed to amount to and be worth £. 5,000 at least, and also was willing that One Third Part of the clear Profits which might arise from the Mines and Minerals which then were, or might be discovered in the said unsetded Estates, should be vested in Trustees, as an accumulating and auxiliary Fund, towards paying off and discharging the Money then to be raised, so far as the same should extend; and after the above Statements, the Act proceeded to vest all the aforesaid setded and unsettled English and Jamaica Estates in Trustees, for raising, by Sale or Mortgage, such Sums as should be necessary for paying the Costs of the said Act, and the Trusts thereby created, and the Portions, Debts, Sums of Monty, and Incumbrances, and redeeming the Annuities specified in a Schedule, and all Interest of the said Debts and Incumbrances, and Arrears of the said Annuities which should be due at the Time of the Payment thereof, the Amount of all which Debts and Incumbrances, and Arrears of Interest, and of Annuities, and of the Monies required to redeem the said Annuities, are calculated in the said Schedule to amount to the said Sum of £. 44,026, for effectuating the other Purposes mentioned in the Recitals of the said Act — And the Witness also produced a Mortgage of all the.English and Jamaica. Estates, settled ana unsettled, dated 26 and 27 June 1772, and several Indorsements thereon, also proved in the before-mentioned Cause, and executed by the Trustees of the before-stated Act, to a Trustee for the Right honourable Richard Rigby, for securing £. 48,000, out of which he says the Trustees paid and satisfied the Debts and Incumbrances, and redeemed the Annuities provided for by the Act, and the Interest and Arrears thereof; but the Court of Chancery, in the aforesaid Cause instituted by the late Richard Rigby for Foreclosure of the said mortgaged Estates, decreed, that the Trustees were only authorized to raise £. 41,386. 13#. 6d. under the Powers given them by the said Act, and accordingly the Trustees, were ordered to pay the difference to Mr. Rigby, which they have done; that there now remains due, for the Principal and Interest, the Sum of £. 53,000 or thereabouts, and that the mortgaged Estates are greatly insufficient for the Payment thereof: — And being further examined, he said.

That all the said mortgaged Estates are in the Possession of Agents appointed by the Representatives of the said late Richard Rigby; and that it further appears, from the Accounts passed before Mr. Holford, one of the Masters of the Court of Chancery, and contained in his Report made in the before-mentioned Cause, dated the 23d December 1786, and also by the Account produced by the acting Executor of the said Richard Rigby, delivered upon Oath, that on an Average for Seven Years, namely from 1785 to 1792, the said Plantation and Estate in Jamaica have not produced more than £. 1,100 per Annum, and that the Estate and Premisses in the County of Monmouth, during the same Period, have not produced more than £. 550 per Annum, and that the Purchase of the unsettled Estate was made for a Sum of £. 3,543.

That the whole Value of the Timber on the Whole of the Monmouthshire Estates, in the Year 1781, both full grown and fit to be cut, and young Timber not fit to be cut, amounted together only to the Sum of £. 3,000.

William Kemeys, Esquire, being examined, said, That no Ore has ever yet been discovered in the said Estates of the Value of Five Shillings; and no Timber has been cut down, save for necessary Repairs, and Sea Stakes.

Joseph Hill, Esquire, being examined, said, That it appears by a Letter from Simon Taylor, Esquire, the late Receiver of the Jamaica Estate, that the said John Gardner Kemeys died in Jamaica in or about the Month of July last.

The said Mr. Robert Sturdy being again examined, said, That the late Richard Rigby, Esquire, on whose Behalf the said Mortgage was taken as aforesaid, died indebted to Government in the Sum of £. 140,000, and upwards; and that Daniel Mc Namara, Esquire, is his sole acting Executor.

James Clitherow, Esquire, being examined, said.

That Jane Gardner Kemeys, the Widow, has no Provision whatever, save what she took under the before-mentioned Settlement: That Jane Gardner Hansard, and Susannah Margaret Gardner Kemeys, the Two Daughters of the late John Gardner Kemeys, have little or no Property, save the Provision made for them under the said Settlement; and that John Kemeys Gardner Kemeys has no Provision or Fortune whatever, save some small Fortune he had with his present Wife:

And that the said John Kemeys Gardner Kemeys has Two Infant Children.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will immediately resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord. TRANSLATION

Article Third.

493

34 Geo. III.

28° Apritis.

TRANSLATION of a Treaty between His Majesty, the King of Prussia, and the States General of The United Provinces, signed at the Hague, the 19th of April *794-

Their Majesties the King of Great Britain and of Prussia, and their High Mightinesses the States General of The United Provinces, being animated by the same Desire of putting a Stop to the Progress of the System of Anarchy and Crimes by which Civil So-'ciety has been menaced, and being desirous of concerting together to support in the most effectual Manner the Common Cause in which they are engaged, in consequence of the unjust and cruel War, which the Persons, who exercise the Powers of Government in France, have raised up against several of the Great Powers of Europe, have agreed, in Conformity to the Bonds of Friendship and Alliance which so happily unite them, to conclude the present Treaty; and for this Purpose, they have named their respective Plenipotentiaries; to wit, His Britannick Majesty, the Lord Baron of Malmesbury, a Peer of the Kingdom of Great Britain, Privy Councillor, Knight of the Order of the Bath; his Prussian Majesty, the Sieur Chretien Henry Ceerce, Comte de His Minis-

ter of State, of War, and of the Cabinet, Knight of the Order of the Red Eagle; and their High Mightinesses the States General of The United Provinces, the Sieurs Laurent Pierre van de Spiegel, Counsellor Pensionary of the Province of Holland and West Frieseland, Keeper of the Seals, and Deputy of the said Province at the Assembly of the States General, and Henry Fagel, Greffier of their High Mightinesses; who, after having communicated to each other their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article First.

His Majesty the King of Prussia engages to furnish an Army which shall be composed of Sixty-two thousand Four hundred Men, conformably to the Establishment which he has caused to be delivered to the Ministers of the Maritime Powers, which Establishment shall be considered as making Part of the present Treaty. This Army shall remain united under a Prussian Commander, and shall act in the most effectual Manner against the Common Enemy, either separately, or jointly with a Body of Troops in the Pay of the Maritime Powers, or of One of them. The said Army shall be and shall remain as complete as possible, and shall be employed, according to a Concert on Military Points between His Britannick Majesty, his Prussian Majesty, and their High Mightinesses the States General of The United Provinces, wherever it shall be judged to be most suitable to the Interests of the Maritime Powers. This Army shall arrive at the Place of its Destination on the 24th of May in the Year 1794, or sooner if possible: It shall be provided with Field Pieces, with their Carriages, and also with the Tents, and all Military1 Equipments necessary for acting in the Field.

Article Second.

It is agreed by the High Contracting Parties, that the Troops which ms Prussian Majesty is bound to furnish to His Britannick Majesty, and to their High Mightinesses, by virtue of the respective Treaties of Alliance between his Prussian Majesty and the Maritime Powers, shall be comprized in this Army of Sixty-two thousand Four hundred Men, and that by employing the said Army in the Manner declared in this present Treaty, his Prussian Majesty shall be deemed to have furnished to his High Allies the Succours stipulated by the said Treaties.

Vo l. 49.

Iii order to facilitate to his Prussian Majesty the Treaty with Means of acting with Vigour, and conformably to the Pru8Uai Sentiments of Zeal and Concern for the Common Cause with which he is animated, His Britannick Majesty and their High Mightinesses agree to furnish to his Prussian Majesty a Subsidy of Fifty Thousand Pounds Sterling, per Month, until the End of the present Year, and to be reckoned from the Beginning of the Month in which the present Treaty is signed.

Article Fourth.

His Britannick Majesty and their High Mightinesses will pay to his Prussian Majesty immediately, the Sum of Three hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, to enable him to defray the Charge of completing the above-mentioned Army, and the first Expences necessary for putting it in a State of Action, and for carrying it to the Place where it is to act; and at the Period of the Return of the said Troops, His Britannick Majesty and their High Mightinesses will moreover pay to his Prussian Majesty the Sum of One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, for the Expences of the Return of the Army into the Territories of his Prussian Majesty. The said Payments for the Expences of completing and putting the Troops in Motion shall be made immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications, as well as that of the first Subsidy, to be paid Monthly, of Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling. The following Months shall be discharged in Advance at the Beginning of each Month. All these Payments shall be made at Berlin, by the Maritime Powers, agreeably to such Arrangement as they shall agree upon between themselves; and the Pound Sterling shall be reckoned at Six Crowns in Frederic's <TOr.

Article Fifth.

The above-mentioned Subsidy and Payments shall satisfy all Demands which his Prussian Majesty might be entitled to make upon the Maritime Powers for the Expences of the Army; all these Expences, of what Nature soever they may be, being to be defrayed by his Prussian Majesty, with the Exception only of the Expences of Bread and Forage, which shall be furnished by the Maritime Powers, as well for the Thirty two thousand Four hundred Men whom his Prussian Majesty engages to employ over and above the stipulated Succours, as for those Succours themselves, in a Manner conformable to the Terms of the Treaties of Alliance subsisting between the Maritime Powers and his said Majesty. But in order to avoid the Difficulties which might arise relative to the furnishing of these Articles in Kind, the High Contracting Parties agree that this Expence shall be satisfied in Money, reckoning at the Rate of One Pound Twelve Shillings (Stg. Money of England) per Month, for each Man of the Sixty-two thousand Four hundred, to be furnished by his Prussian Majesty, according to the Establishment hereinbefore mentioned, and the Payment of this Sum shall be made iii Advance, at the Beginning of each Month, in the same Manner as that of the Subsidy, and shall begin the same Day: But, if it shall happen in future that any Variation shall be made, by Consent of the High Contracting Parties, in the respective Proportions of Infantiy, Cavalry, and Artillery, settled by the said Establishment, in such -Case a new Valuation of the aforesaid pecuniary Aid shall be made, according to the new Proportion of Rations and Portions which may result from the said Variation, so that the said valuation may not be beyond the actual Expences occasioned by the furnishing of the Articles in Question, according to the Proportion of Men and Horses which shall be employed.

It 4s agreed that all Conquests made »by this Army -shall be made in die Names of die Two Maritime iPowers, and shall mmain At their Disposal during the Course of the vWar, and at the Peace to be made such ~Use of as they shall (than judge most proper.

Article Seventh.

The Two Maritime 'Powers shall name Two Persons, commissioned to reside in their Names at the Head Quarters of the Prussian Army, to keep up the necessary Communication and Correspondence between the jeqpeetwre Aqnies.

3Hbs Treaty shall continue in its full Force until tire End the present Year 1794.

Article Ninth.

The present Treaty shall be ratified by all Parties, and the Exchange of the Ratifications shall be made in the Space of One Month, or sooner if possible.

In Witness of which, we, the Plenipotentiaries of His Britannick Majesty, and of his Prussian Majesty, and of the Lords States General of The United Provinces, by Virtue of our respective Powers, have signed the present Treaty, and have hereunto affixed the Seal of our Arms.

Done at the Hague, the 19th of April in the Year of Grace 1794.
