Faction, or a blameable Jealousy, but was founded iu sound Reason and true Policy.

ft may be objected, that the Resolution of the 12 th of May 1679 goeth 00 further than to a Proceeding upon Impeachment

The Letter of the Resolution, it is admitted, goeth no further; but thi6 is easily accounted for: A Proceeding by Impeachment was the Subject Matter of the Conference, and the Commons had no Pretence to interpose in any other. But what say the Lords ? The High Steward is but as a Speaker or Chairman, pro Tempore, for the more orderly proceeding at the Trials; the Appointment of him doth not alter the Nature of the Court, which still remaineth the Court of the Peers in Parliament. From these Premises they draw dm Conclusion I have mentioned. Are not these Premises equally true in the Case of a Proceeding upon Indictment ? — They undoubtedly are.

It must likewise be admitted, that in the Proceeding upon Indictment the High Steward's Commission hath never varied from the ancient Form in such Cases; the Words objected to by the Commons, Ac pro eo qudd Officium Seneschalli Anglia (ague -

sentia in hoc Parte requiritur) ut accepimusjam vacat, are still retained. But this proveth no more than that the Great Seal having no Authority to vary in Point of Form, hath from Time to Time very prudently followed ancient Precedents.

I have already stated the Substance of the Commission, in a Proceeding in the Court of the High Steward. I will now state the Substance of that in a Proceeding in the Court of the Peers in Parliament. And shall make use of that in the Case of the Earl of Kilmarnock and others, as being the latest, and, in Point of Form, agreeing with the former Precedents.

The Commission, after reciting that William Earl of Kilmarnock, &c. stand indicted before Commissioners of Gaol Delivery, in the County of Surrey, for High Treason in levying War against the King; and that the King intendeth that the said William Earl of Kilmarnock, &c. shall be heard, examined, sentenced, and adjudged before Himself in this present Parliament, touching the said Treason, and for that the Qfhce of Steward of Great Britain (whose Presence is required upon this Occasion) Is now vacant as we are informed, appointeth the then Lord Chancellor Steward of Great Britain, to bear, execute, and exercise (for this Time) the said Office, with all Things due and belonging to the same Office, in that Behalf.

What, therefore, are the Things due and belonging to the Office in a Case of this Kind ? Not, as in the Court of the High Steward, a Right of Judicature- For the Commission itself supposeth that Right to reside in a Court then subsisting before the King in Parliament. The Parties are to he there heard, sentenced, and adjudged. What Share in the Proceeding doth the High Steward then take I By the Practice and Usage of the Court of the Peers in Parliament, he giveth his Vote as a Member thereof with the rest of the Peers; but for the Sake'of Regularity and Order, he presideth during the Trial, ami until Judgment, as Chairman or Speaker, pro Tempore. In that Respect, therefore, it may be properly enough said, that his Presence is required during the Trial, and until Judgment, and in no other. Herein I see no Difference between the Case of an Impeachment, and of an Indictment-

I say during the Time of the Trial, and until Judgment, because the Court hath, as I observed before, from Time to Time, done various Acts, plainly judicial, before the Appointment of an High Steward, and where no High Steward hath ever been appointed, and even after the Commission dissolved.

I will to this Purpose die a few Cases,

I begin with the latest, because they are the latest, and were ruled with great Deliberation, and for the most Part, upon a View of former Precedents.

In the Case of the Earl of Kilmarnock and others, the Lords, on the 24th of June, 1746, ordered, that a Writ or Writs of Certiorari be issued for removing the Indictments before the House. And on the 26th the Writ, which is made returnable before the King in Parliament, with the Return and Indictments, was received and read. On the next Day, upon the Report of the Lords Committees, that they had been attended by the Two Chief Justices, and Chief Baron, and had heard them touching the Construction of the Act of the Seventh and Eighth of King William,

" For regulating Trials in Cases of High Treason,

" and Misprision of Treason," the House, upon reading the Report, came to several Resolutions, founded for the most Part on the Construction of that Act What that Construction was, appeareth from the Lord High Steward's Address to the Prisoners, just before their Arraignment. Having mentioned that Act, as One happy Consequence of the Resolution, he addeth,

" However injuriously that Resolution hath been traduced, whatever Attempts have been made to subvert this happy Establishment founded on it, your " Lordships will now have the Benefit of that Law in " its full Extent."

I need not after this mention any other Judicial Acts done by the House in this Case, before the Appointment of the High Steward — many there are. For, the putting a Construction upon an Act relative to the Conduct of the Court, and the Right of the Subject at the Trial, and in the Proceedings preparatory to it, and this in a Case entirely new, and upon a Point, to say no more in this Plaoe, not extremely clear, was undoubtedly an Exercise of Authority proper only for a Court having full Cognizance of the Cause.

I will not minutely enumerate the several Orders made preparatory to the Trial of Lord Lavat, and in the several Cases I shall have Occasion to mention, touching the Time and Place of the Trial, the Allowance or Non-allowance of Counsel, and other Matters of the like Kind, all plainly Judicial, because the like Orders occur in all the Cases where a Journal of the preparatory Steps hath been published by Order of the Peers. With regard to Lord Lavat'& Case,

I think the Order directing the Form of the High Steward's Commission, which I have already taken Notice of, is not very consistent with the Idea of a Court, whose Powers can be supposed to depend, at any Point of Time, upon the Existence or Dissolution of that Commission.

In the Case of the Earl of and the

other Lords impeached at the same Time, the House received and recorded the Confessions of those of them who pleaded guilty, long before the Teste of the High Steward's Commission, which issued merely for the Solemnity of giving Judgment against them upon their Conviction.

This appeareth by the Commission itself: It re-citeth that the Earl of Derwentwater, and others. Coram Nobis in prasenti Parliamento, had been impeached by the Commons for High Treason, and had, Corrm Nobis in prasenti Parliamento, pleaded guilty to that Impeachment; and that the King, intending that the said Earl of Derwentwater and others, de <§T pro proditione unde ipsi ut prafertur imped it', aecusit',

The receiving end recording the Confession of the Prisoners, which amounted to a Conviction, so that nothing remained but proceeding to Judgment, was certainly an Exercise of Judicial Authority, which no Assembly, how great soever, not having full Cognizance of the Cause, could exercise.

In the case of Lord Salisbury, who had been impeached by the Commons for High Treason, the Lords, upon his Petition, allowed him the Benefit of the Act of General Pardon passed in the Second Year of William and Mary, so far as to discharge him from his Imprisonment upon a Construction they put upon that Act, no High Steward ever having been appointed in that Case.

On the 2d of October, 1690, upon reading the Earl's Petition, Setting forth, that he had been a Prisoner for a Year and Nine Months, in the Tower, notwithstanding the late Act of Free and General Pardon, and praying to be discharged, the Lords ordered the Judges to attend on the Monday following, to give their Opinions, whether the said Earl be pardoned by the Act. On the 6th the Judges delivered their Opinions, that if his Offence was committed before the 13th of February 1688, and not in Ireland, or beyond the Seas, he is pardoned. Whereupon it was ordered, that he be admitted to Bail, and the next Day he and his Sureties entered into a Recognizance of Bail, himself in £.10,000 and Two Sureties in £.5,000 each; and on the 30th he and his Sureties were, after a long Debate, discharged from their Recognizance.

It will not be material to esquire, whether the House did right in discharging the Earl without giving the Commons an Opportunity of being heard; since, in Fact, they claimed and exercised a Right of Judicature without an High Steward — which is the only Use I make of this Case.

They did the same in the Case of the Earl of

warth, the Lords Widdrington and Nairn, long after the High Steward's Commission dissolved.

These Lords had Judgment passed on them at the same Time that Judgment was given against the Lords Derwentwater, Nithsdale, and and Judg-

ment being given, the High Steward immediately broke his Staff, and declared the Commission dissolved. They continued Prisoners in the Tower under Reprieves, till the passing of the Act of General Pardon, in the Third of King George the First.

Lords Journ. On the 21st of November 1717, the House being informed that these Lords had severally entered into Recognizances before one of the Judges of the Court of King's Bench, for their Appearance in the House in this Sessions of Parliament; and that the Lords warth and Widdrington were attending accordingly; and that the Lord Naim was ill at Bath, and could not then attend; the Lords Camwarth and Widdrington were called in; and severally, at the Bar, prayed that their Appearance might be recorded; and likewise prayed 3 G. I. c. 19. the Benefit of the Act for His Majesty's General and Free Pardon.

Whereupon the House ordered that their Appearance be recorded, and that they attend again Tomorrow, in order to plead the Pardon. And the Recognizance of the Lord Naim was respited till that Day Fortnight.

On the Morrow the Lords Camwarth and Widdrington, then attending, were called in; and the Lord Chancellor acquainted them severally, that it appeared by the Records of the House,' that they severally stood attainted of High Treason; and asked them severally, what they had to say, why they should not be remanded to the Tower of London?

Thereupon they severally, upon their Knees, prayed the Benefit of the Act, and that they might have their Lives and Liberties pursuant thereunto.

Voju 49.

And the Attorney General, who then attended for Report on that Purpose, declaring that he had no Objection on Pn>* His Majesty's Behalf, to what was prayed, conceiving that those Lords, not having made any Escape since ing»'» Trial, their Conviction, were entitled to the Benefit of the Act; the House, after reading the Clause in the Act relating s?ehSect-45-to that Matter, agreed that they should be allowed the 0 e 3 Benefit of the Pardon, as to their Lives and Liberties; and discharged their Recognizances, and gave them Leave to depart without further Day given for their. Appearance.

On the 6th of December following the like Proceedings were had, and the like Orders made, in the Case of Lord Nairn.

I observe that the Lord Chancellor did not ask these Lords what they had to say why Execution should not be awarded. There was, it is probable, some little Delicacy as to that Point. But since the Allowance of the Benefit of the Act, as to Life and Liberty, which was all that was prayed, was an effectual Bar to any future Imprisonment on that Account, and also to Execution, and might have been

?leaded as such in any Court whatsoever; the whole 'roceeding must be admitted to have been in a Court having complete Jurisdiction in the Case, notwithstanding the High Steward's Commission had been long dissolved — which is all the Use I intended to make of this Case.

I will not recapitulate; the Cases I have cited, and the Conclusions drawn from them, are brought into a very narrow Compass. I will only add, it would sound extremely harsh to say, that a Court of Criminal Jurisdiction, founded in immemorial Usage, and held in Judgment of Law before the King himself, can in any Event whatever be under an utter Incapacity of proceeding to Trial and Judgment, either of Condemnation or Acquittal, the ultimate Objects of every Criminal Proceeding, without certain Supplemental Powers derived from the Crown.

These Cases, with the Observations I have made on them, I hope sufficiently warrant the Opinion of the Judges upon that Part of the Second Question in the Case of the late Earl Ferrers, which I have already mentioned. And also what was advanced by the Lord Chief Baron in his Argument on that Question, " That though the Office of High Steward " should happen to determine before Execution done " according to the Judgment, yet the Court of the " Peers in Parliament, where that Judgment was " given, would subsist for all the Purposes of Justice " during the Sitting of the Parliament." And consequently that in the Case supposed by the Question, that Court might appoint a new Day for the Execution.

A Petition of Thomas Hooton, Gentleman, George Pitt Hurst, Gentleman, and William Davies, Clerk, Stephen Hoddle, John Hollingworth, and William Underwood, Master and Governors of Queen s Hospital, in Newport Pagnel, in the County of Bucks, and John Walton Hooton, Gentleman, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Lands and Grounds lying and being in a certain Open and Common Field, called Port Field, in the Parish of Newport Pagnel, in the VoL. 49.

County of Buckingham; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are Owners and Proprietors of Part of the Lands lying in the said Open and Common Field, and have not been consulted upon, or apprized of, the Terms upon which the said Inclosure is to take place, save by a Perusal of the said Bill; that the Commissioners therein named are altogether unknown to the Petitioners, but have, as the Petitioners apprehend and believe, been named by, or at the particular Instance of, George Lord Viscount Valentia, and Sir John Buchanan Riddell; and, in case of the Death, or Refusal to act, of either of the said Commissioners, the Survivor is authorized to nominate another Commissioner, and that, in Case of Difference between the said Commissioners, the Matter shall be referred to George Maxwell, therein mentioned, a Person also named by the said Lord Viscount Valentia, and Sir John Buchanan Riddell; and that there is a Clause contained in the said Bill, whereby the Commissioners are authorized and required to assign and allot, to the said Lord Viscount Valentia, as Lord of the Manor of Newport Pagnel, such Parcel and Quantity of Ground, in the said Open and Common Field, called Port Field, as by the said Commissioners shall be adjudged to be an adequate Compensation for his Right of Soil of the Lands and Grounds lying Waste in the said Open and Common Fields, and for his Consent to the Inclosure thereof; and that the Commissioners named in the said Bill are to be paid Two Guineas per Day each in travelling to, returning from, and attending in, the Execution of the Act; and if any of the Owners or Proprietors of the said Lands and Grounds, intended to be divided or inclosed, or any other Person or Persons, shall advance any Sum or Sums of Money, for the Purpose of applying and obtaining the said Act, or for putting the same into Execution, they shall be repaid the same with Interest, after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, out of the first Monies that shall be raised by the said Commissioners, in pursuance of the Powders thereby given to them; and that the Petitioners apprehend and believe, that the said Lord Viscount as

Lord of the Manor of Newport Pagnel aforesaid, is not entitled to any Allotment, as a Compensation for Right of Soil, in any Lands lying waste in the said Fields, for there is no Land of that Description, and therefore he is entitled only as any other common Proprietor, and consequently, was any such Allotment to be made him on that Account, or for his Assent to the Inclosure, it must be at the Expence of the Petitioners and the other Proprietors, which is contrary to Justice; and that the Petitioners apprehend and submit, that the Nomination of Commissioners wholly unknown to them, and a Reference to a third Person, named by Part of the Proprietors only, of any Matters, about which the Commissioners may disagree, is by no Means usual, and the Rights and Interests of the Petitioners may be materially affected thereby, and that the Allowance of Two Guineas per Day, to each of the said Commissioners, is a larger Allowance than is generally made on such Occasions, and that an Interest of Five Pounds per Centum, for the Money advanced in procuring the Act, ought not to be charged; and that several of the Petitioners are Proprietors of Land in certain other Common Fields in Newport Pagnel aforesaid, called Tick-ford Fields, and therefore, if the present Bill pass into a Law, and the Port Fields alone be inclosed, the Expences of such of the Petitioners who are Owners of Land in both Fields will be considerably increased in case the Tickford Fields should ever be inclosed; and that the Parish of Newport Pagnel is burthened with a numerous Poor, and, should tire Inclosure take place, there will be much less Employment for the Poor than there is at present, for, that the said Port Fields, the Petitioners apprehend, will be principally

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro- Motion for posed. That the Bill for the Purpose of protecting reading Wooleombers from being injured in their Manufacture ^olc°mbe by the Use of certain Machines lately introduced 60011

for the combing of Wool, be now read a Second Time;

A Petition of the thereunder-signed Persons, in Petition from their own Behalf, and in Behalf of their Partners, Proprietors of Proprietors of Four large and expensive Manufactories ^^inNot-in the Counties of Nottingham and York, was pre- tinghamshire sented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, and York-in a firm Reliance on that Wisdom of the British Le- shire against

n# t> jii

gislature, which has left an unlimited. Field of Exercise to the ingenious Artizan, for the Improvement of Manufactures and Extension of the National Commerce, the Petitioners were not alarmed at the Petition of the Wooleombers, nor apprehended even the Appearance of a Bill in favour of Views, which, in their Principle are partial, in their Operation restrict the Choice of Labour, and, in their Consequences, must inflict a dangerous Wound on the Manufactures and Commerce of the Kingdom: That finding, from the Votes, that a Bill in favour of the Wooleombers has been received and passed a first Hearing, the Petitioners think it behoves them to appear before the House in Behalf of themselves and of their Country, not less confiding, than from the first, in the Wisdom and Justice of the Legislature, but thinking that they should be wanting, both to the House and themselves, if they should omit to lay before the House that Information which is derived from Experience, and which they respectfully submit to the Judgment of the House: That it appears to be the General Right of the Subject, which the Wisdom of the Legislature has for Ages admitted, that he be at Liberty to exercise his Art or Profession in that Way which appears to be the most conducive to his Interest, nor offends against the Laws or the Right of others; that of this Interest he is himself in all Instances the fittest Judge, and that from this unfettered and well-directed Pursuit of Individual Interest, has arisen, and ever will arise, the greatest Aggregate of National Benefit:

That, under the Protection of the Law, vesting in some of the Petitioners and others the Right of certain Patents, the Public has become possessed of a very valuable Improvement in the combing of Wool by Machinery as preparatory to the Spinning of Worsted Yarn, one great Staple of the National Trade: That great Benefit has already resulted from this improved Mode of Combing, but in no Proportion to what is expected to result, whereby a great Saving in the Production of Yam will be obtained, and the Manufactures of the Kingdom be carried to Market with

g eater Advantage both to the Manufacturer and onsumer: That, on a moderate Estimation, the Price of combing of the lower Wools is reduced by this Improvement from Two Pence Half-penny, or Three Pence, to One Penny per Pound, and that, when the finer Wools shall be subjected to the same Operation, the Reduction of Price will most probably be from Six Pence, or more, to One Penny, or Three Half-pence per Pound: That, in Time of Peace, this Difference will be much more considerable,

6 Z as

54 6

2° Mail.

A. 1794.

as the Price of Hand-combing is then greatly enhanced, while the Expence of Machine-combing will remain altogether, or nearly, the same, and that, if the Petitioners and others should be compelled to abandon the Combing of Wool by Machinery, they will severally be subjected to the ruinous Obligation of producing their Yams at an Expence of from £. 1,500 to £. 2,000 per Annum, more than the Production of the same Yam will cost them by Machinery: That if, in the Progress of Time, the Machine-combing, being unrestricted by Law, should supersede the Use of Hand-combing, the saving to the National Produce would, on a moderate Calculation, greatly exceed One Million per Annum; and that, u the Machine-combing be suppressed, the National Manufactures must in Consequence be charged with this additional Load: That the Machine-combing is superior in Quality, it being one continued even Flux of the Material, indefinite in its Length, while the Wool combed by Hand is in short Lengths, with irregular Ends, subject both to Loss and Imperfection in the uniting them; and that the Woollen Manufactures of the Kingdom appear to have been for some Years past considerably on the Increase, and may receive a severe and fatal Check, to the great Injury of the Kingdom, if they cannot be produced on the best and cheapest Terms: That the good Policy of the Law, in leaving Manufactures to their Natural Course, was strikingly evinced in the Business of Cotton, in the Spinning of which the Application of Machinery threatened to deprive of their Maintenance a much more considerable Body of Artizans, while in the Progress the Artizans found Employment, and the Cotton Manufactures of the Kingdom were carried to a Height both of Excellence and Extent, and the National Wealth was multiplied, beyond all Example: That the Woollen Manufactures may, in all Probability, from the same Causes, reach the same Height of Prosperity and Excellence, if unchecked by prohibitory Laws; and it appears to be an unequal Line of Justice, that an Advantage should be granted j;o the Carding of Cotton, and denied to the Combing of Wool; that the latter being, for Ages, the Favourite Produce of the Kingdom, might have expected a special Indulgence; that the Cotton Manufactures have derived their high Reputation and Extent from the very Circumstance which the Petition of the* Woolcombers meditates to withdraw from Wool; and that the Woollen Manufactures may derive the same Improvement from the same Cause to which Cotton has been so much indebted; and that every Landholder in the Kingdom may find his own, and the most solid Interests of his Country, to be materially injured by ,the Denial of Machinery to the Combing of Wool: That the Growth of Wool fit for combing is not limited in the Degree which may be imagined, but will be increased or diminished in Proportion to the Demand for it; and that the Improvement of the Woollen Manufactures must increase the Growth of combing Wool, to the great Advantage of the Land Owner and Farmer, and consequently to the Poor by the Breeding of Sheep, and the Quantity of Mutton brought to Market: That the Petitioners apprehend, that no more Inconvenience will result to the Woolcombers from the Introduction of Machinery, than in the Instance of spinning Cotton by Machinery; that the Use of Machine-combing will be

fradual and progressive; and that the Decrease of land-combers will probably be in Proportion to the Increase of Machines for combing Wool: That, lastly, to the great Injury both to Individuals and the Kingdom, which will ensue from proscribing the free Use of Machinery in the combing of Wool, is to be added the singular Character of the Woolcombers, and the long Experience of the greatest Evils to the 7

Manufactures arising from this veiy Character: That the Woolcombers are a self-constituted Corporation, bound by Laws of their own making in Breach and Defiance of those of the Legislature, and, in consequence of this Combination, they counteract all the Interests and Pursuits of their Employers: That, if a Body of Woolcombers disagree with their Employers, no other Set of Woolcombers dare to succeed them, until the Difference is done away: That they take Advantage of the State of their Employer's Trade to raise their Wages ad libitum, and frequently leave their Employers in the most unwarrantable Manner, and, by their Combination* put a Stop to their whole Operations, by which illegal Conduct from Three to Four hundred poor working People are totally at a Stand, and the Employer has no Resource but in Compliance with their wanton and exorbitant Demands: That, as a Body, their Vices and Intemperance are a Source of infinite Loss and Trouble, and that a Dependance on the Woolcombers alone will

be an Abandonment of the most valuable Manufactures to a Set of Men whom neither Law nor Morals have yet been able to restrain; and that, if the Bill now depending in the House be such as to threaten the Injury which the Petitioners have stated, it is their respectful Petition to the House, that they may be permitted to be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, in Support of the Allegations which they have stated, and of the Interests of themselves and their Country, which are seriously at Stake.

Coctomouth A Petition of the Woolcombers and Manufacturers Woolcombero of the Borough of Cockermouth, was presented to the Petition. House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been alarmed by the Introduction of a newly invented Machine for the combing of Wool, which if not prohibited by the House, they fear, will deprive them of the Means of Subsistence for themselves and Families, many of the Petitioners being advanced in Years, and not able to betake themselves to any other Employment, and the Woollen Manufactory appearing to them to be limited, from the Growth of the Raw Material being confined to these Kingdoms, and no Foreign Nation capable of forming a Competition with this Country in that Branch of Commerce, even in the present State of the Manufactory, they can see no Advantage from the Introduction of such an Invention, but the greatest Evil to the present Wool-combers, by its being brought into immediate Use: And therefore praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and to adopt a Plan to prevent the present Introduction of the said Invention into the Trade.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Jenkinson reported from the Committee, to Dover H*r-whom the Petition of the Warden and Assistants of hou^ the Harbour of Dover, in the County of Kent, was repo referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

James Mom, Harbour Master, being examined said,

That the Number of Ships and Vessels resorting to the said Harbour is of late Years greatly increased, and that the Warden and Assistants have not sufficient Powers for regulating the said Harbour, and the Ships and Vessels coming into the same; and that it is of great Consequence to the Public, that sufficient Powers should be given to the said Warden and Assistants for regulating the said Harbour, and the Mooring of all Ships and vessels upon their entering into the said Harbour.

And the Witness further said. That great Number* of Ships and Vessels come into the said Harbour with large Quantities of Gunpowder on board, and fie in common amongst the other Ships and Vessels where Fires are constantly kept; and that it is absolutely necessary, for the Security of Ships and Vessels in the Harbour, and the Basons belonging thereto, and to all Persons residing in the Town of Dover, that some special Provision should be made respecting Ships and Vessels having on board a certain Quantity of Gunpowder.

Mr. Michael Elwin, Register of the Harbour, confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for better regulating the Harbour of Dover, in the County of Kent: And that Mr. Jenkinson, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Pybus do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Montagu and Mr. Leeds:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enable Subjects of France to enlist as Soldiers in Regiments to serve on the Continent of Europe, and in certain other Places, and to enable His Majesty to grant Commissions to Subjects of France to serve and receive Pay as Officers in such Regiments, or as Engineers, under certain Restrictions; without any Amendment.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That, when any Application is intended to be made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making any Cut or Canal for the Purposes of Navigation, or any Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, for the Purpose of supplying any City, Town, or Place, with Water, or for varying or altering any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, already made, or for making or improving the Navigation of 'any River, or for altering any Act of Parliament, passed for any or either of those Purposes (in which Bill for altering any such Act it is intended to give Power for raising any further or additional Rates, Tolls, or Duties, or for varying the Line of such Canal) Notice of such intended Application shall be inserted Three Times in The London Gazette, in the Months of August and September, or either of them, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made: And that such Notice shall also be inserted in some One Newspaper of every County, through which any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, is intended to be carried, or in which such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, already made, is intended to be varied or altered, or in which such River, or such Part thereof, as is intended to be made navigable, or the Navigation thereof to be improved, is situated (or, if there is not any Newspaper printed in or for such Counties, respectively, then in the Newspaper of some County near or adjoining the reto) Three Times at the least, in the Months of August and September, or either of them, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made: And that such Notice shall also be given at the General Quarter Session of the Peace which shall be holden for every and each County, Riding, or Division, through which any such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, is intended to be carried, or in which such Cut, Canal, or Aqueduct, already made, is intended to be varied or altered, or in which such River, or such Part thereof as is intended to be made navigable, or the Navigation thereof to be improved, is situated, at the Michaelmas preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Application is intended to be made, by affixing such Notice to the Door of the Session Houses, respectively, where such General Quarter Session shall be holden.

whom the Bill for dividing, allotting, and lay- Brockworth, ing in Severalty, the Open and Common Fields,

Common Meadows, Common Pastures, and otherU repo Commonable and Waste Lands and Grounds, in the several Parishes of Elmore and Brochvorth, and also for dividing, inclosing, and allotting, a certain Open and Common Field, called Calmsden Field, and other Commonable and Waste Lands, within the Manor of -den, in the Parish of North Cemey, in the County of Gloucester, was committed; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee (except the Proprietors of 50 Acres, or thereabouts, who refused to sign the Bill; and also, except the Proprietor of One Acre, who could not be met.with; and that the whole Property to be inclosed consists of 1,751 Acres, or thereabouts; and that no Person appeared before the Committee to oppose the Bill); and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table:

Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Ttoyal Assent A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Usher of the t° Bills. Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering His Royal Highness the Prince of JValts, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of „

His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord Kenyon> and the Lord Privy Seal, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money out of the Consolidated Fund; for applying a certain Sum of Money therein mentioned for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-four; and for further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament:

An Act for granting to his Majesty certain Duties of Customs on Slate, Stone, and Marble:

An Act to empower the East India Company to continue a Bond Debt of Two Millions, and to increase the same by a further Sum, as Circumstances may require:

An Act to enable Subjects of France to enlist as Soldiers in Regiments to serve on the Continent of Europe, and in certain other Places, and to enable His Majesty to grant Commissions to Subjects of France to serve and receive Pay as Officers in such Regiments, or as Engineers, under certain Restrictions:

An Act for granting to Foreign Ships, put under His Majesty's Protection, the Privileges of Prize Ships, under certain Regulations and Restrictions; for allowing Aliens in Foreign Colonies, surrendered to His Majesty, to exercise die Occupations of Merchants or Factors; and for repealing an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting a Liberty to carry " Sugars, of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture,

A Petition of George Smith, formerly of Canton, in China, Merchant, now residing in Stoke, next Guildford, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, anterior to the Year 1771, and for near as long a Period as the Europeans have traded to China, there had been established, under the Authority of the Emperor of China, a Co-Hong, or Company of Merchants, consisting of Ten Hongs, or Houses, to transact Business with Europeans, and the Europeans were prohibited from trading with any other Chinese than with the Co-Hong, unless recommended by them; a most extensive Trade was carried on, and unbounded Confidence subsisted betwixt the Europeans and the Co-Hong, in so much, that all Prices of the Imports and Exports rested solely with the Co-Hong: That, in the Month of October, when the Monsoon begins to set in unfavourable for the Arrival at the Port of Canton of any more Ships for the Season, the Co-Hong fixed the Prices at which the Mercats enabled them to give Europeans for the Imports, and also the Prices at which they could furnish the Articles of their Export Cargoes, nor was it ever known that the Co-Hong abused this extraordinary Power of fixing the Profits upon their own Mercantile Transactions; and that, in the Beginning of the Year 1771, the said Co-Hong was dissolved, and the Officers of the Government of China, upon pub-Vot. 49.

lishing its Dissolution, at the same Time declared, that, although the Co-Hong was dissolved, yet that no European was to have any Transaction with a Chinese other than with one of the Ten Hongs, or Houses, which formerly composed the Co-Hong, unless recommended to them by one of the Ten Hongs, or Houses, or by one of the Three Head Linguists, and, in Case of a contrary Conduct in any European, it was declared that the Chinese Government would not be responsible for any Losses the Europeans might sustain by trusting Chinese unknown'to it: That the Ten Hongs, or Houses, thus disunited, became jealous of each other's Success, and, in the Favour which some of them enjoyed over the others, in the Countenance given them by the Officers of Government at Canton, they began to supplant each other, and to effect one another's Ruin; the Property of British Subjects was lavished in Presents to the Officers of the Chinese Government, and they, in Return, screened the Hongs, or Houses, from the Complaints of Europeans, but, these being frequently repeated, at last the Hong Merchants obtained an Order from the Officers of Government at Canton, declaring that they would not, in future, receive any Memorial or Petition from any European, unless it was presented by a Hong Merchant — Thus foiled in every Attempt to obtain Justice, the Petitioner, with the Concurrence of the other British Subjects resident at Canton, drew up a Representation and State of the large Amount of British Property in China, for themselves, and in Behalf of their Constituents, and transmitted one Copy to a Committee of Creditors in London, and also another Copy to the Creditors who were resident at Madras-, the Consequence of these Applications was, that the Committee of Creditors in London were successful in their Applications to the Court of Directors of the East India Company, who took up, and considered the Amount of their Debts as a National Object; the Creditors at Madras were likewise successful in their Applications to the Commander in Chief of His Majesty's Fleet in India, who sent the late Captain Panton, in His Majesty's Ship The Sea Horse, to Canton, for Two Years successively, demanding, in His Majesty's Name, Justice to be done to British Creditors in the full Payment of their just Demands from the Chinese: That the Result of the Application, in the Name of His Majesty, procured a curious Kind of Justice, viz. The Settlement of Two of the Hong Merchants Debts, by making up their Bonds, with Interest, to the End of the Season 1779-80, lopping off One Half of the Debt, and a Promise by the Officers of the Government at Canton to pay the remaining Half, about £. 200,000, by Annual Instalments, in Ten Years, without Interest; and as to the Debt of One of the other Hongs, amounting to near £. 400,000, they gave the Creditors a Promise, when the lopped Debts of the Two Hongs or Houses were once settled, they would then settle this also; with regard to all the other Hongs Debts, One was said to be settled by their Predecessors in the Government at Canton, and as to the remaining Hongs Debts, the Creditors, it was said, had agreed upon Terms, but even these had not been complied with. That His Majesty's Service in India, at this Period, did not permit the Commander in Chief of His Majesty's Fleet to pursue further Measures for the Relief of the unfortunate British Subjects in China, whose Debts the Petitioner can say, with the greatest Confidence, arose from, and are entirely founded on, honourable Mercantile Transactions, and can bear the strictest Investigation: That in this Situation of the Petitioner's Affairs he left China with his. Family in January 1782, and returned to this Country for Two Reasons, First, to meet his Creditors as an honest Man, to do them every Justice in his Power, and, Secondly, to endeavour to obtain the further Aid of the Government of this Country to procure from

7 K the

586

12? M

A. 1794.

the Chinese Govemnment full Payment of the just Debts due by its Hongs to their British Creditors; that the Petitioner arrived in this Country in October 1782, and took the first Opportunity to meet his Creditors, which he did in the Beginning of November following, when he exhibited to them a Statement and Balance of his Affairs, amounting at the Period in which he left China, to £ 201,739. os. 8 owing to him by the Chinese Hong Merchants, in Consequence of honourable Mercantile Transactions with them {only deducting therefrom £4,111. 15 owing to him by British Subjects) out of which he owed to several Persons £ 128,514. 12$. 8 the Balance remaining, his Property, £ 73,224. 8$. the honest Fruits of many Years Industry: That an Assignment was proposed of his Property to his Creditors, and accepted, the Instrument was drawn out, and approved by all his Creditors in Britain, One only excepted, who objected to the Clause of Release by which the Petitioner was to be released from his Debt, although it was only to be binding on his Creditors, provided the Petitioner rendered a fair and honourable Account and Delivery of all his Property, and, upon the Petitioner rejecting this unreasonable Request, his only inimical Creditor issued a Commission of Bankruptcy against him on the 18th of December 1782; and that, upon the 25th of March 1783, the Petitioner exhibited on Oath, before the Commissioners of Bankruptcy, an exact Copy of the aforesaid Statement and Balance of his Affairs, and the Petitioner's Creditors have been since in the regular Receipt of the Annual Dividends paid by the Chinese Government, upon a Part of the Petitioner's large Property, of about £ 2,600, paid by the Officers of the Government of China at Canton, in Part of the lopped Debt, the Annual Instalments of which are now expired: That, so soon as it reached India that a Commission of Bankruptcy had been issued against the Petitioner, his Creditors in that Part of the World gave their Consent, under their Hands and Seals, to his Certificate (except One Creditor only, for a Debt of One Thousand Rupees, most probably from Inadvertency, or from being at the Time in a distant Part of,) and which Consent of his Creditors Abroad he has in his Possession, and all his other Creditors are in England, and they too, One only excepted, have been friendly towards him, and some in a very eminent Degree: That the Petitioner, ever since his Return to this Country, now near Twelve Years ago, has used his utmost Exertions and Abilities for the Benefit of his Creditors, and he hopes his Exertions will prove beneficial to them; and the Petitioner, having done his utmost for the Benefit of his Creditors, can with greater Confidence apply to the House for Relief to enable him to make Use of his Industry to provide for a large Family of Children, for, in the Petitioner's present Situation, he can neither benefit his Creditors or them. That the Petitioner does not claim nor appeal to the Humanity or Compassion of the House, but he relies, and has a firm Confidence in its Justice, upon these Grounds: That his Misfortunes are not owing to his Imprudence, Misconduct, or Extravagance, but to this sole Cause, viz. the Injustice of the Officers of the Government of Canton in China, in Conjunction with the Hong Merchants, his Debtors, in having withheld from him his large Property; and therefore hopes, in Consideration of the peculiar Circumstances attending his Case, that, while the House is engaged in extending its Humanity and Compassion to Thousands in the Insolvent Bill now pending, that the House will extend its Justice by the Admission of a Clause for the Relief of the Petitioner to empowes the Lord Chancellor to sign his Certificate, or in such other Manner as to the House shall seem meet, and that the Petitioner may be heard, by himself, or examined upon Oath, at the Bar of t he House, or be allowed to adduce other Evi-

dence in Support of his very peculiar Case, and of the Allegations in this Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Law, Mr. Francis, c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Secretary Dundas acquainted the House, That King's M«-he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, sage respect-signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to "8 Seditions the House; and it was redd by Mr. Speaker (all the Frac ce*' Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, having received Information, that the Seditious Practices, which have been for some time carried on by certain Societies in London, in Correspondence with Societies in different Parts of the Country, have lately been pursued with increased Activity and Boldness, and have been avowedly directed to the Object of assembling a pretended General Convention of the People, in Contempt and Defiance of the Authority of Parliament, and on Principles subversive of the existing Laws and Constitution, and directly tending to the Introduction of that System of Anarchy and Confusion which has fatally prevailed in France, has given Directions for seizing the Books and Papers of the said Societies in London, which have been seized accordingly; and these Books and Papers appearing to contain Matter of the greatest Importance to the Public Interest, His Majesty has given Orders for laying them before the House of Commons; and His Majesty recommends it to the House to consider the same, and to take such Measures thereupon as may appear to be necessary for effectually guarding against die further Prosecution of these dangerous Designs, and for preserving to His Majesty's Subjects the Enjoyment of the Blessings derived to them by the Constitution happily established in these Kingdoms.

G. R.

Ordered, That His Majesty's said most Gracious Message be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

A Petition of Benjamin Pope, a Prisoner in His Mr. Pope's Majesty's Prison of the Fleet, was presented to the Petition. House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner having instituted a Prosecution against the late Sir Alexander Leith, deceased, for Felony, and which Prosecution was under the Advice of Counsel, upon his Acquittal, an Action of Damages was brought against the Petitioner, and a Verdict obtained for £. 10,000, and Costs, which Damages and Costs the Petitioner being utterly unable to pay, hath been confined in Prison for the said Damages and Costs from the 1st Day of May 1783, being now upwards of Eleven Years; and that the Petitioner's Distress doth not arise from any Misconduct in himself, but from the Misfortune he met with, by being advised to such Prosecution, and the Damages far exceed what the Petitioner's whole Estate and Property amounts unto, and although he was always ready, and willing to make every Satisfaction in his Power, all Proposals of a Compromise have been rejected; and that the Petitioner is Sixty-six Years of Age, and, if not included in the Act now before the House, for the Relief of Insolvent Debtors, so that he may be at Liberty to take the Benefit thereof, he must for the Whole of his Life be confined in Prison: And therefore praying, That a Clause may be inserted in the said Bill (now depending for Relief of Insolvent Debtors) that the Petitioner may have the Benefit of the said Act upon such Terms as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration Lord's the Amendment made by the Lords to the Bill, in- Amend-tituled, An Act for building a new Bridge over the Bridgwater River Parrett, within the Borough of Bridgwater, in Bridge, &c. the County of Somerset, and for repairing, maintaining, Bill agreed to and extending the Quays in the Port of Bridgwater aforesaid, for abolishing the ancient and accustomed Duties, and for imposing certain new Duties at the Port of Bridgwater aforesaid, instead thereof; for regulating the Moorings and Stations of Ships and Vessels in the said Port; and for imposing a certain Toll on Horses, Carriages, and Cattle.

And the said Amendment was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Pr. 30. 1. 40. Leave out from " to

" Provided" in Pr. 31. 1. 13.

And the Clause proposed to be left out by the said Amendment was read; and is as followeth; viz.

" And be it further Enacted, That it shall be lawful for the Owner or Owners of any Ship or Vessel " who shall pay any of the Dues, Duties, and Customs " aforesaid, for any Goods, Wares, or Merchandizes by " them brought to the said Port, to charge such " Dues, Duties, and Customs so paid, in Addition " to their Charge for Freight or Trow Bills, and that " the same shall be recoverable by Action at Law in " any of His Majesty's Courts of Record at " ster."

And the House being informed, that the said Clause was left standing in the Bill as it passed this House by Mistake; for, that by the said Bill, as originally brought into this House, it was intended to apply certain Tolls and Duties on Goods, Wares, and Merchandize therein mentioned, and to impose certain other Tolls and Duties on Goods, Wares, and Merchandize therein also mentioned, brought into the said Port of Bridgwater, for the Purpose of raising a Fund for the building and maintaining the Bridge mentioned in the Bill, to which Tolls and Duties the said Clause was applicable; yet that in the Course of the Bill through this House, and in consequence of certain Petitions presented to this House relating thereto, the original Plan of the said Bill, in respect to such Tolls and Duties, was entirely altered, and the Committee, to whom the Bill was committed, left out those Parts of it by which all the Tolls and Duties on such Goods, Wares, and Merchandize Avere intended to be applied or imposed, and laid a Toll or Duty only on Ships, Trows, and other Vessels, coming into

the

King's Bench A Petition of the Bankrupt Prisoners confined in ®aflkPt the King's Bench Prison, who cannot take the Benefit Petition" *ntended Act of Insolvency, on account of the

Sums for which they are confined amounting to considerably more than what the Act extends to, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been Merchants and Traders, some of them to a large Amount, and Commissions of Bankrupt have issued against them, under which they have long since given up their Effects for the Benefit of their Creditors, notwithstanding which, some of the Petitioners have been confined from Four to Thirteen Years, and that should the impending Bill pass into a Law, without a Clause being added to include Bankrupts, they have nothing to look to, but perpetual Imprisonment, with all the natural Distress attending such Imprisonment, to them, their Wives and Children: And therefore praying, That a Clause may be added to the present intended Act of Insolvency, which may include Bankrupt Prisoners, under whatever Restrictions or Regulations the House may think proper, for the Satisfaction of their Creditors.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

contrary Conduct in any European, it was declared that the Chinese Government would not be responsible for any Losses the Europeans might sustain by trusting Chinese unknown to it:

That the Ten Hongs, or Houses, thus disunited, became jealous of each other's Success, and in the Favour which some of them enjoyed over the others, in the Countenance given them by the Officers of Government at Canton, they began to supplant each other, and to effect one another's Ruin — the Property of British Subjects was lavished in Presents to the Officers of the Chinese Government, and they, in Return, screened the Hongs, or Houses, from the Complaints of Europeans; but these being frequently repeated, the Hong Merchants obtained an Order from the Officers of Canton Government, declaring that they would not, in future, receive any Memorial or Petition from any European, unless it was presented by a Hong Merchant — That thus foiled in every Attempt to obtain Justice, Mr. Smith (the Petitioner) with the Concurrence of the other British Subjects resident at Canton, drew up a Representation and State of the large Amount of British Property in China, for themselves, and in behalf of their Constituents, and transmitted one Copy to a Committee of Creditors in London, also another Copy to the Creditors who were resident at Madras — that the Consequence of these Applications were, that the Committee of Creditors in London were successful in their Applications to the Court of Directors of the East India Company, who considered the Amount of their Debts as a National Object — the Creditors at Madras were likewise successful in their Applications to the Commander in Chief of His Majesty's Fleet in India, who sent the late Captain Panton, in His Majesty's Ship The Sea Horse, to Canton, for Two Years successively, demanding, in His Majesty's Name, Justice to be done to British Creditors, in the mil Payment of their just Demands from the Chinese — that the Result of this Application, in His Majesty's Name, procured a curious kind of Justice, namely, the Settlement of Two of the Hong Merchants Debts, by making up their Bonds, with Interest, to the End of the Season 1779-80, lopping off One Half of the Debt, and a Promise, by the Officers of the Government at Canton, to pay the remaining Half, amounting to about £. 200,000, by Annual Instalments, in Ten Years, without Interest; and that, as to the Debt of one of the other Hongs, amounting to near £. 400,000, they gave the Creditors a Promise, when the lopped Debts of the Two Hongs, or Houses, were once settled, they would likewise settle their Debt — One was said to be settled by their Predecessors in the Government at Canton; and that as to the remaining Hongs Debts, the Creditors, it was said, had agreed upon Terms; but that these have not even been complied with. — And the Witness added, That no further Steps were taken by Government, for the Relief of the British Subjects.

Charles Edward Pigou, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the whole of the above Evidence. — Then,

Several Members present informed the Committee, That on the Petitioner's Arrival in England, in November 1782, he delivered to his Creditors a Statement and Balance of his Affairs, in the Manner stated in the Petition; and that, after several intermediate Circumstances, a Commission of Bankruptcy was issued against him in December 1782.

Joseph Ward, Esquire, (Solicitor to the said Commission of Bankruptcy) being examined, said, That upon the 25th of March 1783, Mr. Smith exhibited on Oath, before the Commissioners of Bankruptcy, an exact Copy of the aforesaid Statement and Balance of his Affairs; and that his Creditors have been since in the regular Receipt of the Annual Dividends paid by the Chinese Government upon a Part of his large Property, of about £. 2,600, paid by the Officers of the

Government of China at Canton, in Part of the lopped Debt, the Annual Instalments of which are now expired. — And the Witness added, That it appeared to him (from the Papers under the Commission of Bankruptcy, and from Two Powers of Attorney, and Affidavits authenticating the same respectively, under the Seal of the Mayor's Court at Bombay, authorizing certain Persons, therein named, to sign Mr. Smith's Certificate under the Commission) that of the Creditors who had proved their Debts, at Home and Abroad, under the Commission of Bankruptcy, all except Thirteen had consented to the granting him his Certificate. —

And,

Several Members present proved the Consent of Eight of the above-mentioned Thirteen Creditors to the granting the same.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Majority of the Prisoners confined for Debt in His Majesty's Gaol of Newgate, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Bill for the Discharge of certain Insolvent Debtors, now under the Consideration of the House, having for its Object the Discharge of Prisoners for Debt, by reason of the present Condition of the Gaols in this Kingdom, the Petitioners, adverting as well to the Principle of the Bill as to their wretched Situation, hold themselves bound in Duty most respectfully to state to the House how far the Bill, as it now stands, and in respect to the said Prison in particular, will operate towards effecting the benevolent Intention of the Legislature: That all the Petitioners have become Prisoners in the said Gaol since the ist Day of January last, and the Number of Debtors now confined therein amounts to Two hundred and Thirteen, of which Number only Seventy-eight will be entitled to the Benefit of an Insolvent Act comprizing those only who shall have been in Prison on the ist Day of January last, leaving a Majority of One Hundred and Thirty-five Prisoners who will be excluded from such Relief, and the Prison remain nearly as full as it has usually been, on an Average for several Years past; and that the principal Part of the Petitioners are Tradesmen, Manufacturers, Seamen, Soldiers, and Labourers, disabled by Confinement from following their respective Occupations, and consequently not only deprived of all possible Means of discharging their Debts, but are, with their Families, plunged into the Extremes of Distress and Penury; and that far the greater Part of the Petitioners had the Misfortune to be taken from their Families, and confined in Prison, before they could possibly know, and before any Intimation was given, of an Intention to relieve Prisoners for Debt by an Insolvent Act, and those of the Petitioners, who have been confined since such Intention became known, are Men in wretched and deplorable Circumstances, compelled by the Necessity of their Affairs to become Prisoners in the said Gaol, and not becoming so with any Intent to deceive or defraud their Creditors, to whom they are ready to give up all they possess, and honestly and rigidly to comply with every Thing which shall be required by the Law in that behalf: That the Bill, as it now stands, will relieve not more than One-third of the Prisoners confined for Debt in the said Gaol, and the Majority, from the present Operation of the Law, have no Prospect but that of miserably ending their Days in Confinement, unless the House, commiserating their wretched Situation, shall condescend to notice the Representation which the Petitioners now presume to offer: And therefore praying, That the House will take into Consideration their peculiar and complicated Hardships, and, by an Extension of the limited Time to a Date, so far subsequent to the 1st Day of January last, as that the Bill shall embrace a Majority of the Prisoners confined for Debt according to the evident Intention of its Principle, or, by such other Measure as the House shall think proper, grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem expedient.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration cif the Committee of the whole House, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for the Discharge of certain Insolvent Debtors, is committed.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Clothworkers and Wool Scribblers, in the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by the Statute of the Fifth and Sixth of Edward the Sixth, Cap. 22. after reciting, " That in many Parts of the " Realm there was then newly and lately devised, " erected, builded, and used, certain Mills, called " Gig Mills, for pearching and burling (now called " Rowing) of Cloth, by reason thereof the true DraDrapery of the Realm was impaired, and the Cloth " thereof deceitfully made; for Remedy thereof it " was enacted, that no Manner of Person should then " after use or occupy any of the said Gig Mills, for " the working of any Woollen Cloth or Clothes made " or to be made within the Realm, upon Pain of Forfeiture for every Cloth so wrought in or by any of " the said Mills called Gig Mills, the Sum of Five " Pounds, one Moiety to the King, and the other " Moiety to him who shall sue for the same in any " of the King's Courts ;" and that, notwithstanding the above Statute, it was afterwards considered be--neficial and expedient, as well to the Clothiers as to Government, to make use of the said Gig Mills in working up Army Cloth and other Cloths of a coarse Nature, as such Cloths are by no means injured or Vol. 49.

impaired thereby, on account of its Coarseness and Strength to withstand the Violence of the Engine, and it was rendered much cheaper to the Contractor, on account of its not being so expensive to the Manufacturer in working it up by the Gig Mill as it is by hand: That very recently several Clothiers of the County of Gloucester have begun, and still do continue, to have their fine Cloth worked up by the above-mentioned Gig Mills; in consequence whereof the true Drapery of such Cloth is considerably affected, deceitfully made, and rendered much less valuable to the Wearers thereof, as the said Gig Mills are driven so violently by the Impetuosity of the Water, that it injures the Texture or Ground of such fine Cloth, winch will not admit of such Violence by reason of its Fineness, and if this Mode of dressing fine Cloth be continued by the Clothiers, the Petitioners are apprehensive Consequences of evil Tendency will ensue, as it must end in the Ruin of many Hundreds of Families who are dependant on the Clothworking Business, and the Land Owners within the said County, or certain Parts thereof, will ultimately be the Sufferers, for, by the Gig Mills doing that Part of the Business which was heretofore done by the Workmen, and which is contrary to the before recited Statute, a great Number of Men must consequently be out of Employ, and, in the end, become burthensome to the respective Parishes to which they belong: That this Country, which has ever been considered so famous, and has stood unrivalled in the making of Broad Cloth, must infallibly lose its Ttrade, by other Nations manufacturing their Goods in a superior Manner, with respect to the real Goodness and Duration of such Cloth, and it is not the Wish of the Petitioners that the Use of Gig Mills should be entirely suppressed, but only to confine them to the working of such Cloth as cannot be hindered thereby, and whereby they will be deprived of Employment, namely, that of the coarser Sort, and which, if so restricted, would then leave sufficient Employment for the Petitioners: That it has been suggested, by some of the Petitioners, that it would be prudent, in order to redress this Grievance, to commence Actions at Law upon the Statute of the Fifth and Sixth of Edward the Sixth, which so effectually prohibits the Use of the said Gig Mills, against such Person offending, and who makes use of the same in the working up of the fine Cloth, in order to recover the Penalty, and which, if done, the Petitioners conjectured would, without Doubt, entirely stop the Progress and Use of the said Mills, in manner aforesaid, as sufficient Proof can be adduced to substantiate the Particulars, and the Fact that the* Cloth which is worked up and wrought by the said Gig Mills, that is, the Supers and best Superfine Cloth, are much inferior in real Value and Worth to that which is done by the hand, and that the Texture or Ground of such Cloth is very immaterially injured thereby, but the Petitioners have been advised, if they were to sue for the Penalties, common Informers would proceed to destroy the Use of Gig Mills in making coarse Cloth entirely as well as that of the Fine, by proceeding against every Person who should use such Gig Mills, for the Penalties incurred by virtue of the said Act, and therefore the Petitioners have suspended and waived the bringing of such Action or Actions: That it has been for Time immemorial, the Custom for the Cloth Manufacturers for the County of Gloucester to have their Wool scribbled and worked up previous to its being put into the hands of the Spinners and Carders hereafter mentioned, by Men called Wool Scribblers, which Business is one of the considerable Branches of the Cloathing Trade, and as such has usually employed a large body of the lower Class of People in the said County, and so essentially convenient and advantageous was the said Branch of

Business

600 ' 16° Mail A. 1794

Business to the Community at large, and the neigh bouring Parishes in particular, that many Individuals who, being advanced in Age, or by Accident or Misfortune disabled from working in other Occupations which require bodily Exertions, could be furnished with the Means of the Necessaries of Life, without applying for Parochial Aid, by Scribbling Wool; and that it has also been universally the Custom, after the Wool has been so worked up by the Scribblers, to be immediately delivered over to be carded and spun, and worked up into Yarn, and this Part of the Business has ever been done by Women and Children, and always employed a numerous Body, whose Earnings are entirely dependent thereon, the Cloathing Manufacture being the only Staple Trade in that Part of the Country: That, within the Space of Two Years ot less, certain Machines or Engines have been introduced into the said County, which are so constructed as to scribble and card Wool, which heretofore was done in the manner before stated; that the Scribbling Engines generally go by Water, attended only by one Man and a Boy, and will do as much Work in Twelve Hours as Twenty Men can do in a like Space of Time, and the Carding Machines will complete as much Work in one Day as Eighty Women can industriously perform in a like Space of Time; and that in consequence of the said new Inventions being so made use of, a very great Number of Persons and their Families are now out of Employ, and nearly deprived of the Means of their future Subsistence, and the Petitioners apprehend, that, if some Means be not speedily adopted to employ the Number of People now destitute of Work, they must become burthensome to the respective Parishes to which they belong: That the Cloth which is made from the Wool scribbled by those Engines, has been found; by Experience, not to be equal in Quality and Goodness to that where the Materials with which it was made were worked up and scribbled by hand, by reason that the Machines, in consequence of the violent Manner in which they are driven by the Impetuosity and Force of the Water, tear the Wool from its true Staple; and notwithstanding the saving of Expence which must naturally accrue to the Clothiers, in consequence of their having the Cloth made by those Machines, they do not in the least reduce the Price of the Cloth, but, on the contrary, they have increased it so, that they alone are the Gainers, and the Public at large by no means benefited; and, that, on account of the great Expence of the Scribbling Machines, some of the inferior Clothiers are not enabled to purchase one for themselves, and therefore send their Wool to another Clothier to have it scribbled by his Machine, who is paid a reasonable Hire for working it up, whereby the more considerable Clothiers alone engross the Benefit thereof, the Expence of the inferior Clothiers for such Hire, making that method of getting their Work completed equally expensive with the original Plan, and the Petitioners are thereby also effectually deprived of the Work of such Persons, who are not able to provide themselves with a Machine; and that there are also other Branches of Business which are connected with, and dependant on, the scribbling and carding of Wool (to wit) the Card Makers, file Card Board Makers, and Wire Drawers, who are very immaterially affected by the before-mentioned Machines, inasmuch as a considerable Number of Persons, who were formerly employed in making Cards (the Instruments made use of in scribbling and carding Wool) are also now out of Employ in consequence of such Machines being so introduced as aforesaid: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to prevent and prohibit any Person or Persons from making use of a Gig Mill, in the working up . of any

fine Woollen Cloth or Cloths, and hitherto suppress the use of the said Scribbling apd Carding Machines, in the scribbling and carding of Wool, or otherwise to limit and confine them to such a certain Number as will not engross the whole of the Labour, but leave sufficient Employment for the Petitioners to support themselves and Families, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie 'upon the Table.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported from Fust Report the Committee of Secrecy, That the Committee had from Com-examined the Matters to them referred, and had di- "^tecof rected him to make a Report to the House; and he recy* read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at she Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee to whom the several Papers referred to in His Majesty's Message of the 12th of May 1.794, and which were presented (sealed up) to the House, by Mr. Secretary Dundas, upon the 12th and 13th Days of the said Month, by His Majesty's Command, were referred; and who were directed to examine the Matters thereof, and report the same, as they should appear to them, to the House; have

proceeded.

601

proceeded, in Obedience to the Orders of the House, to the Consideration of the Matters- referred to them.

They find, on the First Inspection, that the Books and Papers, which they are directed to examine, contain a full and authentic Account of certain Proceedings of Two Societies, calling themselves The Society for Constitutional Information, and The London Corresponding Society, who appear to be closely connected with other Societies in many Parts of Great Britain, and in Ireland; and the Committee also observe, from recent Circumstances, which have already come under their Observation, that these Proceedings appear to become every Day more and more likely to affect the internal Peace and Security of these Kingdoms, and to require, in the most urgent Manner, the immediate and vigilant Attention of Parliament.

The Committee have, therefore, thought it their indispensable Duty, in the First Instance, to submit to the House the general View which they have been enabled to form of these Transactions, reserving a more particular Statement for a subsequent Report.

In the Book containing the Proceedings of the Society for Constitutional Information, which was found in the Custody of the Person acting as Secretary to the Society, there are regular Entries, of what passed on each Day of Meeting, from the End of the Year 1791 to the 9th of May in the present Year.

From these it appears, that during almost the whole of that Period, and with hardly any considerable Interval, except during Part of the Summer in 1792 and 1793, this Society has, by a Series of Resolutions, Publications, and Correspondence, been uniformly and systematically pursuing a settled Design, which appears to your Committee to tend to the Subversion of the established Constitution, and which has, of late, been more openly avowed, and attempted to be carried into full Execution.

The Principles on which this Design is founded are strongly and unequivocally proved, from Resolutions formed as early as the 18th of May 1792, in which the Society applaud the Intention of publishing a cheap Edition of the First and Second Parts of The Rights of Man; and resolve, " That a Copy of Mr. " Paine's Letter [informing them of this Intention] rt together with these Resolutions, be transmitted to " all the Associated Societies in Town and Country; " and that this Society do., congratulate them on the " firm as well as orderly Spirit and tranquil Perseverance manifested in all their Proceedings, and exhort them to a steady Continuance thereinAnd also, " That 3,000 Copies of the Letter and Resolution should be printed for the Use of the Society." This single Circumstance would, in the Judgment of your Committee, leave little Doubt of the read Nature of the Designs entertained by this Society. Their Conduct in other Respects has corresponded with it.

On the 11th of May in the same Year they vote an Address; in Terms of Approbation and Applause, to the Society of Jacobins at Paris.

They adopt a similar Measure, under Circumstances still more striking, by sending, on the 9th of November following, an Address to the National Convention of France, full of Panegyric on the French Resolution, and expressing the strongest Wishes for its Progress and Success. This Address was actually presented at the Bar of the Convention by Two Persons, of the Name of Barlow and Frost; and the Answer of the President was read at the Meeting of the Society on the 7th of December 1792.

On the 14th of the same Month a Letter is received from Persons calling themselves the Friends «rf Liberty and Equality, at Lam, Capital of the Department de L'Aisne, and referred by their Society to their Committee of Correspondence.

Vol. 49-

On the 21st of the same Month, certain Members First Report are expressly appointed a Committee for Foreign Correspondence.

The Proceedings of this Committee are ordered to be entered in a separate Book; and a Letter received, that Day, from the Friends of Liberty and Equality at Macon, is referred to that Committee.

On the 25th of January and on the 1st of February 1793 (at the Eve of the Commencement of the War, and after the repeated Representations which had been made on the Part of the British Government, complaining of the Conduct of France) the Citizens Bar-rere and Roland (then leading Members of the French Convention) are admitted Associated Honorary Members of the Society; and the Speeches of Barrere and St. AndrS (also an Honorary Member of the Society) as given in The Moniteur of the 4th, 6th, and 7th of January, are directed to be inserted in the Books of the Society.

Subsequent to the Declaration of War, which interrupted this System of direct Correspondence and Concert with France, and down to the present Time, the Society have continued, on various Occasions, to manifest their Attachment to the Cause of the French Resolution; and have affected to follow, in their Proceedings and in their Language, the Forms and even the Phrases which are adopted in that County-

The next leading Circumstance which has engaged the Attention of your Committee, is the unremitting Activity and Diligence with which this Society have attempted to disseminate their Principles, both by Publications and Resolutions industriously and extensively circulated, and by endeavouring to establish a general Correspondence and Concert, among the other seditious Societies in the Metropolis, and in different Parts of England and Scotland, as well as in Ireland. With

many of these this Society appears itself to have carried on an immediate Correspondence, particularly with those at Sheffield, Norwich, and Manchester, who have, on all Occasions, taken the most forward and active Part in these Transactions. In their Correspondence with Norwich in particular, as early as the 12th of April 1793, there is a Passage which so clearly marks the real Object which (whatever may have been their Pretexts) they appear uniformly to have had in View, that your Committee think it right here to insert it.

" Extract of a Letter from the Secretary to " the Society for Constitutional Information, to the Secretary to the United Political Societies at Norwich; dated 16th " April 1793.

" Where then are we to look for the Remedy ?

To that Parliament of which we complain? To the Executive Power, which is implicitly obeyed if not anticipated in that Parliament? or, To Ourselves, represented in some Meeting of Delegates for the especial Purpose of Reform, which we suppose you understand by the Term CONVENTION.

" It is the End of each of these Propositions that we ought to look to; and as Success in a good Cause must be the Effect of Perseverance and the rising Reason of the Time, let us determine with Coolness, but let us persevere with Decision. — As to a Convention, we regard it as a Plan the most desirable and most practicable, so soon as the great Body of the People shall be courageous and virtuous enough to join us in the Attempt. Hitherto we have no Reason to believe that the Moment is ^arrived for that Purpose. — As to any Petition to the Crown, we believe it hopeless in its Consequences.
